en: The Dharmapada-avadāna Sūtra, Volume One.
Translated by the Śramaṇas Dharmakṣema and Dharmayaśas during the Jin Dynasty.
Chapter One: On Impermanence. The First Chapter: On Impermanence.

Formerly, when the five virtues had departed from Śakra, Lord of Devas, he knew for himself that his life was exhausted and that he would descend to be born in the world, taking the form of a donkey’s womb in the house of a potter.
What are these five virtues?

First, the light upon his body faded; second, the flowers upon his head withered; third, he took no pleasure in his original seat; fourth, sweat from his armpits became foul-smelling; fifth, dust and dirt adhered to his body.
By these five signs, he knew for himself that his merit was exhausted and fell into great sorrow and anxiety.
He thought to himself, "Within the three realms, the Buddha alone can deliver people from suffering and calamity. Thereupon, he hurried on his way until he arrived at the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the Buddha was in a stone cave on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, sitting in meditation and having entered the Samādhi of Universal Salvation.

When Śakra, Lord of Devas, saw the Buddha, he prostrated himself in homage, bowing his head to the ground, and with a sincere heart took refuge three times in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha. Before he had even risen, his life suddenly ended, and he was reborn as a son within the womb of a she-ass belonging to a potter.

At that time, the donkey untied itself and ran among the unbaked clay vessels, breaking them. Its owner struck it, and immediately the fetus was injured. The spirit then returned to its former body; its five virtues were restored, and it became the Heavenly Emperor once again.
The Buddha, awakened from samādhi, praised him, saying:
"Excellent, O Lord of Devas!
That you were able to take refuge in the Triple Gem at the moment of death, your karmic retribution is now complete, and you shall no longer undergo further suffering."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"All conditioned things are impermanent; They are subject to the law of arising and decaying. Whatever is born must die;
This cessation is bliss."
"Just as a potter fashions vessels from clay, all must eventually break; so too is the life of man.

Upon hearing this verse, Śakra understood the essence of impermanence, grasped the transformation between demerit and merit, comprehended the root of rise and fall, and followed the practice of nirvana. Receiving it with joy and reverence, he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Once, when the Buddha was staying in a monastery in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, he was preaching the Dharma for the sake of devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits.

At that time, the chief consort of King Prasenajit, who was over ninety years old, suddenly fell gravely ill; though she sought medical treatment and medicine in hopes of recovery, she eventually passed away.
The king and the ministers of the state performed the funeral rites according to the Dharma and interred the spirit in the tomb.
When the funeral ceremonies were completed, they returned and passed by the Buddha’s dwelling; there they removed their robes, went barefoot, and approached to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha bade him sit and asked him, saying:
"From where have you come, O King, that your clothing is coarse and your appearance so different? What have you been doing?
The king bowed his head and replied:

"The Great Lady of the State was over ninety years of age when she fell gravely ill and suddenly passed away. Her remains were escorted to the grave for burial, and we have only now returned to pay our respects to the Holy One."
The Buddha told the king:
"From antiquity until now, there have been four great fears:
birth leads to the withering of old age and the loss of luster through illness; death leads to the departure of the spirit and separation from one's kin. These are called the four."
One does not make an appointment with others; the myriad phenomena are impermanent and difficult to dwell upon for long, as each day passes away.
Human life is likewise: like the five rivers that flow day and night without ceasing, the swift passage of human life is just the same.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as a river flows swiftly, going on and never returning, so it is with human life:
that which passes away does not come back."
The Buddha told the Great King:
"In all worlds this is so; nothing endures forever. All must return to death, and none can escape it.

Kings of the past, the Buddhas, the True Persons, and the seers with the five supernatural powers have also all passed away; none were able to remain. It is in vain that you grieve and cause your physical form to perish."

"Now, as a filial son, one should feel compassion for the deceased and perform meritorious deeds and virtuous acts to dedicate their benefits to them; such blessings will follow after them like provisions sent to someone on a distant journey.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, the king and his ministers were all filled with joy; they forgot their sorrows and cast off their afflictions, and all who had gathered there attained the stage of the Path (srotāpanna).

Formerly, when the Buddha was at the Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, he entered the city with his disciples to accept an invitation. Having finished preaching the Dharma, they left the city in the late afternoon.
On the road, they encountered a man driving a large herd of cattle back toward the city; the animals were fat and well-fed, leaping about and repeatedly butting one another.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as a man holding a staff goes to pasture his cattle for their food, so too do old age and death sustain life and lead it away."
Thousands and hundreds, not just one—men and women of noble lineage who have amassed wealth and property—all shall suffer decay and loss.
For those born, day and night their lives are eroded away; the exhaustion of their lifespan is like the water of a leaking jar.
When the Buddha arrived at the Bamboo Grove, he washed his feet and sat down. Ānanda immediately stepped forward, prostrated himself, and asked:
"World-Honored One!
Earlier on the road, you recited these three verses; I do not yet understand their meaning."
"I pray that you will grant me transformation.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you see anyone driving a herd of cattle?"
“Yes, I have seen them. The Buddha told Ānanda:

“This herd of cattle from the butcher’s house originally numbered one thousand heads. Every day, the butcher sent men out of the city to seek fine water and grass to nourish them so they would grow fat; then he would select the fattest ones and lead them away daily to slaughter.”
Of those killed, more than half have died, while the remainder remain unaware; they are currently goring one another, leaping about, and roaring. Because they lack wisdom, I have spoken this verse.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
“Not only these oxen;
worldly people are likewise.”

In calculating for our own selves, we do not realize that all things are impermanent; we greedily crave the five desires to nourish our bodies, seeking to satisfy our minds and exhaust our intentions, yet we continue to harm one another. When the karmic retribution of impermanence suddenly arrives without appointment, we remain in a state of blinding ignorance, failing to perceive it—how is this any different from the aforementioned?

At that time, there were two hundred bhikṣus among those seated who were attached to gain and sustenance; upon hearing the Dharma, they exhorted themselves, attained the six supernormal powers, and became arhats.
The assembly, filled with both grief and joy, paid homage to the Buddha.
In the past, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, he was preaching the Dharma to his disciples.

At that time, there was a daughter of a brahmin, fourteen or fifteen years of age, who was handsome, intelligent, and eloquent; her father cherished her dearly. She suddenly fell gravely ill and passed away. It was as if a field of ripening wheat had been consumed by a wild fire. Upon learning this, the brahmin was overcome with grief and distress, so bewildered and disoriented that he was like a madman, unable to compose himself.
It was rumored that the Buddha was a Great Sage and Teacher of Gods and Men, who expounded the Way of the Sūtras to dispel sorrow and eliminate affliction.
Thereupon, a Brahmin went to where the Buddha was, paid his respects, knelt for a long time, and said to the Buddha:

"I have always had few children; I have only this one daughter, whom I loved so much that I forgot my sorrows. Suddenly she fell gravely ill and passed away, leaving me behind. By nature I am grieved and pained, and my emotions cannot be restrained."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to transform me with his divine power and release me from the knots of my grief.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"In the world there are four things that cannot endure for long."

What are the four? First, that which is permanent must become impermanent; second, that which is wealthy and noble must become poor and lowly; third, that which is joined together must inevitably separate; fourth, that which is strong and healthy must inevitably die.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"That which is eternal must come to an end; that which is high will surely fall; meeting implies separation, and those who are born are subject to death."

Upon hearing these verses, the brahmin’s mind was immediately opened and liberated; he wished to become a bhikṣu, whereupon his beard and hair fell away of their own accord and he became a bhikṣu. Reflecting deeply on impermanence, he attained the path of an arhat.
Long ago, when the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, there was a courtesan in the city named Padmā.
Her beauty and grace were peerless in the land, and among the sons of the high ministers, there were none who did not seek her out with respect.

At that time, a virtuous mind arose spontaneously within Padmā, and desiring to renounce worldly affairs to become a bhikṣuṇī, she immediately set out for the mountains to reach the Buddha’s dwelling. Before she had reached her destination, there was a flowing spring; as Padmā drank water and washed her hands, she saw her own reflection. Her complexion was radiant and glowing, her hair was deep blue-black, and her features were perfectly proportioned and exceptionally distinguished beyond compare. She felt remorse in her heart and said:
"If one is born into this world with such a physical form as this, why should I abandon it to go forth as a śramaṇa?"
"For now, let me follow the season to satisfy my private desires.
Having thought this, he returned.

The Buddha, knowing that Padma was ready to be transformed and delivered, manifested as a woman of peerless beauty, surpassing Padma by many millions of times, and approached him along the road from the opposite direction.
When Padmāvatī saw him, her heart was filled with great love and reverence; she immediately asked the transformed man, "From where have you come?
Where are your husband, children, father, brothers, and all your kin?"
"How is it that you travel alone without any attendants?

The transformed person replied, "I have come from within the city and wish to return home. Although we do not know one another, would it not be fitting for us to return together, sit by a spring to rest, and converse?"
The Lotus said, “Very well.
The two of them went back together to the water’s edge and explained their intentions in full detail.

The emanated person came and lay down to sleep, resting his head upon the lotus and sleeping on his knees; in a mere moment, he suddenly passed away. His body became bloated, foul-smelling, and putrid; his belly burst open and worms emerged; his teeth fell out, his hair dropped off, and his limbs fell apart. When the Lotus saw this, his heart was filled with great terror.
"How can it be that this good man has suddenly passed away?
If even he is thus, how could I possibly endure for long?
Therefore, I must go to the Buddha and diligently train in the Path."
He immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and having completed his salutation, he related in detail to the Buddha all that he had seen.
The Buddha told Padma:
"There are four things upon which a person cannot rely."
What are these four?

First, youth and vigor must inevitably return to old age; second, physical strength and health must inevitably return to death; third, the joyful gatherings and entertainments of one's six kin must inevitably end in separation; fourth, the accumulation of wealth and treasures must inevitably result in dispersal.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"With old age, the complexion fades; The body, afflicted by illness, naturally decays. The form collapses and rots;
such is the end of life."
Of what use is this body?
It is a place of constant leakage and stench, beset by illness, and plagued by the afflictions of old age and death.
Indulging in desires to one's heart's content increases what is unrighteous; failing to perceive or hear of change, one overlooks that life is impermanent.
"It is not that one has sons to rely upon, nor fathers or brothers; when pressed by death, there is no kinsman to provide refuge.

Having heard this teaching, Liánhuá was delighted and attained understanding. She contemplated her body as being like an illusion, its life not remaining for long, and realized that only the Way, its virtue, and *nirvāṇa* offer eternal peace. She immediately stepped forward and said to the Buddha, "I pray to become a *bhikṣuṇī*."
The Buddha said, "Excellent!
Her hair fell off of its own accord, and she immediately became a bhikṣuṇī; through contemplating śamatha and vipaśyanā, she attained arhatship.
All those seated there who heard what the Buddha had spoken were filled with joy.

Formerly, when the Buddha was teaching the Dharma at the Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, there were four brothers who were brahmins, each of whom had attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Knowing that their lives would end in seven days, they deliberated among themselves, saying:

"With the power of the five supernormal faculties, one can overturn heaven and earth, touch the sun and moon with one's hand, move mountains, and stop flowing rivers; there is nothing one cannot do—how then could one fail to avoid this confrontation with death?"
Another person said:
"I shall enter the great ocean; neither appearing above nor reaching the bottom, but dwelling precisely in its midst—how could the ghost of impermanence know my location?"
One person said:
"I shall enter into Mount Sumeru and merge myself with its exterior so that no trace remains; how could the demon of impermanence know my whereabouts?"
One person said, "I shall ascend lightly and hide within the void; how could the ghost of impermanence know my whereabouts?
Another person said:
"I shall hide myself within the great marketplace; when the Ghost of Impermanence goes about seeking a victim, why must it seek me?
Having finished their deliberations, the four men went together to take leave of the King, saying:

"Our allotted lifespans have but seven days remaining. We now wish to flee for our lives in the hope of escaping death; we shall return to pay our respects and pray only that Your Majesty may further advance in virtue."
Thereupon they departed separately, each going to their respective destinations.
When the seven-day period was complete, they all met their deaths, like fruit falling when it has ripened.
The market supervisor informed the king:
"A certain brahmin has suddenly died in the marketplace.
Upon hearing this, the king realized:
"Four people were avoiding their karmic retribution; now that one has already died, how could the remaining three possibly escape alone?"
The king immediately prepared his carriage and went to where the Buddha was staying. Having paid his respects, he withdrew to sit down and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Recently there were four brahmin brothers who each attained the five supernormal powers. Knowing that their lives were coming to an end, they all fled together. I do not know whether they have now been able to escape [their fate] or not?"
The Buddha told the Great King:
"There are four things with which a person cannot be separated. What are these four?
First, while in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one cannot avoid taking birth.
Second, once born, one cannot avoid aging.
Third, once aged, one cannot avoid falling ill.
"Fourth, once one is ill, one cannot avoid undergoing death.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Not in the sky, nor in the midst of the sea, Nor by entering into mountain clefts or rocks, [Can one escape death]."
There is no place on earth where one can escape and not undergo death.
This is my task, this is what I must do; I must act so as to bring it to completion.
People are restless for this sake, treading upon the sorrows of old age and death.
"Knowing this, one can bring oneself to stillness; seeing thus the exhaustion of birth, the bhikṣu grows weary of Māra’s armies and attains deliverance from saṃsāra.
Hearing the Buddha’s words, the king sighed in admiration and said:
"Excellent! It is truly as Your Majesty has taught: when four people avoid facing one, that one dies; since fortune and destiny have their allotted portions, it is likewise for the rest.
None among the ministers and attendants failed to believe and accept this.
Chapter Two: On Teaching. *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*. Once, when the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should diligently cultivate the Path and cast off the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); with a clear mind and settled spirit, you may escape all suffering."

There was a bhikṣu whose resolve was not clear or penetrating; having eaten his fill, he entered his room and closed the door to sleep in silence. Cherishing his body and seeking pleasure, he did not contemplate impermanence; shrouded in darkness and indolent, he knew no distinction between day and night.
Seven days hence his life will come to an end; the Buddha, pitying him and fearing he would fall into the evil realms, immediately entered his room, snapped his fingers to awaken him, and said:
"Ho! Rise! Why do you sleep?"
Wasp-like insects, snails, clams, and woodworms dwell hidden within impurity; deluded, they imagine this to be their self.
How can one whose body is scarred by wounds, whose mind suffers like that of a child in pain, and who is beset by manifold calamities, yet still indulge in sleep?
Reflecting without negligence, practicing benevolence and studying its traces,
one will thereby have no sorrow, always mindful of extinguishing one's own defilements.
Cultivating right view and striving for its increase— this is the light of the world.
"The merit produced shall be a thousandfold, and one will never fall into the evil realms.

Upon hearing this verse, the bhikṣu was immediately startled awake; seeing the Buddha personally instructing him, he felt increased reverence and awe, and immediately rose to prostrate himself in salutation before the Buddha.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Do you recognize your own past lives?
The bhikṣu replied:
"Shrouded by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), you truly did not recognize [the truth] yourself.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

"In the past, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, you once left the household life; yet, out of greed for bodily comforts and gain, you did not attend to the sūtras or the precepts. Having eaten your fill, you would sleep and fail to contemplate impermanence. When your life ended, your spirit was reborn among the *vāyasa* insects, where it remained for fifty thousand years."
When their lifespans end, they again become conch and clam insects, or wood-boring worms within trees, each for fifty thousand years.

These four kinds of insects grow in darkness; they crave their bodies and cling to life, delighting in dwelling in hidden seclusion. Taking darkness as their home, they take no pleasure in light; when they sleep, they remain so for a hundred years before awakening, entangled in the net of sin and seeking no way of escape.
"Now that my transgressions have finally come to an end and I have become a śramaṇa, how can I sleep and remain ignorant of the need for contentment?

Thereupon, the bhikṣu heard again of his past causes and conditions; filled with shame and fear, he reproached himself. The clouds of the five hindrances were dispelled, and he immediately attained arhatship.
In the past, when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, he was preaching the Dharma to the devas, humans, and the fourfold assembly.

At that time, there was a young bhikṣu who was dull-witted, simple-minded, rustic, and unrefined; he did not yet understand the essentials of the Path. His passions were rife and his thoughts were set upon desire; his vital energy was so intense that he could not control himself. Distressed by this, he failed to attain liberation from the world.
Sitting in meditation, he thought to himself:
"Only when the roots [of defilement] are severed can one attain purity and enter the tracks of the Path.

He immediately went to the house of a donor and borrowed an axe; returning to his room, he locked the door, stripped off his clothes, and sat upon a wooden board intending to cut off his own genitals.

"It is precisely these aggregates that cause me such diligent suffering, leading me through birth and death for countless kalpas; the three miserable realms and the six destinies all stem from form and desire. Unless one severs this, there is no way to attain the Way."

The Buddha, knowing that his mind was so deluded, taught that the path lies in governing the mind, for the mind is the root; yet he did not realize that by seeking his own destruction, he would fall into transgression and suffer long-lasting pain.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One went into his room and asked the bhikṣu, "What do you intend to do?
Setting down his axe, putting on his robes, and prostrating before the Buddha, he spoke of his own situation:

"I have studied the Way for a long time yet have not understood its dharma-gates. Whenever I sit in meditative concentration on the verge of attaining the Way, I am overwhelmed by desire; my vital energy becomes excessive, my mind is deluded, and my vision darkens, such that I am unaware of heaven and earth."
He reproached himself, thinking, "All these matters arise from this; therefore, I shall borrow an axe to cut it off and bring it under control.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu, "How can you be so foolish as not to understand the principle?"
Those who seek the Way must first sever their delusion and then restrain the mind; for the mind is the root source of both good and evil.
Those who wish to sever the root must first restrain the mind; when the mind is settled and the intellect is liberated, one then attains the Way.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One who first severs the mother, Leads the king and his two ministers, And abandons all retinues—
Such a person is a supreme practitioner."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The twelve links of dependent origination have ignorance as their root; ignorance is the source of all transgressions.
Wisdom is the foundation of all practices; one must first sever ignorance before the mind can become concentrated.”
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣu felt ashamed and reproached himself, saying:
"I have been deluded by folly for a long time; it was because I did not understand the ancient scriptures that I acted in this way. How truly marvelous is what the Buddha has now taught!"

Internally contemplating right concentration and the mindfulness of *ānāpāna*, he restrained his mind, subdued his passions, and blocked off all desires; he immediately attained a concentrated mind and, in the presence of the Buddha, realized arhatship.
In the past, when the Buddha was at Vulture Peak Mountain in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, he was preaching the Dharma of Ambrosia for the sake of devas, humans, kings, and ministers.

There was a bhikṣu who was fierce, bold, and courageous; the Buddha, knowing his disposition, sent him to the Ghost Valley behind the mountain, instructing him to sit beneath a tree and practice breath-counting to seek meditative concentration (*samādhi*). By observing the length and brevity of the breath through *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing), he would sever craving, extinguish suffering, and attain *nirvāṇa*.

The bhikṣu accepted the instruction and went into the valley, intending to sit and compose his mind. However, he heard only the voices of mountain spirits and deities; their forms were not visible, yet their sounds were present. Trembling with fear and unable to find peace, he wished to repent and return, thinking to himself:

"I come from a wealthy family with a great clan, yet I have forcefully left the home life to study the Way. Here in this deep mountain inhabited by spirits, I am alone without any companions or fellow travelers; there are only various ghosts who frequently come to terrify people."
While he was reflecting thus and had not yet departed, the World-Honored One went to his side, sat beneath a tree, and asked him:
"Are you not afraid, being here all alone?"
The bhikṣu bowed his head and said:

"I have never before entered this mountain, and I was truly anxious while here. Just a short while ago, a wild elephant king came by and lay down beside a tree; his heart alone was filled with joy. To be far removed from all other elephants—how delightful!"
The Buddha, knowing the elephant’s thoughts, addressed the bhikṣu, saying:
"Do you know from where this elephant has come? He replied:
"I do not understand.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

"This elephant has over five hundred followers, both large and small. Having grown weary of the young elephants, he abandoned them and came here to lie down leaning against this tree. He thinks to himself: 'How joyful it is to have escaped the prison of affection and love!'"
Even an elephant, though a beast, still seeks solitude; how much more so you, who have left the household life seeking liberation from the world, yet now seek a companion when you are already alone?
A foolish companion brings about much ruin and failure; dwelling alone without a counterpart, one has no need for counsel. It is better to practice the Path alone than to have a foolish companion.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"One who studies without companions, Failing to find a virtuous friend, Would rather dwell alone in goodness Than associate with the foolish."
Delighting in the training of the precepts, what need is there for companions?
To be solitary and virtuous without sorrow is like an elephant in the empty wilderness.
When the Buddha spoke these words, the bhikṣu’s mind was liberated; reflecting inwardly upon the holy teaching, he immediately attained arhatship.
The spirits and deities within the valley also all heard and understood, receiving the Buddha’s vows and instructions as his disciples; they would no longer harass the people.
The Buddha and the bhikṣus then returned together to the vihāra.

2. Chapter on Guarding the Precepts. *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Chapter Two: Guarding the Precepts. Formerly, when the Buddha was at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī, he expounded the Dharma for the sake of devas and humans.
At that time, there were two newly ordained bhikṣus in the kingdom of Rājagṛha who wished to go and see the Buddha.

Between the two kingdoms, the land was vast and devoid of people; at that time, due to a drought and intense heat, the springs had run dry. The two men were parched with thirst and exhausted by the heat, gasping for breath. Within one of the springs there was a little more than a *sheng* of water, but because it contained tiny insects, they could not drink it.
The two faced each other and said, "We have come from afar specifically wishing to see the Buddha; we did not expect that today we would lose our lives here.
One of them spoke further, saying:
"Let us drink water to sustain our lives and proceed forward to see the Buddha; what else could we know?
One man replied, "The Buddha’s clear precepts take benevolence and compassion as their primary principle. To live out one's life through such cruelty serves no purpose in seeing the Buddha."
"It would be better to die while observing the precepts than to live while violating them.
One person immediately rose and drank to his heart's content, and they then proceeded on their way.

The other did not drink and consequently lost his life; he was reborn in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Reflecting and examining himself, he recognized his past lives: that he had maintained the precepts without violation and had now come to be born here.
Truly, the retribution of merit is not far off!
He immediately took flowers and incense and descended to where the Buddha was, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Those who had drunk water arrived after being exhausted by the journey for many days; seeing the Buddha’s divine virtue, most supreme and majestic, they bowed their heads in worship and, having finished their prostrations, wept as they spoke of themselves:
"One of my companions passed away there; I feel regret that he did not reach his destination. I pray that the Buddha may take note of this.
The Buddha said, "I already know it clearly."
The Buddha pointed with his finger and said, "This celestial being is your companion; having perfected the precepts, he has been reborn in heaven and arrived here before you.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One bared his chest to show him.
"If you observe my form but do not uphold my precepts, though you claim to see me, I do not see you;
yet if one who is ten thousand *li* away from me upholds the sutras and the precepts, that person is as if before my very eyes."
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Learning much through study and maintaining the precepts without fail, one will be praised in both worlds and obtain all that is wished for."
To study yet hear little, and to maintain the precepts incompletely, leads to suffering in both worlds and the loss of one’s original vow.
Now, there are two ways of studying: always draw near to those who have heard much, and understand the meaning with settled composure; even in adversity, do not waver.
Thereupon, upon hearing the verse, the bhikṣu felt shame and fear; he prostrated himself, repented his transgressions, and silently reflected upon his conduct.
Hearing the verse, the devas and humans were filled with joy in their hearts and attained the Dharma-eye; among the assembly of devas and humans, there was none who did not reverently practice it.

Chapter Three: On Much Learning (*Bahusruta-varga*). From the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*. In the past, there was a poor household in the kingdom of Śrāvastī. The husband and wife were stingy and wicked, having no faith in the Way or its virtue. The Buddha, pitying their ignorance, manifested himself as an ordinary, impoverished śramaṇa and went to their door to beg for alms.
At that time, her husband was away, and his wife reviled him with improper words.
The śramaṇa said to her, "I am a practitioner of the Way who lives by begging; I must not be reviled, for I seek nothing but a single meal."
The hostess said, "If you were to die right now, you would still not even obtain food; how much less so when you are currently healthy and strong—why do you hope for my food?
You are merely delaying the time; it would be better for you to leave early."

Thereupon, the śramaṇa stood before him, rolled his eyes upward, and exhaled his vital breath, manifesting the signs of death: his body became bloated, worms emerged from his nose and mouth, his belly burst open, his intestines rotted away, and impurities flowed out and spread.
Upon seeing this, his wife was struck with terror and lost her voice; she abandoned him and fled.
Thereupon, the practitioner suddenly departed and, having traveled several li from the house, sat beneath a tree to rest.
When her husband returned home and saw his wife on the road, he marveled at her extreme terror.
The wife said to her husband,
"There was a śramaṇa who frightened me so greatly."
Greatly enraged, he asked where she was.
His wife replied, "She has already left; I think she has not gone far."

The man immediately took up his bow and girded on his sword, following the tracks to pursue him. Drawing his bow and unsheathing his sword, he ran straight forward, intending to strike the practitioner.

The practitioner then transformed himself into a small city of lapis lazuli to surround himself; the man circled the city several times but could not enter, so he asked the practitioner, "Why do you not open the gate?"
The practitioner said,
"If you wish to have the gate opened, you must cast away your bow and sword.
The man thought to himself:
“I shall follow your word; if you succeed, I will strike you with my closed fist.
He then cast away his bow and sword.
Yet the gate still would not open, so he spoke again to the practitioner:
"You have already cast away your bow and sword; why then is the gate not opened?
The practitioner replied, "I meant for you to cast away the bow and sword of evil intentions within your mind, not the bow and sword in your hands."
Thereupon, his heart was startled and his body trembled with fear, thinking:
"This practitioner is so divine and sagely that he even knows my thoughts.
He immediately prostrated himself to repent his transgression and bowed his head to the practitioner, saying:

"I have a lowly wife who does not recognize the True Man; she incites me toward evil. I pray that you will show me some small measure of compassion and not abandon me so quickly. I wish now to bring her here to exhort her to practice the Way."
He immediately rose and returned home.
His wife asked him, "Where is the śramaṇa?"

The husband recounted in detail the virtues of the divine transformations, saying, "He is there now; you should go yourself to repent and extinguish your sins. Thereupon, the husband and wife went to the place where the practitioner was.

Prostrating themselves with their five limbs to the ground, they repented their transgressions and requested to become his disciples. Kneeling for a long time, they asked, "The practitioner’s divine transformations and holy attainments are such as these.

You possess a city of lapis lazuli, firm and difficult to surpass; your resolve is clear and your mind is settled, forever free from sorrow and affliction. What path of virtue and what conduct have you practiced to achieve such wondrous spiritual power?"
The practitioner replied:

"I have studied extensively without weariness and served the Dharma without slackening; through diligent application, upholding the precepts, and wisdom free from negligence, I have attained the Way and reached Nirvana for myself."
Thereupon, the practitioner spoke this verse:
"Because of being well-learned and able to uphold [the teachings], One honors the Dharma as a protective wall;
Through diligence, it is difficult to overcome or destroy, And from this, precept and wisdom are perfected."
Much learning makes the will firm; with a firm will, wisdom increases.
Wisdom leads to a broad understanding of meanings; seeing the meaning, one dwells in peace through practicing the Dharma.
Much learning can remove sorrow; it enables one to find joy in meditative concentration.
Well-spoken is the Dharma of the Deathless; by it one personally attains Nirvāṇa.
Hearing leads to knowledge of the Law and Discipline; through hearing, doubt is resolved and the Right Path is seen.
By hearing, one abandons what is not the Dharma; through practice, one reaches the deathless state.
After the practitioner had spoken the verse, he manifested the radiant marks of a Buddha; its vast brilliance blazed forth, illuminating heaven and earth.

The husband and wife were struck with awe, their spirits trembling with fear; they repented their evils, cleansed their hearts, and prostrated themselves with their heads striking the ground. They destroyed twenty billion evils and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
In the past, when the Buddha was at the Monastery of Beautiful Sound in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, he was extensively expounding the Great Dharma to the fourfold assembly.

There was a brahmin practitioner whose wisdom was vast and penetrating; he had mastered all the scriptures and there was nothing he did not comprehend. Arrogant and self-conceited, he praised himself as being peerless in the world, traveling about seeking an opponent, yet none dared to respond.
One day, he walked through the city holding a torch. People asked him, "Why are you walking through the city by day carrying a torch?
The brahmin replied:
“The world is entirely ignorant and blind, with eyes that see nothing; it is for this reason that I hold up a torch to illuminate it.
Observing the world, there is no one who dares to speak thus.

The Buddha knew that although the brahmin had accumulated merit in past lives and was ready for deliverance, he acted with arrogance, seeking superior fame and reputation, and disregarded impermanence while relying on his own pride and indulgence. Such a person shall fall into the Great Mountain Hell, where it will be exceedingly difficult to seek escape for incalculable kalpas.
The Buddha then transformed himself into a wise man sitting at the head of a stall and called out to the brahmin,
"Why are you doing this? The brahmin replied:
"Because the multitude is shrouded in darkness and does not see the light by day or night, I have taken up this torch to illuminate them.
The worthy man asked the brahmin again:
"In the scriptures there are four types of clear knowledge; do you know them?"
He replied, "I do not understand.
What is meant by the Dharma of the Four Clarities?"

"First, he is clear regarding celestial phenomena and terrestrial geography, and knows how to harmonize the four seasons; second, he is clear regarding the constellations and distinguishes the five elements; third, he is clear regarding the governance of a state and possesses skillful methods for pacification and transformation; fourth, he is clear regarding leading troops, remaining steadfast and without error."
“Are you, as a brahmin, possessed of these four types of vidyā-knowledge?
The brahmin felt ashamed; he cast aside his torch, joined his palms, and felt a sense of inadequacy.
The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, immediately restored his physical form, his radiance brilliant and illuminating heaven and earth. Then, with a Brahma-voice, he spoke this verse for the brahmin:
"If one has heard even a little and yet is conceited and arrogant toward others, this is like a blind person holding a torch: it illuminates others but does not illuminate oneself.
Having spoken this verse, the Buddha addressed the brahmin, saying:
"In the darkness, nothing surpasses you; yet by day, you carry a torch as you enter a great kingdom—is this, as you yourself know, any different from a single speck of dust?
Upon hearing this, the Brahmin was filled with shame and immediately prostrated himself, vowing to become his disciple.
The Buddha immediately accepted him and ordained him as a śramaṇa; with his mind liberated and delusions ceased, he attained arhatship.
Formerly, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a great elder named Sudatta who had attained the stage of srotāpanna.

There was an elder named Xiàoshī (Good Giver) who was a close friend [of the Buddha]. He did not believe in the Buddha’s Way nor in various medical arts. At that time, he contracted a severe illness and became so debilitated that he was confined to his bed.
His kinsmen and friends all came to visit and inquire after him, urging him to seek medical treatment, but he refused until death.
He replied to the crowd, saying, "I serve the sun and moon and am loyal and filial toward my sovereign and father; I shall devote my life to this cause and never alter my resolve.
Sudatta said to him:

"The master I serve is titled 'Buddha. His divine virtue is widely pervasive, and those who behold him obtain blessings. You may test him by requesting that he preach a sutra and offer prayers; then listen to how his speech, conduct, and progress compare to those of other paths. Whether you serve him or not shall be according to your own will."
"Since your illness has persisted for a long time and has not yet been cured, I urge you to invite the Buddha,
hoping that you may receive his blessings. Haoshi replied, "Excellent."
"You should then request the Buddha and his assembly of disciples on my behalf.
Sudatta immediately invited the Buddha and the Sangha, who proceeded to his gate.
The Buddha emitted a radiance that penetrated both inside and outside; seeing this light, the elder was filled with joy and felt his body become light.
The Buddha sat down before him and inquired of the elder:
"How is your illness? Which deity did you formerly serve?"
"What treatment should be administered? The elder addressed the Buddha: "I have served the sun and moon, the sovereigns, and my ancestors;

I have observed fasts and precepts with reverence, offering ten thousand kinds of prayers. Yet, though I have been ill for a long time, I have received no grace or protection. Medicine, herbs, and acupuncture are things forbidden within my household; the sutras, the precepts, and the merit they bring are things I have never known since the days of my forefathers. My ancestors have maintained this way until now, awaiting death right here."
The Buddha told the householder:
"When people are born into this world, there are three kinds of untimely deaths:

first, failing to treat an illness; second, treating it but lacking care; and third, being arrogant, self-indulgent, and willful, failing to understand the principles of what is contrary and what is compliant."
Such illnesses cannot be dispelled by the sun, the moon, heaven, earth, ancestors, sovereigns, or fathers; rather, they must be pacified and relieved at the appropriate time through the clear Way.

First, for the cold and heat of the four elements, one must rely on medicine; second, for the various malevolent spirits and demons, one must rely on the sutras and precepts; third, one must serve the worthy and holy ones to show compassion and rescue those in distress.

With virtuous majesty and spiritual power, they bestow blessings upon all living beings; through great wisdom, they eliminate the hindrances of the aggregates. By practicing in this way, one will enjoy peace and security in the present life and never suffer injustice or calamity; with pure precepts and wisdom, one shall always abide in tranquility throughout successive lifetimes.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One serves the sun for the sake of light; one serves one's father for the sake of his kindness;
one serves a ruler with one's strength; but one serves a person of the Path because of what has been heard."
When people entrust their lives to physicians, they desire to overcome illness by relying on the powerful;
yet the Dharma resides in the sphere of wisdom, and meritorious conduct brings clarity through every generation.
One examines a friend in times of business, and distinguishes a companion in moments of urgency.
To observe one’s wife in the chamber is pleasure; to know where wisdom lies is in speech.
To be able to see the Path as a teacher, to resolve doubts and cause learning to become clear, and furthermore to bestow the root of purity—such a person is able to uphold the treasury of the Dharma.

Hearing brings benefit in this present life—bringing one's wife, children, brothers, and friends [peace]—and it also secures merit for future lives; by accumulating what is heard, one achieves noble wisdom.
One who is able to grasp what is heard understands its meaning; through understanding, one’s precepts remain unbroken.
Those who receive the Dharma and rely upon the Dharma will swiftly attain peace from this.
This can dispel sorrow and anger, and also remove inauspicious decline.
If you wish to obtain tranquility and good fortune, you should attend to those who are learned.

Thereupon, having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, the knots of doubt and confusion in the elder’s mind were suddenly dispelled like clouds clearing from the sky. He entrusted himself to the Way and its Virtue as a skilled physician applies his treatment. His four elements became tranquil and his manifold ailments vanished; as if drinking ambrosia, he was joyful within and without, his body at ease and his mind settled. He attained the stage of Srotāpanna, and there was no one among his clan or the people of the land who did not revere and honor him.
In the past, to the south of the kingdom of Rājagṛha there was a great mountain, two hundred *li* from the city; the roads to the various kingdoms of the southern lands passed through this mountain.

The mountain paths were deep and remote, and five hundred bandits relied on these precipices to plunder travelers. Subsequently, they acted with such impunity that the victims were so numerous as to be a chaotic mass of corpses; merchants were afflicted by their cruelty and the royal highways became impassable. Although the king pursued them to punish them, he could not capture them.

At that time, the Buddha was in the kingdom, out of compassion for all living beings, he reflected: "Those bandits do not understand the nature of sin and merit; though a Tathāgata exists in the world, they do not behold him with their eyes, and though the Dharma drum resounds daily, they do not hear it with their ears."
"If I do not go to deliver them, it would be like a stone sinking to the bottom of a deep pool.

He then transformed himself into a man dressed in fine garments, riding a horse while wearing a sword at his side and holding a bow and arrows in his hands. His saddle and bridle were finely adorned and decorated with gold and silver, and a bright moon pearl was draped across the horse’s body. Leaping onto the horse and sounding his bowstring, he entered the mountains.

When the bandits saw this, they thought their purpose was accomplished; having been thieves for many years, they had never before encountered such an opportunity. How is this any different from throwing an egg against a stone?
The bandits all moved forward together to surround him, drawing their bows and unsheathing their swords, vying with one another to strip him naked.

Thereupon, the conjured man raised his bow and fired a single arrow, causing each of the five hundred bandits to be struck by one shaft; as he pointed his sword at them, each was wounded by a gash, and with the wounds severe and the arrows deep, they all immediately fell prostrate.
The band of five hundred thieves rolled upon the ground, prostrating themselves with their heads at his feet to surrender.
"What deity is this whose power is so great?
We beg for your pardon and forgiveness so that our humble lives may be spared. Please pull out the arrow at once so that the wound may heal; currently, the pain of the wound is unbearable."
The transformed person replied:
"This wound does not cause pain, and this arrow is not deep; yet among all wounds in the world, none is more grievous than sorrow, and none is more destructive than folly."
You harbor the anxiety of greedy acquisition and the folly of violent slaughter; the wounds from blades and the poison-tipped arrows can never be healed.
These two matters have deep and firm roots; even a valiant and powerful warrior cannot uproot them.

Only by means of the sutras, the precepts, extensive learning, wisdom, and their meaning can one clarify the Way to heal the diseases of the mind, uproot sorrow, craving, ignorance, and arrogance, and subdue stubbornness, haughtiness, wealth, and greed; only through the accumulation of merit and the cultivation of wisdom can these be eliminated, thereby attaining lasting peace and security.

Thereupon, the emanated person immediately manifested the body of a Buddha, with the marks and signs of excellence standing out prominently and a golden countenance of exquisite beauty. He then spoke this verse:
"Nothing surpasses sorrow in inflicting wounds; Nothing surpasses folly in shooting arrows.
These are too strong to be pulled out by force; Only through extensive learning can they be removed."
The blind gain sight from him; the dark receive a lamp.
He guides the people of the world as one with vision leads those without.
Therefore, one should abandon delusion and leave behind pride and the pleasures of wealth.
"Those who apply themselves to learning and seek out what is heard, this is called the accumulation of merit.

Thereupon, the five hundred people beheld the Buddha’s radiant marks and, hearing these verses once more, prostrated themselves in submission, resolved their minds to repent of their transgressions. Their wounds from blades and the poison of their arrows were naturally healed; with joyful hearts opened, they immediately received the five precepts. The realm became peaceful and stable, and there was no one who did not rejoice.

Chapter Four: On Profound Faith. *The Sutra of Parables from the Dharmapada*. In the past, to the southeast of the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a great river. Its waters were both deep and wide. More than five hundred households lived upon its banks; they had not yet heard of the path of morality that leads across the world. They practiced violence and deception as their primary pursuits, greedily seeking profit, indulging themselves, and following their every whim and desire.

The World-Honored One constantly keeps in mind those who are ready to be delivered and should go to deliver them; knowing that these families possessed the merit to be delivered, the World-Honored One went to the water's edge and sat beneath a tree.

When the villagers saw the Buddha’s radiant and extraordinary appearance, they were all struck with awe and solemnity; they all went to pay their respects, some prostrating and others bowing, inquiring after his well-being.

The Buddha bade them sit and preached the Dharma for them, but when the multitude heard it, their hearts did not believe, for they were accustomed to deceit and indolence, and could not trust the true words.
The Buddha then manifested a person who came from south of the river, walking upon the water with his feet submerged only up to the ankles, and approached the Buddha to prostrate and pay homage.

When the multitude saw this, there was no one who was not struck with wonder and asked the manifested person, "Since the time of our ancestors, we have lived by this river, yet we have never heard of anyone walking upon the water; who are you?"
"What kind of spiritual art allows one to walk upon water without sinking?
I wish to hear its meaning.
The transformed person replied:
"I am a simple and straightforward man from Jiangnan. Hearing that the Buddha was here, I yearned for his Way and virtue; however, when I reached the southern bank, I could not cross at will.
I asked those on the opposite shore how deep the water was."
That person saw me and said, "The water is only ankle-deep; why do you not wade across?
Believing his words, I simply came over; there was no other extraordinary method involved.
The Buddha then praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
One who clings to faith and the ultimate truth can cross the abyss of birth and death; what is so remarkable about a river of only a few li?"
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Faith can cross the abyss; restraint serves as the helmsman; Vigor eliminates suffering;
wisdom reaches the further shore."
The person who possesses faithful conduct is praised by the sages; those who delight in non-action have all their bonds released.
Through faith one attains the Way, and through the Dharma one reaches extinction (nirvāṇa). From hearing one gains wisdom, and wherever one goes, there is clarity.
"Faith and precepts, wisdom and intention—if one can practice these, the steadfast man crosses over by means of wisdom and is thereby liberated from the abyss.

When the villagers heard what the Buddha had said and witnessed the proof of his faith, their minds were opened and their conviction became firm; they all received the five precepts and became lay disciples (*upāsaka*). With clear understanding, they practiced the Dharma daily, and the teachings spread far and wide.

In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a great elder named Śūdra who possessed immeasurable wealth and placed his faith in the Way and its Virtue. He made a vow to always invite the Buddha and the Sangha on the eighth day of the twelfth month, and throughout his life, his descendants continued to practice this without fail.
When the elder was on his deathbed, he entrusted his son with the instruction not to let [the offerings] be neglected.

The son’s name was Virūḍhaka; later, as days passed, his wealth gradually diminished until he possessed nothing. When the month of Mārgaśīrṣa arrived, he had no means to prepare the offerings, and he was filled with grief and distress, finding no joy.
The Buddha dispatched Maudgalyāyana to go and ask Bhīradvāja:
"Your father’s month of service is about to end; what plan do you intend to employ? Bhīradvāja replied:
"I dare not disobey the instructions of my deceased father; I only pray that the World-Honored One will not neglect or abandon me.
On the eighth day, at the hour of noon, may you turn your light to look upon me.
Maudgalyāyana returned and reported this.
Vīradatta immediately took his wife to his maternal relatives to pawn their belongings for one hundred taels of gold; returning home, he prepared the offerings until everything was complete.

The Buddha, together with a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty monks, went to his house. Once they were seated, the water for washing was served, followed by the meal; when the cleansing was finished, they returned to the vihāra.
Vīradatta was filled with joy and did not dare feel regret; at midnight that very night, the various old treasuries were naturally filled with precious objects just as they had been before.
When Vīradatta and his wife saw this the next morning, they were both joyful and afraid, fearing that the authorities would see them and ask where they had obtained these things.
The husband and wife consulted together that they should go to question the Buddha.
They soon arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling and reported the matter to him in detail.
The Buddha addressed Bhīradvāja:

"Be at ease and use it freely without hesitation or difficulty. You have practiced faith without disobeying your father's instructions; you have maintained the precepts with shame and remorse, remaining steadfast until death. You have heard the teachings on generosity and wisdom, and the seven riches are fully complete within you. This is the result of your merit and virtue, not a portent of calamity."
"The wise are able to practice this; it does not matter from where they were born, whether male or female—for their merit will manifest spontaneously.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The wealth of faith and the wealth of precepts, The wealth of shame and the wealth of remorse, The wealth of learning and the wealth of giving."
Wisdom is the seventh of the riches.
Guarding the precepts through faith, constantly and purely contemplating the Dharma, practicing with wisdom, and never forgetting the teachings one has received.
"Those born with this wealth—regardless of whether they are male or female—will never be poor at the end of their lives; the wise recognize the truth.

Having heard what the Buddha had said, Bhīradvāja’s faith grew even more profound. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and returned home with joy. He fully proclaimed the Buddha’s teachings to his wife and children, and through their mutual succession of practice, they all attained the fruit of the Path.

Chapter Five: On Heedfulness. *The Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Chapter Five: On Heedfulness. Long ago, there was a mountain in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, located forty or fifty *li* from the city, where five śramaṇas dwelt and practiced the Way.

At dawn he would leave the mountain to beg for food among the people, and having finished his meal, he would return to the mountain only at dusk; being utterly exhausted from this coming and going, he was unable to sit in meditation or contemplate right concentration, and though years passed in this manner, he could not attain the Way.

The Buddha, pitying them for their toil without gain, manifested as a wandering ascetic and went to where they were. He asked the practitioners, "In your seclusion and cultivation of the Way, have you not grown weary?"
The śramaṇas said: "We are here far from the city;

this body composed of the four great elements requires food and drink. Daily providing for these needs causes us exhaustion on our journeys back and forth. Having endured such toil for years and ages, we travel by day and are always weary and spent by evening, leaving no leisure to practice the Way; it seems we shall simply bring our lives to an end in this very state."

The practitioner said: "One who practices the Way takes the precepts as the foundation and the restraint of the mind as the practice. One deprecates the physical form to honor the Truth, casting aside even life itself; one eats merely to sustain the body and guards the mind in right concentration. By internally studying *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, extinguishing the defiled will, one attains the Way. How could one who nourishes the body and follows its passions ever escape suffering?"
"I pray that you, venerable practitioners, do not travel tomorrow; I shall provide for your needs so that you may rest for one day.
At that time, the five śramaṇas were filled with great joy, marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence; they settled their minds in composure and no longer worried about traveling.

At noon the next day, this transformed person arrived bringing food. Having finished eating, his mind was peaceful and his spirit was tranquil. Thereupon, the transformed person spoke these verses for him:
"The bhikṣu establishes the precepts, Restrains and gathers his sense faculties, Knows moderation in eating, And awakens the mind to make it responsive."
Subdue the mind with the precepts, maintain the mind in right concentration, internally train in śamatha and vipaśyanā, and do not forget right wisdom.
With clear discernment, guard the precepts; contemplate right wisdom within; practice the Path as it truly is, and purify yourself to eliminate suffering.

After the transformed person had spoken this verse, he manifested the radiant countenance and physical marks of a Buddha’s body. Thereupon, the five śramaṇas were deeply moved in spirit; they all contemplated the precepts and immediately attained the path of arhatship.
Chapter Six: On Mindfulness (Vimamsa-varga). From the *Dharmapada-avadana-sutra*. Once, when the Buddha was in the world, King Pukkasati and King Bimbisara were close friends.

King Pukkasāti, not yet knowing the Buddha-way, fashioned flowers of the seven treasures and sent them as a gift to King Bimbisāra. Upon receiving them, King Bimbisāra offered them in turn to the Buddha, saying to him:

"King Pukkasāti is my friend; he has sent me these flowers. Now that they have been offered to the Buddha, I pray that the king’s mind may be opened and his understanding awakened, so that he may see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and pay reverent homage to the Noble Assembly."
"What should be given as a gift in return for what he has bestowed?
The Buddha told Bimbisāra,
"Transcribe the Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination and send it to him."
"That king will surely attain faith and understanding upon reading this sutra.
He then transcribed the scroll and wrote a separate note saying:

"You have presented me with precious flowers; I now offer you the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in return. Contemplate its meaning in detail, for its karmic fruition is profound and sublime; once you receive it, recite and practice it so that we may share the flavor of the Way."

When King Puṣya attained this sūtra and read it, he examined it repeatedly and understood it with profound clarity. He sighed deeply and said: "The transformation of the Way is truly wondrous; its refined meaning brings peace to the spirit.

National glory and the five desires are the source of anxiety and affliction. Having practiced delusion through successive kalpas, I have only now awakened. Looking back at worldly customs, there is nothing therein to be craved or enjoyed."

He immediately summoned his ministers and entrusted the kingdom to the crown prince; then, shaving his own head, he became a śramaṇa. Clad in dharma-robes and carrying an alms-bowl, he went to the outskirts of Rājagṛha and took up lodging for the night in a potter’s kiln. "Tomorrow I shall enter the city to beg for alms; after the meal, I shall go to the Buddha's dwelling to receive the sūtras and precepts."

The Buddha, through his supernormal knowledge, perceived that Puṣya’s life would come to an end at the time of the next day’s meal; thus, having traveled from afar, he would not have the opportunity to see the Buddha nor hear the scriptures, which was truly pitiable. Thereupon, the World-Honored One manifested as a śramaṇa and went to a potter’s house seeking lodging for the night.
The potter said, "A while ago there was a śramaṇa in that kiln; you may go there and stay the night with him.
Taking some straw, he entered the kiln and sat to one side, then asked Pukkusa:
"From where have you come?
Who is your teacher? For what cause and condition have you gone forth as a śramaṇa?"
"Have you seen the Buddha? Puṣya said, "I have not yet seen the Buddha;
having heard of the twelve links of dependent origination, I became a śramaṇa. Tomorrow, after entering the city to beg for alms, I shall go to see the Buddha."
The transformed śramaṇa said:

"Human life is precarious and fragile, subject to change from morning to evening. Impermanence and past karmic conditions arrive suddenly without fixed time; one should simply contemplate how the body arises from the four great elements, and that its aggregation and dissolution each return to their own source."

Contemplate the awakening mind as empty, pure, and signless; single-mindedly recollect the Triple Gem, practicing generosity and the virtue of precepts. Being able to know the impermanence [of all things], one perceives the Buddha as no different [from oneself]; only then should one consider that tomorrow’s planting of seeds is of no benefit.
Then the transformed śramaṇa spoke these verses:
“If a person attains a wholesome benefit, They then come to take refuge in the Buddha;
For this reason, day and night, One should constantly mind the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.”
One who knows this self-awakening mind is a disciple of the Buddha;
they should constantly, day and night, be mindful of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
They should be mindful of the body and its impermanence, and mindful of the virtues of ethical discipline and generosity.
"Emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness—day and night you should contemplate these.

At that time, the transformed śramaṇa remained within the kiln and expounded for Puṣkarasārin the essentials of impermanence. King Puṣkarasārin contemplated with a concentrated mind and immediately attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
The Buddha, knowing that he had understood, manifested for him the Buddha-body with its radiant marks and signs of excellence.
King Pukkasāti was filled with wonder and leaped for joy; he prostrated himself and paid homage.
The Buddha addressed him once more, saying:
"Since offenses are impermanent, once they are exhausted,
there is no need for fear. King Pukkusāti said,
"I respectfully accept your noble teaching."
He suddenly departed.

On the following day at mealtime, King Pukkasāti entered the city to beg for alms; at the city gate, he encountered a recently calved cow protecting her calf, which gored him, tearing open his abdomen, and he died, immediately being reborn in the Anāgāmin heaven.
The Buddha dispatched his disciples to perform the funeral rites and erect a stupa for him. The Buddha said to his disciples:
"One must not fail to be cautious regarding the root of karmic retribution.

Chapter Seven: On Compassion and Benevolence (*Maitrī-karuṇā-varga*). *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*. In the past, when the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, there was a mountain five hundred *li* from the capital. Within that mountain lived a family consisting of one hundred and twenty-two people.

Born and raised among the mountains and marshes, they made their livelihood by hunting; clad in skins and eating meat, they never practiced agriculture. They worshipped ghosts and spirits and were ignorant of the Three Jewels.
The Buddha, through his noble wisdom, perceived that they were ready for deliverance, so he went to their village and sat beneath a tree.

The men had gone out hunting, leaving only the women behind. Seeing the Buddha’s radiant countenance illuminating heaven and earth, such that the trees and stones of the mountains all turned golden, they were filled with wonder and joy. Realizing the Buddha was a divine being, they all went to prostrate themselves before him, making offerings and providing seats for him.
The Buddha taught the women the sin of taking life and the merit of practicing loving-kindness, explaining that even those bound by affection must eventually part.
Upon hearing this sutra, the women were filled with joy and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"The mountain folk are greedy and harmful, making their food of meat; we wish to offer you a modest gift, and pray that you will accept it."
The Buddha told the women:
"The Dharma of the Buddhas does not involve eating meat; since I have already eaten, there is no need to prepare any more.
He then said to them:

"Indeed, throughout one's life in this world, the food consumed is countless; why not instead prepare nourishment that is beneficial, rather than sustaining oneself by harming living beings? Upon death, one will fall into the evil realms, resulting only in loss and no benefit."

When humans consume the five grains, they should take pity upon all sentient beings; among the wriggling creatures of every kind, there is none that does not cherish life. To kill others to sustain oneself results in calamity and guilt that do not perish; through compassion and benevolence in refraining from killing, one shall be free from suffering throughout successive lifetimes.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Practicing benevolence by refraining from killing, And always being able to restrain the body— In such a state one does not die;
wherever one goes, there is no affliction."
Non-killing is benevolence; guarding the mind with caution in speech, one dwells in the deathless state and encounters no misfortune wherever one goes.
With hands folded and acting without effort, not harming any living being and free from all affliction—this is to correspond with the Brahma Heaven.
"Always with compassion and pity, purifying yourself according to the Buddha's teaching, knowing contentment and knowing when to stop—this is how one crosses over birth and death.
After the Buddha had spoken these verses, the men returned from hunting; the women, having listened to the sutra, did not go out to meet them.

Her husband was startled, suspicious, and marveled that things were not as usual; he abandoned the meat and returned home, suspecting some calamity had occurred. Upon seeing all his wives sitting before the Buddha with palms joined, listening to the sutra, his anger flared up and he intended to destroy the Buddha.
The wives admonished them, saying, "This is a divine being; do not harbor ill intentions.
They immediately repented their faults and prostrated themselves before the Buddha.
The Buddha again explained for them the blessings of refraining from killing and the transgressions of causing harm.
Upon this, their minds were opened; they knelt long and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We have grown up in the deep mountains, making our living through hunting. Our sins have accumulated; what dharma should we practice to escape these heavy calamities?"
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Practicing benevolence and exercising compassion, Loving all extensively to rescue the multitude— One will possess eleven forms of renown,
And blessings will constantly follow one’s person."
Protected by the gods with benevolence and love, one is not harmed by poison or weapons;
one does not perish by water or fire, gains profit wherever one goes, and upon death ascends to the Brahma Heaven—this is the eleventh.
After the Buddha had spoken these verses, one hundred and twenty-two people—men and women, both young and old—rejoiced with faith and acceptance, and all received and upheld the five precepts.
The Buddha said to King Bimbisāra:
"Grant them fields and bestow upon them grain and food."
"His benevolent transformation was vast and universal, and the kingdom was at peace.

In the past, there was a great king named Huo Mo who lived on the borders where he had not yet seen the holy and wondrous transformation of the Three Honored Ones. He served Brahmins, non-Buddhist practitioners, and sorcerers; the entire nation followed false paths, making it their constant practice to kill living beings for sacrifice."

At that time, the King’s mother fell ill with a wasting disease and was bedridden; she provided no medicinal decoctions for her physicians and sent female attendants to seek treatment everywhere, yet after years had passed, her condition remained unrelieved.
He further summoned two hundred brahmins from within the kingdom, invited them to enter and take their seats, provided them with food and drink, and addressed them, saying:
"My chief queen has been afflicted by illness for a long time; I do not know what cause has brought her to such a state."
"You all possess great wisdom and clearly understand the signs of phenomena, the heavens, and the constellations; why then do you not fully observe and inform us of what is happening?
The Brahmins replied, "It is simply because the constellations are disordered and the Yin and Yang are out of harmony that this has occurred."
The king asked,
"What remedy should be employed so that he may be cured?
The brāhmaṇa replied:

"You must level and purify a site outside the city and perform suburban sacrifices to the four mountains, the sun, the moon, and the constellations. You shall obtain one hundred head of livestock of various different species, as well as a young child, and slaughter them to sacrifice to the gods."
The king personally escorted his mother there, prostrating himself to beg for her life; only then would she be released.

The king immediately prepared everything as she had instructed, driving out a hundred heads of people, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep. As they followed the road, their mournful cries shook heaven and earth. They departed through the eastern gate, intending to go to the sacrificial altar to slaughter them as offerings to Heaven.

The World-Honored One, with great compassion, universally rescues all sentient beings; you should pity this king for being so exceedingly stubborn and ignorant—how can he give rise to evil by killing the lives of many to seek to save a single person?

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, leading his great assembly, proceeded toward that kingdom; at the eastern gate of the city, on the road, he encountered the king and a group of brahmins, whose draft animals were coming along while uttering mournful cries.

From afar the king saw the Buddha, like the sun first rising or the full moon at its peak; his radiant marks were brilliant, illuminating heaven and earth. Among the people, there was none who beheld him without love and reverence. As for the livestock he drove and the implements used for sacrifice, they all aspired to seek liberation.

The king immediately stepped forward, descended from his carriage, and set aside his parasol; he prostrated himself before the Buddha, joined his palms, knelt for a long time, and inquired after the World-Honored One’s well-being.
The Buddha bade him sit and asked where he intended to go.
With hands folded in reverence, he replied:

"The Great Lady of the state has been ill for a long time; we have sought out skilled physicians and divine spirits without exception. Now we wish to perform rites of expiation and thanksgiving toward the stars, the four mountains, and the five sacred peaks, praying for my mother’s life so that she may hope to recover."
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Listen well to these words.

If you wish to obtain grain and food, you must practice cultivation; if you wish to attain great wealth, you must practice giving; if you wish to attain long life, you must practice great compassion; if you wish to attain wisdom, you must practice study."
By performing these four deeds, one receives their fruit in accordance with what was sown.

Now, those of wealthy and noble families do not covet the food of the poor and lowly; the devas take the seven treasures as their palaces, where clothing and food appear spontaneously. How could they possibly abandon the meal of ambrosia to come and eat coarse and impure food?

To perform sacrifices through sexual licentiousness, taking what is perverse to be correct; to kill living beings in the hope of seeking life, thereby distancing oneself from the Way of Life—how can one who kills and harms the lives of many in an attempt to save a single person ever succeed? How could such a thing be possible?
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“If a person lives for a hundred years, Diligently serving the gods of the world,
And using elephants and horses for sacrifice, It is not equal to practicing a single act of loving-kindness.”

When the Buddha spoke these verses, he immediately emitted a brilliant light that illuminated heaven and earth; those in the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties were all filled with joy, each attaining their proper place.
King Huo-mo, hearing the exposition of the wondrous Dharma and beholding the radiance, was greatly delighted and immediately attained the fruit of the Path (srotāpanna).
The sick mother, having heard the Dharma, felt her five senses rejoice and her ailment was eliminated.
Two hundred brahmins, beholding the Buddha’s radiant marks and hearing his words once more, felt shame and remorse for their transgressions, and vowed to become his disciples.
The Buddha accepted them all, and they all became śramaṇas, each attaining his wish.
The king and his ministers invited the Buddha to receive offerings for one month before departing; they governed the kingdom with the Dharma, and it consequently flourished.
Chapter Eight: On Speech. *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*. Once, King Puṣya entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms; at the city gate, he was gored to death by a cow that had recently calved.
The owner of the ox was terrified and sold it, passing it on to another person.
When that man led the ox out intending to water it, the ox turned back and gored its new master to death.
The deceased had a son who, filled with rage, slaughtered the ox and sold its meat in the marketplace.

A man from a village purchased an ox-head and, carrying it on a pole, returned toward his home. After traveling some distance, he sat beneath a tree to rest; he hung the ox-head upon a branch, and after a short while, the rope snapped. The ox-head came down and fell directly onto the man; the horns pierced him, and he died instantly.
In a single day, he killed three people in total.

When King Bimbisāra heard of this, he marveled at such occurrences and immediately went with his ministers to the Buddha’s dwelling. Upon arrival, after performing his prostrations, he withdrew to his royal seat and, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How truly strange! This is most extraordinary!"
“World-Honored One!
A single cow has killed three people; will there be some portentous event?
We pray you will explain its meaning.”
The Buddha told King Bimbisāra:
"The retribution for offenses has its origins; it is not something that began only now.
The king said:
"I wish to hear the reason for this.
The Buddha said:

"In the past, there were three merchants who traveled to another country to seek their livelihood. They stayed in the house of a solitary old woman and were required to pay her rent. Seeing that the old woman was alone and destitute, they sought to deceive her and did not wish to give it; waiting until she was away, they departed in silence without paying the rent at all."
When the old woman returned home and did not see the merchant, she immediately questioned her neighbors, who told her that they had all already departed.
The old woman became enraged; she pursued him from behind, and after becoming exhausted, she finally caught up with him and demanded the payment for lodging.
The three merchants rebuked him in return, saying, "We have already given it to you previously; why do you ask for it again?
They all raised their voices together to refuse and were unwilling to pay the price.
The old woman, weak and helpless, could do nothing; in her distress, she uttered curses and oaths to the three merchants:
"I am now in dire straits; how can you bear to deceive and insult me?"

"I vow that in whatever place I am reborn in future lives, if I should encounter you, I must certainly kill you; even if you attain the Way, I shall never let you go. I will kill you and then rest; otherwise, I will not cease."
The Buddha said to King Bimbisāra:
"The old woman at that time was this very cow;
the three merchants were those three men, Puṣkarasārin and his companions, who were gored to death by the ox."
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Uttering evil words and insults, Arrogantly treating others with contempt— By giving rise to such conduct,
Swift resentment is born."
Humble speech and compliant words show respect for others; by abandoning resentment and enduring evil, hatred and enmity perish of themselves.
Now, the gentleman is born with an axe in his mouth; it is by means of his evil words that he cuts himself down.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, King Bimbisāra and all his officials were filled with profound reverence; they vowed to honor virtuous conduct, paid their respects, and departed.

Chapter Nine: The Twin Essentials (*Yuga-nidāna*). From the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Chapter Nine: The Twin Essentials. Formerly, the king of Śrāvastī was named Prasenajit. He came to the place where the Buddha was staying; he alighted from his carriage, set aside his parasol, unsheathed his sword, removed his shoes, and advanced straight forward with hands clasped in reverence. Prostrating himself fully upon the ground, he bowed his head to the Buddha’s feet and knelt for a long time, addressing the Buddha:
