“I wish to provide a modest meal at the crossroads tomorrow, desiring that the people of the nation may know the Buddha is most supreme. I pray that sentient beings may distance themselves from ghosts, demons, and sorcery, and that by all observing the five precepts, the calamities of the state may be extinguished.”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! As a ruler of a nation, one ought to provide enlightened guidance, leading the people through the Way to seek the blessings of future lives."
The King said, "Most Venerable One,
please withdraw while I prepare the offerings.
He personally prepared the meal and went in person to welcome the Buddha and the assembly of monks, meeting them together at the crossroads.
When the Buddha arrived and took his seat, [the king] immediately served water for washing and personally attended to the pouring of the meal.
Once the Buddha had finished eating, he preached the Dharma for the king at the crossroads; those who came to witness it were innumerable.
At that time, there were two merchants, one of whom thought to himself:

"The Buddha is like an emperor, and his disciples are like loyal ministers. The Buddha expounds the clear Dharma, and the disciples recite and proclaim it; thus the King is illustrious. Knowing that the Buddha is worthy of veneration, one should humble one's will to serve him."
One person thought to himself:
"How foolish this king is!
Being a king, what more could he possibly seek?"

The Buddha is like an ox and his disciples are like a cart; that ox pulls the cart east, west, south, and north, and the Buddha is likewise. What path do you possess such that you humble yourself to serve him?
The two men went together for thirty *li* and stayed overnight at an inn, where they bought wine and drank together while discussing their respective affairs.

The one with virtuous thoughts was protected by the Four Heavenly Kings, but the one with evil thoughts was targeted by the spirits of Mount Tai. These spirits caused the wine to burn his body like fire once it entered his belly; he left the inn and lay down by the road, twisting in the ruts of the carriage tracks, where in the morning he was run over and killed by five hundred merchant carts.
The companion sought him the following day and found it as he had said:
"Upon returning to my country, I was suspected of having killed someone and taken their property.
Disregarding his own life on account of what was not righteous, he abandoned his wealth and departed.
The king of another country had passed away, but he had no heir apparent. A prophetic book stated:
"A humble person from the central land shall rule this territory.
Consequently, the king possessed a divine horse that would surely kneel before whoever was destined to be king.
He immediately prepared his carriage with divine horses, seals, and ribbons, setting out to seek the ruler of the land; thousands flocked to watch him.
The merchants also came forth, and the Grand Astrologer of the state said:
"That man is shaded by a canopy of yellow clouds; this is the vital energy of a king."

The divine horse knelt down and licked the merchant’s feet; the ministers prepared fragrant water for him to bathe in and installed him as king, whereupon he took up his station and attended to the affairs of state.
He reflected deeply within himself, saying:
"I possess not even a trace of merit; by what cause have I obtained this?
It must surely be the Buddha's grace that has brought it about."
Thereupon, together with his ministers, he headed toward Śrāvastī and bowed his head from afar, saying:

"I am a lowly man devoid of virtue; having received the compassionate grace of the World-Honored One, I have become king of this country. I pray that tomorrow you and the assembly of Arhats will deign to turn your attention toward this place for a period of three months."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Instruct all the bhikṣus that tomorrow, at the king's invitation, they shall all manifest miraculous transformations so as to bring joy to that king and his people."

Each performed a feat of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and traveled to that kingdom; they all took their seats one after another in solemn accordance with the Dharma, and when the meal was finished and they had washed their hands, they preached the Dharma for the king.
The King said, "I was originally a man of humble station and have never possessed superior virtue; by what cause have I obtained this?
The Buddha told the King:
"Formerly, when that great king provided a meal for the Buddha at the crossroads, he thought to himself:
'The Buddha is like a king, and his disciples are like his subjects.
Having planted this seed, he now reaps the fruit himself."
Another person later said:
"The Buddha is like an ox, and his disciples are like a cart.
That person himself sowed the seeds of being crushed by a cart; he now dwells in the Mount Tai hell, being crushed by a fire-cart.

One obtains its fruit for oneself; however, this is not something that even a king’s prowess can bring about. When one does good, blessings follow; when one does evil, calamity pursues. This is what one has created oneself; it is not something that devas, nāgas, or spirits can bestow upon another.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The mind is the root of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign, the mind is the driver. If one harbors evil thoughts within the mind, they immediately manifest in speech and action.
Suffering follows as a consequence of one's transgressions, just as a wheel follows the ruts of its tracks."
The mind is the foundation of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign and the mind is the driver.
When one dwells upon wholesome thoughts within the mind, they immediately manifest in speech and action; thus, happiness and merit follow of their own accord, like a shadow following a form.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these verses of the sutra, the king, his ministers, and the common people—countless listeners—all rejoiced greatly and attained the Dharma-eye.

Formerly, the elder Sudatta purchased the prince’s garden and land to build a vihara together to offer to the World-Honored One; each invited the Buddha and the Sangha for a month of offerings. The Buddha extensively expounded the clear Dharma for the two men, and they both attained the fruits of the Path.
Prince Jeta returned to the Eastern Palace in great joy, praising the Buddha’s virtues and amusing himself with music.

Prince Vairāṭī, the younger brother of Jeta, was always by the King’s side. On this occasion, the King, dressed in plain garments, went together with his close ministers and the ladies of the harem to the place where the Buddha was. Having prostrated themselves in worship, they listened to the sutra with single-minded devotion, while Vairāṭī remained behind to guard the royal throne.
At that time, the sycophantic ministers, Asaṭha and others, presented a wicked scheme, saying:
"Let us try on the Great King’s seal and insignia and sit upon the royal throne; would we not appear like the King?"
Thereupon, Virūḍhaka followed those words; having donned his robes and ascended the throne, the sycophantic ministers all bowed together in congratulation, saying:
"He truly resembles the Great King!"
"To encounter this once in a thousand years is the long-cherished wish of the common people; how could we allow the Crown Prince to be excluded from this?
How could one ascend this imperial throne and then descend from it again?"

He immediately led his followers, donned his armor, and drew his sword, proceeding in person to the Jetavana Monastery. He expelled the Great King, preventing him from returning to the palace, and fought with the king’s officials and retainers within the grounds of the Jetavana, killing more than five hundred of the king’s close attendants.

The King and his consort fled in haste, traveling day and night until they reached the kingdom of Śākyas. On the way, they were overcome by hunger; the King ate radishes and died from abdominal distension.
Thereupon, Virūḍhaka assumed sole control of power; he drew his sword and entered the Eastern Palace, where he slew his elder brother Ghaṭīkāra.

Knowing only impermanence, his mind felt no dread and his countenance did not change; with a smile and a joyful expression, he welcomed the blade with a willing heart. Before his life had even ceased, he heard the sound of celestial music spontaneously arising from the void to welcome his spirit.
At the Jeta Grove, the Buddha spoke this verse:
"Creating joy brings joy later; practicing goodness brings joy in both worlds. That joy is indeed delight;
seeing merit, the mind is at peace."
"Joy now and joy hereafter—doing good brings joy in both places. This constitutes one's own protection; one shall receive blessings and rejoice.

At that time, King Virūḍhaka immediately raised an army to attack the Śākya kingdom, slaughtering the Śākyas who were followers of the Path. He was cruel and unprincipled, committing all five heinous crimes.

The Buddha prophesied that Virūḍhaka was unfilial and disloyal, and that his grave offenses were so heavy that in seven days he would be burned to death by the fires of hell; furthermore, the records of the Grand Astrologer matched the Buddha’s account exactly.
The king was struck with great terror and immediately boarded a boat to enter the river, thinking, "Now that I am situated within the water, how could fire come here?

At noon on the seventh day, a spontaneous fire emerged from the water, burning the boat until it capsized and sank; the king was also burned, and overcome by the poisonous heat of his terror, he suddenly drowned and died.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Creating sorrow brings sorrow later; practicing evil brings sorrow in both ways. That person is filled with anxiety and fear, their heart trembling as they behold their transgressions."
"Regret now and regret later; to do evil is to regret twice. This brings about one's own calamity, and one shall receive the retribution of feverish affliction.
Having spoken thus, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"As for Prince Jeta, he did not covet glory or rank, but remained faithful to the Way even unto death; he has been reborn in the heavens, where his peace and joy are spontaneous."
King Vaidūrya was mad, foolish, and indulged in his whims; upon death, he fell into hell and suffered immeasurable pain.
Whether one is noble and wealthy or poor and lowly in this world, all return to impermanence; nothing endures forever.
"For this reason, high-minded gentlemen sacrifice their lives to preserve their conduct, regarding it as a treasure for the spirit.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, there was none who did not believe and accept them.

Formerly, behind Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, there were more than seventy households of Brahmins whose past merits made them ready for deliverance. When the Buddha arrived at their village and manifested the divine transformations of the Way, all who beheld the Buddha’s majestic and towering radiance were filled with reverence and submission.
The Buddha sat beneath a tree and asked the brahmins,
"For how many generations have you resided in these mountains?
What means of livelihood do you employ to support yourselves?"
He replied, "For more than thirty lifetimes since I first lived here, I have made my livelihood through agriculture and animal husbandry.
He asked again:
"What practices should one cultivate to seek liberation from birth and death? He replied:
"One should serve the sun, moon, water, and fire, performing sacrifices according to the seasons."
"If there are those who die, they gather in large or small assemblies and proclaim that they have been born into the Brahma Heaven to escape birth and death.
The Buddha said to the brahmins:

"Now, as for farming, raising livestock, performing sacrifices to the sun and moon, water and fire, or crying out to be born in heaven—these are not the methods for eternal existence or for escaping birth and death."
The ultimate merit does not exceed that of the twenty-eight heavens; yet without the wisdom of the Path, one will fall back into the three miserable realms.
Only by leaving the household life to cultivate pure resolve and practicing the meaning of tranquility can one attain Nirvana.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"To take the true for the false, And to take the false for the true— This is a perverse calculation,
By which one does not obtain the true benefit."
To know the true as true and to see the false as false is the correct calculation; one will surely obtain true benefit.
All in the world must die, and there is no peace within the three realms; though the heavens are pleasant, even they are lost when merit is exhausted.
"Observe all the worlds: there is none that does not end in death. If you wish to leave behind birth and death, you must practice the True Path.
When the seventy brahmins heard what the Buddha had said, their minds were joyfully liberated, and they vowed to become śramaṇas.
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, bhikṣus! Their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, and they all became śramaṇas.

The Buddha returned to the vihāra together with the bhikṣus; while on the way, he looked back with longing for his wife and children, each harboring thoughts of retreat. At that time, they encountered rain, which only served to increase their sorrow and distress.
The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, manifested several dozen huts by the side of the road. He entered one to take shelter from the rain, but the hut leaked.
Because of the leaking hut, the Buddha spoke this verse:
"If a roof is not sealed tight, When it rains from heaven, it leaks; If the mind does not contemplate its conduct,"
Lust is like a hole in a roof;
if the covering is well-sealed, rain will not leak through. By restraining the mind and practicing accordingly, lustful secrecy will not arise.
When the seventy śramaṇas heard this verse, although they forced themselves forward, they still harbored a sense of bewilderment; when the rain ceased, they proceeded further.
Seeing some old paper on the ground, the Buddha told the bhikṣus to pick it up; having received his instruction, they immediately took it.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"What kind of paper do you consider it?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
"The incense paper within this bundle remains fragrant as before, even though it has now been discarded.
The Buddha proceeded further, where there was a broken cord on the ground; the Buddha told the bhikṣu to take it, and having received the instruction, he immediately took it.
The Buddha asked again,
"What kind of cord is this?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
"That rope has a foul odor; it is the rope used for tying fish.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"All things are fundamentally pure; it is solely through causes and conditions that demerit and merit arise. By associating with the worthy and wise, the Way and its principles flourish; by befriending the foolish and ignorant, calamity and transgression arrive."
"It is like that paper rope: if it is near fragrance, it becomes fragrant; if it binds fish, it becomes fishy. Through gradual staining and habitual practice, each remains unaware.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The base person stains others, Just like being near a foul object; Gradually deluded by practicing what is wrong,"
Unaware, one becomes evil;
when a virtuous person associates with others, it is like being perfumed by incense. By advancing in wisdom and practicing goodness, one’s conduct becomes fragrant and pure.
Upon hearing this verse for a second time, the seventy śramaṇas realized that household desires are a thicket of filth and that wives and children are shackles; their faith became firm and steadfast.
They went to the vihāra, restrained their minds, and practiced meditation, thereby attaining the path of arhatship.

Chapter Ten: On Heedlessness (*Pramāda-varga*). *The Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Chapter Ten: On Heedlessness. Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, there were five hundred merchants who had emerged from the sea. Carrying a great quantity of the seven treasures, they were returning to their own country. As they passed through a deep mountain range, they were led astray by malevolent spirits and could not find their way out. Their provisions were exhausted, and being utterly weary and distressed, they all died of starvation; the precious goods they had brought were scattered throughout the mountains.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa studying in the mountains who, seeing this, gave rise to this thought:
"I have diligently practiced the Way for seven years already, yet I have not attained the Way; moreover, I am poor and destitute, with no means to sustain myself."
"These treasures have no owner; let us take them back and use them to establish our households.
Thereupon, he descended the mountain to gather the treasures, and having hidden them in one place, he left the mountain to call his brothers to carry them back home.

When they had reached the midpoint of their journey, the Buddha thought that these bhikṣus should be delivered; he then transformed himself into a bhikṣuṇī with a shaved head and dharma robes, yet adorned with powdered face, painted brows, and gold and silver necklaces, as she followed the valley into the mountains.
On the road she encountered a śramaṇa; she bowed her head to the ground in salutation and inquired after his well-being.
The practitioner rebuked the bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Is this the proper way for one who practices the Path?"
“Having shaved your head and donned the dharma robes, why do you further apply face powder, paint your eyebrows,
and adorn your body with necklaces? The bhikṣuṇī replied,
“Is this how the Dharma of the śramaṇas ought to be?”
Having bid farewell to your kin to study the Way and dwell in the mountains with a tranquil mind, how can you again take what is not rightfully yours?

To greedily forget the Way and indulge your desires and impulses—failing to reckon with impermanence and that life in this world is like a temporary lodging—will result in the prolongation of karmic retribution.
Thereupon, the bhikṣuṇī spoke these verses for him:
“The bhikṣu who is heedful in the precepts Is free from the many sorrows of negligence;
But strife, though small at first, leads to the great, And the accumulation of evil brings one to be consumed by fire.”
"Those who guard the precepts bring forth joy through their merit; those who violate them harbor fear.
One who can sever the outflows (*āsrava*) of the triple world—this one draws near to *nirvāṇa*.
When the bhikṣuṇī had spoken this verse, she manifested for them the Buddha’s physical marks, signs, and radiance.
Upon seeing this, the śramaṇa was struck with such terror that his hair stood on end; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, repented, and confessed:
“In my folly and delusion, I have transgressed the True Teaching; having gone astray and failed to return, what shall I do?”
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one was formerly heedless, but later is able to restrain oneself, This person illuminates the world;
mindfulness and concentration are appropriate for them."
When one covers over faults with evil, it is like darkness; when one covers over faults with goodness, it illuminates the world—therefore, it is fitting to mind what is good.
To leave the home life in youth and vigor and diligently cultivate the Buddha’s teachings illuminates the world, like the moon when the clouds have vanished.
"To commit evil before others, yet afterwards to cease and refrain from it—this illuminates the world like the moon when the clouds have vanished.

Thereupon, the bhikṣu, having heard this verse again, untied his bonds, ceased his greed, and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet. Returning to the foot of a tree, he practiced counting the breaths and following them, through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* returning to purity; he attained the fruits of the Path and realized the state of an Arhat.

Chapter Eleven: The Mind and Heart. *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Chapter Eleven: The Mind and Heart. Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a practitioner who dwelt under a tree by a river to study the Way. For twelve years, his greedy thoughts were not eliminated; his mind ran wild and his thoughts were scattered as he contemplated only the six desires: forms for the eyes, sounds for the ears, fragrances for the nose, flavors for the tongue, tangibles for the body, and mental phenomena for the mind. When the water dog moved slightly away, the tortoise again extended its head and feet and walked as before; the dog could do nothing to it and was thus able to escape.

The transformed śramaṇa replied: "I observe that people of the world are not like this tortoise; unaware of impermanence, they indulge their six sense-faculties. At that time, there was a brahmin in the city who was nearly eighty years old and possessed immeasurable wealth. At that time, the brahmin was constantly managing and directing various affairs himself. Possessing brilliant natural talent, he soon surpassed his teacher in every task. Having given away all he possessed, he took leave of his teacher and departed.

He traveled throughout the world, visiting all sixteen great kingdoms; when he challenged opponents to test their skills, no one dared to respond to his solitary words or single steps. In his heart, he became arrogant and said:
"Within heaven and earth, who is there that can surpass me?"

The Buddha, staying at the Jetavana, saw from afar that this man was ready to be converted; by means of his supernormal powers, he transformed himself into a śramaṇa and approached him, carrying a staff and holding an alms bowl.
The brahmin thought, "In this country, there has long been no path of the Dharma; I have never seen such śramaṇas. What kind of person is this?
I must wait until he arrives to ask.
After a short while, the man arrived, and the brahmin asked him:

"Among the models of a hundred sovereigns, we have never seen your kind; among the regulations for robes and garments, there is no such attire as this. Among the various objects used in the ancestral temple, we have never seen such a vessel. Who are you, that your appearance and clothing deviate so from the norm?"
The śramaṇa replied,
“I am one who disciplines the body.
He asked again:
“What is meant by ‘disciplining the body’?
Thereupon, the śramaṇa spoke these verses according to what [the king] had practiced:
“The bow-maker disciplines the horn; the boatman disciplines the boat; the skilled carpenter disciplines the wood.”
The wise person disciplines the body;
like a massive rock, the wind cannot move it. The mind of the wise is heavy; they are not swayed by praise or blame.
"Just as a deep abyss is tranquil, still, and clear, so too does the wise person, upon hearing the Way, become pure of heart and filled with joy.

When the śramaṇa had spoken this verse, his body ascended into the void and transformed back into the form of the Buddha, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. His radiance penetrated everywhere, illuminating heaven and earth. Descending from the void, he said to the man:
"My transformation through the power of the Way and my virtue is the result of the strength of bodily cultivation."
Thereupon, that man prostrated himself on the ground with his five limbs and, bowing his head, asked:
"I wish to hear about the disciplining of the body; is there a key method for it?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
“The five precepts and ten wholesome acts, the four immeasurables and six perfections, the four dhyānas and three liberations—these are the methods for disciplining the body.

As for archery, navigation, carpentry, the six arts, and extraordinary skills, these are all matters of ornate adornment and hollow reputation; they are paths that dissipate the body and indulge the will, leading further into the cycle of birth and death.”
Upon hearing this, the brahmin was filled with joy and, having gained faith and understanding, wished to become a disciple.
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, śramaṇa!"
His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
The Buddha again expounded for him the essentials of the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Emancipation; at that very moment, he attained the path of Arhatship.

In the past, when the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a mountain village of fifty or sixty households located five hundred *li* from the capital. In that village lived a poor family; the wife of the head of the household became pregnant for ten months and gave birth to twin boys. They were exceptionally handsome and peerless, and their parents, out of love for them, gave them names: the first was named Śubhadatta (Double Virtue) and the second was named Puṇyadatta (Double Fortune).

When they were fifty or sixty days old, their father returned from tending cattle; exhausted, he lay down to rest upon his bed. Their mother had gone out to the fields to gather firewood and had not yet returned. Seeing neither parent as they looked around, the two young children began to reproach one another.
He said to one person:

"In a previous life, I was on the verge of attaining the Way, yet because of my foolish mind, I believed that life is permanent. Consequently, I fell back into the cycle of birth and death for incalculable kalpas. Now I have been born as a son in this poor family; covered only by felt and coarse cloth amidst piles of straw, my food and drink are so coarse and vile that they barely sustain my body. Having remained in such a state for so long, how could I ever attain the Way?"

All of you, because in previous lives you were attached to wealth and honor, indulging yourselves and letting your minds wander for a fleeting moment of pleasure, have since then suffered upon this long road. Now, in the midst of such grief and affliction, what can you rely upon?
One person replied:

"At that time, I was slightly negligent for a single moment and failed to apply myself with diligence; consequently, I have had to endure various sufferings and afflictions for many lifetimes. This was my own doing and not something done by my parents; we must simply share this burden together—what more is there to say?"

When the father heard his two sons rebuking one another in this manner, he was greatly astonished and thought: "Is this some malevolent spirit that has come to cause calamity? How could infants of only several days old speak such words?"
Fearing that he might later kill his parents and exterminate his clan, Manxiang thought, "He is still small and not yet grown; it is best to kill him now.
His father, startled, came out, closed the door, and fled. Arriving at the fields, he gathered firewood, intending to burn him to death.
When his mother returned, she asked her husband, "What are you doing with this firewood?

Her husband replied, "It is truly most strange that what he says is like this; he seems to be a ghost who will surely destroy our family line. Because he is so small and long-limbed, I wish to burn him to death."
When the mother heard this, she was struck with astonishment in her heart; hesitant and lacking full conviction, she waited for several days to listen further to their words.

On the following day, the husband and wife both went outside and secretly overheard the two children inside reproaching one another as before. Hearing it again together, they were greatly perplexed by the reason for this and immediately gathered firewood, intending to burn them in secret.

With his divine eye, the Buddha saw that this couple intended to burn their two children to death. Moved by compassion for their pitiable state and knowing they were destined for deliverance due to their past merit, he went to their village and radiated light everywhere. Heaven and earth shook violently, and the mountains, rivers, trees, and forests all turned the color of gold.

The villagers, both young and old, came in alarm to where the Buddha was; they prostrated themselves before him and were all filled with joy, realizing that the Buddha’s spiritual power was supreme and beyond compare within the three realms.

When the Buddha arrived at the home of the twin infants, the two children saw the Buddha’s radiance and leaped for joy beyond measure. Their parents were also struck with alarm; each took one child and brought them to where the Buddha was. They asked the World-Honored One:

"These children have been born for only fifty or sixty days, yet what they say is like this. We find it most extraordinary and fear they will bring calamity, so we wished to burn them to death with fire. It happened that the Buddha arrived just as we were about to do so."
"I do not know what kind of ghost or demon this child is;
I only pray that you will explain what calamity or strange apparition he is.
Upon seeing the Buddha, the child leaped for joy; the Buddha, seeing the child, laughed aloud, and from his mouth issued five-colored light that shone everywhere throughout heaven and earth.
The Buddha addressed the parents of the two children and the villagers, both great and small: "These two children are not demons; they are sons of merit.

In the time of the previous Kāśyapa Buddha, they were once śramaṇas and were childhood friends. With the same aspiration, they left the household life and each applied themselves with diligence. As they were about to attain the Way, they suddenly gave rise to perverse thoughts and undermined one another. Delighting in worldly glory and relying on their merit to be reborn in heaven, they subsequently became nobles, kings, national rulers, or elders. Having suddenly given rise to these thoughts, they fell into regression and failed to attain nirvāṇa."
Through successive births and deaths, for many kalpas, we have always been bound together and born as twins.
It is only now that we have been born during my era.

Because of the merit from having made offerings to Buddhas in the past, the remaining blessings should now deliver us; our transgressions are extinguished and our fortune has arisen. We ourselves recognize our past lives; therefore, the World-Honored One has come specifically to deliver us. Had I not delivered them, they would have been pointlessly burned by fire.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The body of a Great Man is free from desire; Wherever he is, he shines with radiant clarity.
Though he may encounter suffering or joy, He does not manifest his wisdom through elation."
The great sage has no concern for worldly affairs; he does not desire sons, wealth, or a kingdom.
He constantly maintains the path of precepts and wisdom, never coveting perverse riches or honor.
The wise man knows that instability is like a tree in the sand.
"The friend's will is not yet firm; it follows the colors that dye its plainness.
When the Buddha spoke these words, the child saw the Buddha and his body immediately leaped up, appearing like an eight-year-old boy. He then became a śrāmaṇera and attained the path of an arhat.

The villagers, both old and young, beheld the Buddha’s radiant countenance; they also saw the child’s form transform and leap to a great size. All were filled with immense joy and attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. Their parents’ doubts were resolved, and they too attained the Dharma-eye.

Chapter Fifteen: The Arhats. *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Chapter Fifteen on the Arhats. Long ago, there was a country named Nāli, situated near the shores of the South Sea; its inhabitants made it their regular occupation to gather pearls and sandalwood.

In that country, there was a family consisting of two brothers whose parents had passed away; they wished to divide their inheritance. In the household, there was a slave named Bhāṇḍaka who was young and intelligent, skilled in trade, commerce, and buying and selling, and there was nothing he did not know regarding making a living at sea. The family property was divided into one share, while the slave Bhāṇḍaka constituted the other share. The brothers cast lots, and the younger brother won Bhāṇḍaka; consequently, the elder brother departed from the house with only his wife and children, leaving his hands empty.
At that time, there was a famine in the world, and he received only a portion of the rice; fearing they would not survive together, he became filled with anxiety.
Then the slave Pūrṇa said to his master:
"Please do not worry; Pūrṇa has devised a plan by which, within a few months, I shall surpass my elder brother."
The mistress said, "If you can truly do this, I shall release you to be a free person.
The mistress had some private pearls and goods, which she gave to Panṇaka as his capital.
At that time, the tide came in, and the people within the city went to the water’s edge to gather firewood.

Pūrṇa, carrying his jewels and goods, went outside the city and saw a beggar carrying a load of wood. Within the wood was ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣacandana*), which could cure serious illnesses; one *liang* of it was worth a thousand *liang* of gold, and such as this appears only once in an age and cannot be found constantly.
He divided that consciousness and purchased it for two gold coins, bringing it back home where he broke it into several dozen pieces.
At that time, there was an elder who fell gravely ill and required two *liang* of this ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣa-candana*) to compound his medicine, yet despite searching, he could not obtain it.
Bhadraka took it and sold it, immediately obtaining two thousand taels of gold.
He continued selling his possessions until they were all exhausted; the wealth he acquired was beyond measure, making him ten times richer than his elder brother.
The master of the house, moved by Bhadraka’s kindness, did not go back on his word and released him as a free man, allowing him to live according to his own pleasure.
Thereupon, Punna took his leave to study the Way. Arriving in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, he prostrated before the Buddha, knelt for a long time, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am of humble and lowly origin, yet my heart delights in the Way and its virtue; I only pray that the World-Honored One will bestow compassion upon me and deliver me."
The Buddha said, "Welcome, Pūrṇa!
His hair fell off of its own accord and the dharma robes clothed his body; he immediately became a śramaṇa. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he soon attained the path of an arhat.
Sitting in meditation, he thought to himself:

"Now that I have attained the six supernormal powers and can move freely between life and death, all is due to the kindness of my master; I must now go to deliver him and transform the people of the country."

At that time, Pūrṇa returned to his native land and went to the house of his host. The host was delighted and invited him to sit and provided him with food. Having finished eating and washed his hands, he ascended into the void; he manifested his body by dividing it and dispersing its parts, emitting water and fire from his half-body, his radiance penetrating everywhere.

Descending from above, he addressed the host, saying: "This divine power is all due to the merit of your generosity in providing me with sustenance; such is what is learned upon reaching the presence of the Buddha."
The host replied, "The Buddha’s divine transformations are so subtle and wondrous; I wish to see the World-Honored One and receive his instruction. Pūrṇa replied:
"Simply set your mind on providing the offerings with a sincere heart; the Buddha, possessing the three types of transcendent knowledge, will surely come of his own accord.
Thereupon, they prepared the offerings overnight until they were complete, then prostrated themselves toward Śrāvastī, knelt for a long time, and burned incense to invite the Buddha, saying:
"We only pray that you will deign to humble yourself and extensively deliver all beings."
The Buddha, knowing his intention, immediately accompanied five hundred arhats, each traveling by means of their supernatural powers to that house.

The king and the people were all filled with reverent solemnity; they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves on the ground with their five limbs touching the earth, and withdrew to sit upon the royal throne. When the meal was finished and they had washed their hands, the Buddha extensively expounded the clear Dharma for the host, the king, and the royal officials; they all received the five precepts and became disciples of the Buddha.
Rising before the Buddha, he praised Pūrṇa, saying:

"While at home he was diligent, and having left the household life, he has attained the Way. His spiritual virtue is lofty and far-reaching, and both his family and the nation have received his deliverance. How should I repay his kindness?"
Thereupon, the World-Honored One further praised Pūrṇa and spoke these verses:
"The mind has come to rest, And speech and action have also ceased; Through right liberation, He has returned to extinction in profound stillness."
Having abandoned desire and being without attachment, with the obstacles of the three realms shattered and worldly aspirations utterly severed—such a person is called a superior man.
Whether in a village or the wilds, on level ground or high embankments, wherever the Arhat passes, there are none who do not receive his deliverance.
"He delights in solitude, which others cannot; how joyful it is to be without expectations and to have no desires to seek!
When the Buddha had finished speaking these verses, the host and the king were filled with even greater joy; they made offerings for seven days and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

Chapter Sixteen: Narrating the Thousandfold Chapter from the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*. Formerly, when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was an elder bhikṣu named Paṇḍaka. Having newly entered the monastic order, he was by nature dull-witted and obstructed. The Buddha ordered five hundred arhats to instruct him daily; yet for three years, he could not master even a single verse. Consequently, the fourfold assembly throughout the kingdom all recognized his ignorance and obscurity.

The Buddha took pity on him and immediately called him forward, bestowing upon him a verse: "Guard the mouth, restrain the mind, and let the body commit no transgression; one who practices in this way shall attain deliverance from the world."
At that time, Pāṇṭaka, moved by the Buddha’s compassionate grace, felt his heart open with joy and recited the verse fluently.
The Buddha said to him, "You are now old, yet you have only just mastered a single verse; it is known by all people and is not worth marveling at."
"I shall now explain its meaning for you; listen with single-minded attention.

Paṇḍita received the instruction and listened as the Buddha explained for him the origins of the three actions of body, four of speech, and three of mind. He observed their arising and examined their cessation, showing how beings revolve incessantly through the three realms and five destinies. "By these one ascends to heaven; by these one falls into the abyss; by these one attains the Way and the natural state of Nirvana. Thus he analyzed and expounded upon immeasurable sublime dharmas.
At that time, Pāṇṭaka’s mind suddenly opened and he immediately attained the path of an Arhat.
At that time, there were five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who had a separate vihāra; the Buddha would daily dispatch a bhikṣu to preach the Dharma to them, saying, "Tomorrow it is Pāṇṭaka’s turn to go."
When the nuns heard this, they all smiled with suppressed mirth,
saying, "If he comes tomorrow, we shall join together to counter his verses, leaving him so ashamed that he will not utter a single word."

The next day, when Paṇḍaka went there, all the bhikṣuṇīs, both senior and junior, came out to pay their respects; they looked at one another and smiled. Once they were seated, food was served. After they had finished eating and washed their hands, he was invited to preach the Dharma.
Then Pāṇḍaka ascended the high seat and, feeling self-reproach, said:

"I am one of meager virtue and inferior talent who has recently become a śramaṇa; being naturally dull-witted, I have studied little. I know but a single verse and have a rough understanding of its meaning; I shall now expound it for you, so please listen with quiet minds."
The young bhikṣuṇīs, wishing to respond with verses, were unable to open their mouths; struck with fear and self-reproach, they prostrated themselves to repent their errors.

Puṇṇa then, according to what the Buddha had taught, analyzed in detail the origins of the body and mind, the internal and external aspects of demerit and merit, and the methods for ascending to heaven, attaining the Way, concentrating the spirit, severing discursive thought, and entering meditative absorption.
Immediately, when the bhikṣuṇīs heard what he had said, they were struck with great wonder and marvel; with single-minded joy, they all attained the path of arhatship.

On a later day, King Prasenajit invited the Buddha and the assembly of monks to a gathering in the main palace hall. Desiring to manifest the majestic spiritual power of Pāṇṭaka, the Buddha gave him his almsbowl and had him follow behind him as he walked.
The gatekeeper recognized him and detained him, refusing to let him enter:
"If you, a śramaṇa, cannot even understand a single verse, what is the point of accepting an invitation?
I am but a layman and yet I know verses; how much more so for a śramaṇa who possesses no wisdom? To give to you would be of no benefit; there is no need to enter the gate."
At that time, Pāṇṭaka stood outside the gate.
After the Buddha had sat in the main hall and finished washing his hands, Pāṇṭaka held up his bowl, extended his arm, and offered it from afar to the Buddha.

The king, along with his ministers, the queen, the crown prince, and the fourfold assembly, saw the arm enter but could not see its form; marveling at this, they asked the Buddha, "Whose arm is this?"
The Buddha said, "This is the arm of the bhikṣu Paṇḍita; he has recently attained the Way.
Previously, when I sent him to carry my bowl, the gatekeeper would not allow him to enter, so he extended his arm to hand me the bowl."
He immediately invited him inside, whereupon [Panthaka’s] majestic spiritual power was twice his usual.
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have heard that Panthaka was by nature dull-witted and only recently learned a single verse; by what cause has he attained the Way?"
The Buddha told the king:
"Learning need not be extensive; practice is what is supreme.
Paṇḍita understood the meaning of a single verse, its refined principles penetrating to the divine; his body, speech, and mind were as tranquil and pure as celestial gold."
"Though a person may study much, if they do not understand or practice, they merely waste their consciousness and perceptions; what benefit is there in that?
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Though one recites a thousand chapters, If the meaning of the phrases is not correct, It is not as good as a single essential point."
Hearing can extinguish evil.
Though one may recite a thousand words, what benefit is there if they are not righteous?
It is better than a single principle; by hearing and practicing it, one may cross over to liberation.
"What benefit is there in reciting many sutras if one does not understand them?
To understand even a single verse of Dharma and practice it, one may attain the Way.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this verse, three hundred bhikṣus attained the path of Arhatship; the king, his ministers, the queen, and the crown prince were all filled with joy.
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the monastery at Śrāvastī, he was preaching the Dharma for the sake of devas and humans.
At that time, there was in Śrāvastī a brahmin elder named Lambada, who was immensely wealthy; his family’s assets were beyond counting.

According to the dharma of the brahmins, one should construct a great altar to manifest one’s reputation; exhausting the family’s wealth, they used it for almsgiving to perform a *pañcavārṣika* festival, providing for more than five thousand brahmins over the course of five years with clothing, bedding, seats, medicine, rare treasures, and sacrificial implements, giving up everything they cherished.

For five years, these various brahmins, on behalf of the elder Rāmadatta, performed sacrifices to the heavens, the four mountains, the five sacred peaks, the constellations, water, and fire, leaving nothing undone; they offered incantations and prayers that the elder might receive blessings throughout the long night.

When the five years had fully elapsed, on the final day he performed a most magnificent act of giving according to the custom of a great householder: golden bowls filled with silver grain and silver bowls filled with golden grain; elephants, horses, chariots, slaves, and wealth; ornaments of the seven jewels, parasols, canopies, and sandals; deer-skin garments, mendicant’s staffs, couches, water-pitchers, and basins; beds, stools, mats, and cushions—whatever was appropriate to obtain, eighty-four thousand items of each kind, he gave away entirely as alms.

On that day, they all gathered for a great assembly; spirits, ghosts, kings, ministers, brahmins, and those of noble lineage all came and took their seats, the crowd so vast and the clamor so great that there was not one who did not rejoice.
The Buddha, seeing this, sighed and said:
"How can this brahmin of noble lineage be so foolish?
His offerings are vast, yet his karmic reward is meager; it is like sowing seeds in fire—how could one expect a harvest?"
"If I do not transform them, they will remain forever estranged from the Dharma-gate.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One rose and adjusted his robes; he manifested a transformation that emerged from the earth, emitting a great radiance that shone universally upon the assembly. When those of both small and great capacity saw this, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, struck with awe and trembling, not knowing what deity it was.
The elder Ramadatta and the great assembly prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground to pay homage to the Buddha.
Seeing that all the people possessed hearts of reverence, and because of their solemnity, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"One might offer sacrifices a thousand times a month, Never ceasing throughout one's entire life; Yet this is not equal to [offering] for even a moment..."

To mind the Dharma with single-mindedness and to perform a single act of merit surpasses that which one might do throughout an entire lifetime—though one were to spend a hundred years serving the fire god;
it is not equal to a brief moment of making offerings to the Triple Gem. A single act of offering brings merit that surpasses that of a hundred years.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Randa, saying:
"There are four matters regarding giving. What are these four?"
First, giving much but receiving little merit; second, giving little but receiving much merit; third, giving much and receiving much merit; fourth, giving little and receiving little merit.
What is meant by giving much yet receiving little in karmic reward?
It refers to one who, out of folly, slaughters living beings for sacrificial offerings, indulges in wine, song, and dance, and squanders wealth and treasures, possessing neither merit nor wisdom.
What is meant by giving little and receiving little in return?
It is when one gives to an ordinary practitioner with a stingy and malicious mind; since both parties are ignorant, there is no merit.
What is meant by giving little and receiving great merit?

If one can serve a person of virtue with a compassionate heart, and that practitioner, having eaten, applies themselves with diligence to study and recitation, then although the gift is small, its merit is exceedingly great.
What is meant by "giving much and receiving much merit"?

If there is a worthy person who perceives the impermanence of the world and, with a benevolent heart, provides wealth to establish stupas, temples, monasteries, and fruit orchards, and makes offerings to the Triple Gem of robes, sandals, beds, and food, this merit is like the five rivers flowing into the great ocean; such a flow of merit continues uninterrupted from generation to generation. Thus, the more one gives, the greater the retribution becomes, just as farmers obtain different yields depending on whether their land is fertile or poor.

At that time, the people gathered in the assembly hall of the elder Randa, seeing the Buddha’s miraculous transformations and hearing his words of Dharma, were all filled with great joy. All the devas, humans, and spirits attained the stage of Srotāpanna;
five thousand brahmins all became śramaṇas and attained the path of Arhatship;
and all members of the host, the elder Randa’s household, both great and small, received the five precepts and likewise attained the traces of the Path.
The king and his ministers all received the three refuges and became upāsakas; they also attained the Dharma-eye.

Formerly, while the Buddha was teaching at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī, there was a man in the kingdom of Rājagṛha who was cruel and foolish, unfilial toward his parents, and who treated the virtuous with contempt and showed no respect for his elders. His household suffered decline and he was constantly frustrated by misfortune, so he began to serve the fire in hopes of seeking blessings.
Regarding the method of serving the fire: when the sun was about to set, he would kindle a great mass of fire and prostrate toward it, continuing until midnight when the fire was extinguished.
Having practiced this for three years without obtaining its blessings, he further served the sun and moon.

Regarding the method for serving the sun and moon: during the day one faces the rising sun, and at night one faces the bright moon; one bows toward them until they have set, at which point one ceases.
Even after practicing this for three years, one still does not obtain merit.

They returned once more to serving the gods, burning incense and prostrating themselves, offering sweet-scented flowers, wine, dried meats, and the flesh of pigs, sheep, oxen, and calves; yet they eventually fell into poverty and could not obtain blessings, becoming weary and haggard from their toil, with illness never leaving their doors.
Hearing that there was a Buddha in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, revered by all the devas, he thought, "I shall go to serve him;

I surely hope to obtain merit. He immediately went to the Buddha’s location and, arriving at the gate of the vihāra, gazed upon the World-Honored One. His radiant marks were brilliant and his countenance was extraordinary, like the moon among the stars. Seeing the Buddha, he rejoiced and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet.

Joining his palms, he addressed the Buddha: "Born and raised in ignorance, I did not know the Triple Gem. I served fire, the sun, the moon, and various heavenly deities for nine years with diligent devotion, yet I never obtained any blessing. My complexion is haggard and my strength has declined; my four elements are plagued by many ailments, and there is no day when death will not come."
"I have humbly heard that the World-Honored One is the teacher who delivers sentient beings; therefore, I have come from afar to take refuge, wishing for you to bestow upon me blessings and joy.
The Buddha told him:

"Those whom you serve are entirely demons, goblins, and malevolent spirits. Your sacrifices are as vast as mountains, yet your sins are like the rivers and seas; seeking blessings by killing living beings is to distance yourself even further from blessings."

Even if one were to labor diligently for a hundred kalpas, slaughtering pigs and sheep throughout the world to offer in sacrifice, the resulting sin would be as vast as Mount Sumeru while the merit would not equal a single mustard seed; to squander oneself in vain—how deluded this is!

Furthermore, you are unfilial toward your parents, treat the virtuous with contempt, and show no respect for your elders; arrogant and conceited, the three poisons blaze within you. As your transgressions deepen day by day, by what means could you possibly obtain merit?

If one can reform the heart to pay respectful homage to the worthy, maintain dignified deportment and ritual propriety in serving the elders, abandon evil and believe in the good, cultivate oneself and honor benevolence, then these four blessings will increase daily and one shall be free from affliction throughout successive lifetimes.

What are the four? First, one's complexion will be upright and handsome; second, one's physical strength will be abundant and robust; third, one will be peaceful and free from illness; and fourth, one's lifespan will be extended without premature or violent death.
"If one practices this without slackening, one may likewise attain the Way.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"To sacrifice to the gods in pursuit of blessings, And then observe the retribution that follows,"
One-fourth of that merit does not equal the honoring of the worthy;
those who can skillfully practice the rules of propriety and always revere their elders will naturally increase in four blessings: physical beauty, strength, longevity, and peace.
Thereupon, having heard these verses of the Buddha, the man was filled with joy and faith; he prostrated himself in homage and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Obscured by the defilements of my sins, I have accumulated transgressions for nine years. Fortunately, by relying on your compassionate transformation, I have now attained understanding."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to become a śramaṇa.
The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣu!"
His hair fell off of its own accord and he immediately became a śramaṇa; by contemplating *ānāpāna* internally, he attained the path of Arhatship.

Chapter 17: On Evil Conduct (*Duścarita-varga*) from the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*. Formerly, when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, he dispatched an arhat named Sumana to take the Buddha’s hair and nail-clippings to the southern mountains of Kaśmīra to construct a Buddhist monastery. Five hundred arhats constantly resided therein, burning incense morning and evening and circumambulating the stupa in worship.

At that time, there were five hundred monkeys on that mountain who, seeing the practitioners making offerings to the stūpas and temples, immediately led one another to the edge of a deep ravine. There they carried stones on their backs to construct a model of a Buddhist temple; they erected wooden poles for *śāla* staffs, fastened ceremonial banners to their heads, and performed prostrations morning and evening just like the practitioners.

At that time, the mountain waters surged in a torrential flood, and five hundred monkeys were swept away and drowned simultaneously; their spirits were immediately reborn in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where palaces of the seven treasures and clothing and food appeared spontaneously.
Each thought to themselves:
"From what place have we come to be born in the heavens?

They then used their divine eyes to see their own original forms; they were the bodies of monkeys who had imitated the various practitioners by playfully constructing stupas and temples. Although their bodies had perished and sunk, their spirits had attained birth in heaven.
"Now we must repay the kindness of this former corpse.
Each leading their attendants with flowers, incense, and music approached the former corpse, scattering flowers and burning incense while circumambulating it seven times.

At that time, there were five hundred brahmins in the mountains who followed external teachings and held false views, having no faith in the retribution of sin and merit. Seeing the devas scattering flowers and performing music as they circled the monkey’s corpse, they were astonished and asked:
"The radiance and majesty of the various devas are so sublime; for what reason do you deign to offer worship to this corpse?"
The devas and humans said: "This corpse was our own former bodies.

In the past, while we were here, we imitated various practitioners by playfully constructing stupas and temples. When the mountain waters swelled in a torrential flood, they swept us away and killed us. By virtue of this slight merit, we have been reborn in the heavens; therefore, we now scatter flowers to repay the kindness of our former bodies."

"If playing with the construction of stūpas and temples yields such blessings as these, how much more inconceivable must be the merit of those who serve the Buddha, the World-Honored One, with a sincere heart!

You all hold false views and do not believe in the True and Right; though you toil and suffer for a hundred kalpas, you shall gain nothing at all. It would be better for you all to go together to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, where by paying homage and making offerings, you will obtain infinite blessings."
They all immediately went joyfully to the place where the Buddha was, prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and scattering flowers as an offering.
The devas and humans said to the Buddha:

"In our recent lives we were monkeys; having received the grace of the World-Honored One, we have been born in the heavens. We regretted not having seen the Buddha, and therefore we have now come to take refuge."
They addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"What offenses did we commit in previous lives to receive these bodies of monkeys?
Though we have built stūpas and monasteries, our bodies have been swept away and killed."
The Buddha told the deva:
"This has causes and conditions; it does not arise from emptiness. I shall explain to you its origins.
In the distant past, there were five hundred young brahmins who traveled together into the mountains, desiring to seek the way of the immortals."

At that time, there was a śramaṇa on the mountain who wished to plaster the vihāra with mud. He went down the valley to fetch water, moving as lightly as if he were flying. Five hundred brāhmaṇas, conceiving feelings of jealousy, laughed at him in unison, saying:
"Now this śramaṇa moves up and down with such rapidity that he is just like a monkey; what is so remarkable about him?"
"If you continue to draw water like this, before long a mountain torrent will come and drown you.
The Buddha told the devas and humans:
"The ascetic from above at that time was my own self; the ascetic from below was Śāriputra."
"The five hundred young Brahmins were these five hundred monkeys.
Having committed offenses in jest, they now receive their retribution in this body.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Committing evil in jest, yet having performed it as bodily action, one receives retribution with wailing cries;
as the deed was done, so does the transgression arrive.
The Buddha told the devas and humans:

"Although you were recently in the form of a beast, you were able to joyfully construct a stupa and temple; thus, you have now attained rebirth in heaven as your transgressions have been extinguished and merit has flourished.
Now, having come once more to personally receive the True Teaching, by virtue of these causes and conditions, you shall be forever separated from all suffering."
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, five hundred devas and humans immediately attained the fruit of the Path.
The five hundred brahmins who had come with them to the water’s edge, having heard the retribution for sin and merit, sighed to themselves:

"We have studied the arts of the immortals for many years, yet we have not received their fruits. It is not as good as this monkey, who through the merit of playful laughter has been reborn in the heavens. The Buddha’s Way and virtue are truly as wondrous as this!"
Thereupon, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and requested to become a disciple.
The Buddha said, “Welcome, bhikṣu.”
He immediately became a śramaṇa; through diligent daily cultivation, he eventually attained the path of arhatship.
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the monastery at Śrāvastī, he preached the Dharma for the sake of devas and humans.

At that time, the king’s second son, named Virūḍhaka, was twenty years old; leading his retinue of officials, he deposed his father the king and attacked his elder brother, the crown prince, in order to seize the throne for himself.
There was an evil minister named Yeli who said to King Vairadeva:

"When Your Majesty was originally a prince, you went to the home of your maternal relatives in the country of Śākya. There you saw the Buddha’s vihāra, where you were rebuked by the sons of the Śākyas, who reviled you with words that made no distinction between good and bad."
At that time, he saw the command:
"If I become king, you shall report this matter.
Now the time has arrived; as the troops and horses are flourishing, it is fitting that one should avenge the grievance.
He immediately ordered his chariots to be prepared and led forth his troops to invade the kingdom of Śākyas.

The Buddha had a second disciple named Mahāmaudgalyāyana, who saw that King Virūḍhaka was leading his soldiers to attack the kingdom of the Śākyas to avenge an old grudge, intending now to slaughter the fourfold assembly of disciples. Thinking of their pitiable state, he went to the Buddha’s dwelling and said to him:

“King Virūḍhaka is currently attacking the kingdom of the Śākyas; I consider that those within it will suffer great hardship. I wish to rescue the people of the Śākya kingdom by means of the four skillful methods.”

First, he lifted all the people of Śrāvastī and placed them in mid-air; second, he lifted all the people of Śrāvastī and placed them in the great ocean; third, he lifted all the people of Śrāvastī and placed them between the two Iron Ring Mountains; fourth, he lifted all the people of Śrāvastī and placed them in the center of another great kingdom, so that King Vairāṭya could not know their location.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"Although I know that you possess such wisdom and virtue as to be able to bring peace to the people of Śrāvastī, there are seven things among all beings and the myriad phenomena that cannot be avoided."
What are these seven?
First is birth; second is aging; third is illness; fourth is death; fifth is demerit; sixth is merit; and seventh is causal conditions.
Regarding these seven matters, though the mind desires to avoid them, one cannot attain mastery over them.
As for your majestic power, you may achieve such things; however, the retribution of past offenses and debts cannot be escaped.

Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana performed his prostrations and departed. Acting on his own private judgment, he gathered four or five thousand acquaintances and donors from the land of Śrāvastī, placed them within his bowl, and lifted it up into the midst of the stars in the void.
King Virūḍhaka, having conquered the Śākya kingdom and slain three hundred million people, was leading his army back to his own country.
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana went to where the Buddha was, paid homage to the Buddha, and spoke with pride:

"King Virūḍhaka has conquered the Śākya kingdom; however, relying on the Buddha’s majestic power, I, your disciple, have saved four or five thousand people from the Śākya nation, who are now all safely in the void and have attained liberation."
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Will you go and see who is in the bowl? He replied:
"I have not yet gone to look at them.
The Buddha said,
"You should go first and look at the multitude of people within the bowl."

Maudgalyāyana used his supernatural power to bring down the bowl and saw that all those within were dead. Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana was despondent and wept with grief, pitying their suffering; he returned and said to the Buddha, "Those within the bowl are now all dead;
even the power of the Way and spiritual transformations cannot exempt them from the retribution of their past karma."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"There are these seven matters that even a Buddha, the various sages, seers, and practitioners of the Way cannot avoid, even when they conceal their forms or disperse their bodies."
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Not in the sky, nor in the midst of the sea, Nor by hiding among the mountain crags—
Nowhere can one find a place To escape the retribution for past evils."
“Sentient beings suffer affliction; they cannot escape old age and death.
Only those who are benevolent and wise do not dwell upon the faults or evils of others.

When the Buddha spoke these words, countless people in the assembly, hearing the Buddha’s teaching on impermanence, were all moved to sorrowful reflection that such opposition is difficult to avoid; yet they joyfully attained the Way, realizing the fruit of *srotāpanna*.

Chapter 18: On Weapons. *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*. Chapter Eighteen: On Weapons. In the past, there was a kingdom named Bhadra. At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu who had been long ill, prostrate with exhaustion, emaciated, and covered in filth. He lay within the Bhadra monastery, yet no one attended to him.

The Buddha led five hundred bhikṣus to where he was, instructing them to take turns looking after him and preparing gruel for him; however, upon smelling its odor, the bhikṣus all looked down upon it with contempt.

The Buddha sent Śakra, Lord of Devas, to fetch hot water; the Buddha then washed the body of the sick bhikṣu with his adamantine hand. Immediately, the earth shook and a brilliant light flashed forth, such that all were struck with awe and solemnity.
The king, his ministers and subjects, devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits—countless people in all—went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves in worship, and said to the Buddha:
“The Buddha is the World-Honored One; your moral virtue is peerless in the three realms and already perfected. Why do you deign to humble yourself to wash this emaciated and defiled bhikṣu?”
The Buddha addressed the king and the assembled multitude:
"It is precisely for the sake of those who are destitute, afflicted, and without protection that the Tathāgata has appeared in the world."

To provide offerings for sick and emaciated śramaṇas and practitioners, as well as for the poor, the destitute, the solitary, and the elderly, brings immeasurable merit and fulfills all wishes. Just as the five rivers flow, so does merit come; as one's merit gradually fills, one shall surely attain the Way.
The king said to the Buddha,
“What transgression did this bhikṣu commit in a previous life such that he has been afflicted by illness for many years, and though treated, his condition does not improve?
The Buddha told the king:
"In the past, there was a king named Duṣkṛta whose administration was harsh and violent. He appointed a powerful official, Pañcaśata, to flog people.

These five hundred men, feigning the king’s majesty and wrath, arbitrarily inflicted cold and heat [tortures]. When they wished to flog someone, they would demand a ransom; if they received wealth, the lashes were light, but if they received nothing, the lashes were heavy. The entire kingdom suffered from this."
There was a virtuous man who was falsely accused by others and ought to have been flogged; he replied to the five hundred [officials] with these words:
"I am a disciple of the Buddha; I have never committed any offense, yet I have been wronged by others. I pray that you will show me some small measure of leniency."
When the five hundred [attendants] heard this, they thought, "These are disciples of the Buddha," and they lightly passed their whips over him without anything striking his body.

When their lives ended, the five hundred fell into hell, where they were tortured by ten thousand poisons; once their offenses were extinguished, they emerged and fell among the animals, where for more than five hundred lifetimes they were constantly beaten with clubs. When their retribution was finished, they became humans, yet they always suffered from grave illnesses that never left their bodies.
The king at that time was none other than Devadatta;
the five hundred at that time were these present sick bhikṣus;
and the worthy man at that time was my own self.
Because I was forgiven by him in a previous life, the whip did not strike my body; for this reason, the World-Honored One personally washed it for me.
When people perform good or evil deeds, calamity or fortune follows them like their own shadow; even after undergoing birth and death through many lifetimes, one cannot escape them.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"To strike the virtuous with a staff, Or to slander the innocent, Brings tenfold calamity;
Such sudden disaster shall not be forgiven."
Naturally afflicted by illness, they lose their minds and become dazed; they are slandered by others, or face calamities from government officials;
their wealth and property are exhausted, and they are separated from their kinsmen;
all that they possess—houses and dwellings—is consumed by the fire of disaster; and at death, they enter hell.
"These are the ten.

At that time, the sick bhikṣu, having heard these verses from the Buddha and the account of his past lives, recognized his own former conduct. He reproached himself with a keen mind, and immediately before the Buddha, his ailment was cured. With body at peace and mind settled, he attained the path of Arhatship.

King Kṣemadatta was filled with joy and faith; he immediately received the five precepts and became a lay follower (*upāsaka*), practicing them until the end of his life and attaining the stage of *srotāpanna*.
Long ago, when the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery in Śrāvastī, he preached the Dharma for devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits.

In the east there was a country named Uttara-pāṭha. Formerly, five hundred Brahmins led one another toward the Ganges River; on its bank were three sacred bathing pools for deities, where they would bathe to cleanse their impurities and seek immortality naked, according to the methods of the Nirgranthas.

On his way through a vast marsh, he became lost and could not pass; midway, his provisions ran short. From afar he saw a great tree that seemed imbued with a divine spirit, and thinking someone might dwell there, he hurried toward it, but upon reaching its base, he saw nothing at all.
The brahmins and others raised their voices and wailed aloud; famished, parched, and exhausted by their misfortunes, they were on the verge of death in this marsh.
A tree deity manifested in human form and asked the brahmins, "O practitioners of the Way, from where have you come?"
"What do you intend to do now?
They replied with one voice, "We wish to go to the Divine Pond to bathe and seek immortality; we are hungry and thirsty today, so we pray you will have compassion for us and save us."

The tree deity immediately raised her hand, and food and drink of a hundred flavors flowed forth from it; she provided meals for the assembly until all were fully satiated, and there remained enough food and drink to serve as provisions for their journey.
As he was about to depart, he went to the deity to inquire:
"What virtues did I practice in my past lives to have attained such a magnificent state?
The deity replied to the brahmin:

"My original residence was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a chief minister of the state named Sudatta who was providing meals for the Buddha and the assembly of monks. While he was purchasing curd in the marketplace, there was no one to carry it; looking around, he asked me to carry it for him. Upon arriving at the vihāra, he requested that I distribute it."
Having finished distributing the water for washing, he sat solemnly to listen to the Dharma; everyone rejoiced and praised him boundlessly.
At that time, I had observed the fast and returned home at dusk without eating. My wife asked me in wonder:
"Why do you not eat? What is your grievance?"
He replied: "I have no regrets.
While walking through the market, I saw the elder Sudatta providing a meal for the Buddha in his garden; I went there to observe the fast, which is called the Eightfold Precepts."
His wife, filled with indignation and anger, said:
"Gautama disturbs the common ways; why should he be worthy of acceptance?
You have destroyed the inherited norms, and calamity will arise from this."
Being pressed and constrained without end, they ate together.
At that time, on that very night, my allotted lifespan came to an end at midnight, and my spirit was reborn here.
It was because of this foolish woman that she ruined my practice of the *upavāsa* (fasting) and I did not complete my task.

Having been reborn in this marsh as a tree deity, he offers food and drink from his hands through the merit of carrying curd; had he completed the fasting ritual, he would have been reborn in the heavens to enjoy natural abundance.
He then spoke a verse for the brahmin:
"Sacrifices plant the roots of calamity, Which grow their branches and twigs day and night;
They are empty toil that ruins the very foundation of the self— The laws of fasting are for the transcendent immortals."

Upon hearing the verse, the brahmin’s delusions were dispelled and he accepted it with faith. He then returned to Śrāvastī, traveling by way of a certain country named Kūlani. There lived an elder named Surūpa, who was benevolent and virtuous, and whom all people revered.
After the brahmin had stayed overnight, the elder asked him:
"Where have you come from, ascetic?
Where do you intend to go now?"
He related in detail the virtues of that tree deity of the marsh:
"I wish to go to Śrāvastī to visit Sudatta, so that by collecting and practicing the rules for the fast, I may hope to obtain merit.
Delighted and leaping with joy, his past deeds having pursued him, he felt a natural clarity and proclaimed the command to his clan:
"Who can go together to receive the precepts of the fast?
Five hundred people responded in unison to this call; led by their original vows, they set forth with solemn dignity and proceeded together to Śrāvastī.
Before reaching the Jetavana, he encountered Sudatta on the road; not recognizing him, he asked his attendants, "What kind of man is this?
They replied:
"It is Sudatta! The assembly of brahmins rejoiced and pursued him, saying,
"Our wish has been fulfilled!"
Seeking someone to receive him, he hurried to meet him; they greeted one another with a single voice, sighing in admiration:

"The tree deity has praised your virtue, looking up to you with a humble and open heart while fully recounting what he admires. Therefore, we have come to seek refuge in you, hoping that you will show us the ritual of the Dharma."
The charioteer replied, "What you seek is most excellent!
I have a venerable teacher titled Tathāgata and World-Honored One, who delivers humanity and resides nearby at the Jeta Grove; we may go together to pay him our respects."

They all respectfully agreed and proceeded forward with solemnity. Seeing the Tathāgata from afar, their joy was immeasurable; they prostrated themselves on the ground and withdrew to sit at one side. All together, kneeling upright, they addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"From our initial departure from home, we intended to go to the Three Pools to bathe and seek immortality. As we passed by, it was as the tree deity described to us. Therefore, we have come to seek conversion; we pray that you will manifest your supreme spiritual power."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, in accordance with his conduct, spoke these verses:
"Though one goes naked and shaves the hair, Wears long robes of grass, And bathes while squatting upon stones—
What does this avail against the knots of doubt?"
"He does not strike, kill, or burn, nor does he seek victory; he loves all under heaven, and wherever he goes, there is no resentment.
Upon hearing these verses, the five hundred brahmins were filled with joy; they all became śramaṇas and attained the path of arhatship, while Meṇḍaka and his followers attained the Dharma-eye.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What virtues did these five hundred brahmins and householders practice in the past, that they have attained the Way so swiftly?
The World-Honored One replied:
"In the distant past, there was a Buddha in the world named Kāśyapa, who preached the Dharma to his disciples concerning the future age of the five turbidities."
At that time, there were one thousand brahmin householders who together made this declaration:
"May we encounter and behold Śākyamuni Buddha.
Those brahmins of that time are these very brahmins here today.
"The elder at that time was none other than the present-day Sundarī and her companions.
It is because of these causes and conditions that they were liberated upon seeing me.
The bhikṣus rejoiced, paid homage, and practiced accordingly.
*Faju piyu jing*, Scroll II; *Faju piyu jing*, Scroll III.
Translated by the Śramaṇas Dharmakṣema and Dharmayaśas during the Jin Dynasty.
19. Chapter on the Simile of Old Age.

Once, when the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, after his meal, he preached the Dharma of Ambrosia for devas and humans, kings, ministers, and subjects, and for the fourfold assembly of disciples.

At that time, there were seven elderly brahmins from a distant land who came to where the Buddha was staying. They prostrated themselves on the ground, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"We are men from afar who have humbly heard of the Sage’s transformation. For a long time we have intended to take refuge in you, but many obstacles hindered us. Now we have finally come to behold your holy countenance; we pray to become your disciples so that we may extinguish all suffering."
The Buddha accepted them and ordained them all as śramaṇas, instructing that these seven men should dwell together in one room.

However, upon beholding the World-Honored One, these seven failed to attain the Way by contemplating impermanence; instead, while sitting in their room, they thought only of worldly affairs, speaking in low voices and laughing loudly without considering success or failure. Life’s days are shortening and reach their end without appointment, yet they merely shared in joyful laughter, their minds deluded within the three realms.
The Buddha, through his threefold knowledge, perceived that their lifespans were coming to an end; moved by compassion for them, he rose and went to their room, where he addressed them, saying:
"You who practice the Way should seek transcendence from the world; why do you laugh so loudly?"
All sentient beings rely on five things for their self-assurance.
What are these five? First, relying on youth; second, relying on physical beauty; third, relying on great strength; fourth, relying on wealth; and fifth, relying on noble lineage.
"You seven, why do you speak in whispers and laugh so loudly? On what do you rely?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"What joy, what laughter?"
Thoughts are constantly ablaze, deeply shrouding the dark and obscure; it is better to seek meditative concentration.
One perceives the form and proportions of the body and leans upon it for security, yet many thoughts bring about illness—how could one know this is not real?
