In old age, the complexion fades; in sickness, there is no luster. The skin becomes slack and the muscles shrink; death draws near and hastens.
When the body dies, the spirit departs, like a driver abandoning his chariot. Flesh wastes away and bones scatter;
how can this body be relied upon?
After the Buddha had spoken these verses, the minds of the seven bhikṣus were liberated and their cravings ceased; they immediately attained the path of Arhatship before the Buddha.
Formerly, when the Buddha was at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī, he preached the Dharma for the sake of devas, humans, kings, and emperors.

At that time, there was a Brahmin village consisting of more than five hundred households, among whom were five hundred young Brahmins who practiced the Brahmanical arts. They were haughty toward others and did not respect their elders; they were arrogant and self-important, making this their constant habit.
Five hundred brahmins suddenly deliberated among themselves, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama claims for himself to be a Buddha; his triple-knowledge and skillful wisdom are such that no one dares to debate with him.
We should join together to request a formal discussion, questioning him on every point to discover what he truly is."
He immediately prepared the offerings and went to invite the Buddha.
The Buddha, together with his disciples, arrived at the village of the brahmin; once they were seated, water was served for washing, and after the meal was finished, they washed their hands.

At that time, there were an elderly brahmin couple who were wandering together for alms in this village. The Buddha, knowing that they had originally been immensely wealthy and had once served as high ministers, asked the young brahmins:
"Do you recognize this elderly brahmin?"
They all said, "We have known him.
He asked again:
"What was his original status? He replied, "Originally,
he was a great minister with immeasurable wealth."
"Why do you now go about begging again?
They all replied, "We have squandered our wealth without principle; that is why we remain in poverty."
The Buddha told the brahmins:
"There are four things in the world that people are unable to practice; those who do practice them will obtain blessings and shall not fall into such poverty. What are these four?

First, when one is in the prime of life and possesses great strength, one must be careful not to be arrogant; second, when one is old, one should be diligent and not crave lustful indulgence; third, when one possesses wealth and treasures, one should always keep in mind the practice of giving; fourth, one should approach a teacher to study and inquire, listening to and receiving the correct words of the Dharma.

If an old husband does not practice these four matters—namely, maintaining constancy and disregarding success or failure—and they suddenly part ways, it is like an old crane guarding this empty pond, forever obtaining nothing.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Day and night negligent and indolent, Old yet ceasing not from lust, Possessing wealth yet not practicing giving,
Not receiving the words of the Buddha."
Possessing these four obscurations, one deceives and betrays oneself; alas, old age arrives, and the complexion changes into decrepitude.
Seeing that one has been overtaken by old age, yet one has neither cultivated the holy life nor amassed wealth—like a white crane guarding an empty pond—one fails to maintain the precepts.
Furthermore, one does not accumulate wealth; when old and frail, one's vital energy is exhausted. Thinking of the past, what can be attained?
Old age is like autumn leaves; one’s conduct is recorded in a foul mirror. Life swiftly departs; there is no room for regret.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"There are four seasons in the world when one who practices the Path attains merit and liberation, and may escape all suffering.
What are these four?"

First, when one is young and possesses physical strength and power; second, when one is wealthy and possesses material goods; third, when one encounters the Three Honored Ones, who are excellent fields of merit; and fourth, when one reflects upon all things and contemplates the sorrow of their inevitable dispersal.
"By practicing these four things, one shall obtain all that is wished for and will surely attain the traces of the Path.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
Life is wasting away day and night; One should exert oneself with diligence while there is still time.
The truths of the world are impermanent; do not be deluded and fall into darkness.
You should learn to light the lamp of the mind, purifying yourself to seek wisdom.
Free from defilement and untainted by impurity, hold the torch and observe the stages of the Path.

When the Buddha spoke these words, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated heaven and earth. Thereupon, five hundred young brahmins attained realization; their hair stood on end with awe, and they rose to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, saying to him:
“We take refuge in the World-Honored One; we pray to become your disciples.”
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, Bhikṣu! and he immediately became a śramaṇa and attained the path of arhatship.
The villagers, both young and old, all attained the traces of the Path, and there was none who did not rejoice.

Chapter 20: Cherishing the Body. *Faju Piyu Jing* (Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra), Chapter Twenty: Cherishing the Body. Formerly, there was a kingdom named Tāmraliptī. Seven *li* from the city stood a monastery where five hundred *śramaṇas* constantly resided, reciting the scriptures and practicing the Way.

There was an elder bhikṣu named Mahālu who was dull-witted and obtuse. Five hundred practitioners of the Way taught him together for several years, yet he could not master even a single verse. The assembly collectively despised him and would not allow him to participate in their gatherings; they constantly kept him at the vihāra, ordering him to sweep and clean.
On a later day, the king invited various practitioners into the palace to provide them with offerings. The bhikṣu Mahālu thought to himself:
"I have been born into this world so shrouded in darkness that I do not know even a single verse; I am despised by others—what is the use of living like this?"
He then took the rope and went beneath a large tree in the back garden, intending to hang himself.
The Buddha, seeing this from afar with his eye of the Way, manifested as a tree spirit with a human torso appearing from the trunk and rebuked him, saying: "Ho! Ho! Bhikṣu!"
"Why have you done this? Mahālu then related his hardships in detail.
The manifested deity rebuked him, saying:
"Do not act in this way; listen now to my words.

In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, you were a Tripiṭaka śramaṇa with five hundred disciples. Because you considered yourself wise, you looked down upon others and were stingy with the meaning of the scriptures, never instructing or admonishing them. For this reason, in every birth since then, your faculties have remained dull and obtuse."
"You should only reproach yourself; why do you act as your own enemy?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One manifested a radiant image and spoke this verse:
"One who loves their own person Should vigilantly guard what they maintain; If they desire liberation from craving,"
The Master of Learning does not sleep;
being foremost in person, he constantly exerts himself in study. Being capable of benefiting others through instruction, his wisdom is such that he never tires.
In learning, first rectify oneself, and only then rectify others; by harmonizing the body, one enters wisdom, and will surely be transformed into a superior being.
If one cannot benefit oneself, how can one benefit others?
When the mind is disciplined and the body is upright, what wish could remain unfulfilled?
What I have originally created, I myself shall later receive; having committed evil, one undergoes its consequences alone, like a hard diamond drilling through a pearl.

When the bhikṣu Mahālu beheld the Buddha manifesting his radiant form, he was moved with a mixture of sorrow and joy and trembled with awe; bowing his head at the Buddha’s feet, he contemplated the meaning of the verses and immediately entered a state of meditative concentration. Thereupon, in the presence of the Buddha, he attained the path of an Arhat, recognized his own past lives through countless eons, and mastered the various sūtras of the Tripiṭaka within his mind.
The Buddha said to Mahālu:

"Put on your robes, take up your bowl, and go to the royal palace for a meal. Sit at the head of the five hundred practitioners; these practitioners were your five hundred disciples in a previous life. Preach the Dharma to them so that they may attain the fruits of the Path, and cause the king to clearly believe in the retribution of sin and merit."
He immediately accepted the Buddha’s instruction and went straight into the palace, taking his seat at the head of the assembly.

The people were filled with resentment and wondered at the reason for this; each one, out of deference to the king’s wishes, dared not rebuke him, yet they were weary at heart, thinking of his ignorance and lack of understanding regarding the distribution of offerings (*dakṣiṇā*).

The King then set down the food and served it with his own hands; Mahālu immediately offered a *dakṣiṇā*, the sound of which was like a thunderclap and his eloquent words fell like rain. The practitioners seated there were struck with awe and repented of themselves, and all attained the state of an Arhat.
He preached the Dharma for the king, explaining it so thoroughly that there was nothing he did not clarify; consequently, the ministers and all the officials attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Long ago, when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there were five hundred Brahmins who constantly sought an opportunity to slander him.

The Buddha’s wisdom of the three types of supernormal knowledge perceives the minds of all people universally; out of compassion, he desires to deliver them. Yet, because their fruits have not yet ripened and the conditions have not yet converged, when the time arrives for all their transgressions and merits to manifest, they must encounter those transgressions and merits through the causes and conditions they themselves have created. These brahmins possess a slight residue of merit from past lives and ought to attain liberation; thus, drawn by their own merit, they must create the appropriate conditions for it themselves.
Five hundred brahmins deliberated among themselves, saying:

"We shall have a butcher kill living beings and invite the Buddha and the assembly of monks; the Buddha will surely accept the invitation and praise the butcher, whereupon we shall step forward together to revile him."
Thereupon, the butcher entreated the Buddha on his behalf, and the Buddha accepted the invitation, saying to the butcher:
"When fruit is ripe, it falls of its own accord; when merit is ripe, one is liberated of its own accord."
The butcher returned home and prepared a meal.
The Buddha, leading his disciples, arrived at the butcher's village and went to the house of the donor; the brahmins, both great and small, all rejoiced together.
"Today is precisely the opportunity to deal with the Buddha; for if he were to praise the donor's merit, I would use his past sins of killing to mock him;
and if the Buddha were to speak of the sins from his origins, I would challenge him with the merit of today."
"Of these two appropriate times, today is the very moment when the Buddha has found his opportunity.

Upon arriving, the Buddha sat down; water was served and food was distributed. Thereupon, the World-Honored One observed the minds of the assembly, and for those who were ready to be saved, he extended his tongue to cover his face and lick his ears, emitting a great radiance that illuminated the entire city.
Then, with a Brahma-voice, he spoke this verse as a blessing: "As the True Man teaches, One sustains one's life through the Way; The foolish envy it,"
Seeing and doing evil—by practicing evil one obtains evil, just as planting bitter seeds brings bitter fruit; the wicked receive their own punishment, while the virtuous receive their own blessings.
"Each must likewise ripen for themselves; one cannot substitute for another. By practicing good, one obtains good, just as planting sweetness [yields sweet fruit].

When the Buddha had finished speaking these verses, the minds of the five hundred brahmins were spontaneously opened and liberated. They immediately came forward, prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:
"We were dull-witted and ignorant, failing to comprehend the Sage’s instruction. We only pray that you will compassionately nurture us and allow us to become śramaṇas."
The Buddha immediately granted them permission to receive ordination as śramaṇas.

When the villagers, both old and young, witnessed the Buddha’s miraculous transformations, there was none among them who did not rejoice; they all attained the fruit of the Path and were hailed as worthies and sages, no longer bearing the name of butcher.
When the Buddha had finished his meal, he returned immediately to the vihāra.

Chapter 21: On the Worldly (Lokadhātu-varga). The Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra, Chapter Twenty-one: On the Worldly. In the past, there was a Brahmin king named Ta-mei-xie (Tasmiśa). This king served ninety-six different types of heterodox paths.

One day, the king suddenly gave rise to a virtuous mind and desired to practice great giving. Following the Dharma of the Brahmins, he accumulated the seven treasures like mountains to bestow as alms; whenever anyone came to beg, he permitted them to take as much as they could carry in a single handful and depart. In this manner, for several days, the accumulation did not diminish.
The Buddha, knowing that this king’s past merit made him ready for deliverance, manifested as a brahmin and went to his kingdom.
When the king came out and met him, they exchanged greetings, and the Buddha asked after his well-being, saying: "What is it you seek?"
"Do not harbor doubts or difficulties within yourself. The brahmin replied,
"I have come from afar wishing to beg for precious treasures to build a dwelling."
The king said,
"Excellent! Take for yourself as much as one large handful."
The brahmin took a handful [of earth], walked seven paces, and returned to place it back in its original spot.
The king asked,
"For what reason did you not take it?"
The brahmin replied, “This is barely sufficient to build a hut; furthermore, I must marry a wife, so it will not suffice for both. For this reason, I do not take it.”
The king said,
"Take three more handfuls.
The brahmin immediately took them.
He walked seven steps and then returned to place it back in its original position.
The King asked the brahmin,
"Why did you do this again?"

He replied: "This is sufficient for taking a wife; yet, as I possess no fields, slaves, oxen, or horses, even this would be insufficient when calculated. For this reason, I have ceased my worldly ambitions."
The king said,
"Take another seven handfuls.
The brahmin immediately took them, walked seven paces, and then returned to place them back in their original spot.
The king asked,
"For what further reason?
The brahmin replied:
"If there are men and women who must marry again, the expenses for auspicious and inauspicious occasions would be beyond what we can afford; therefore, we do not take them.
The King said, "I shall give you all my accumulated treasures to provide for your needs."
The brahmin accepted [the food] and departed.
The king, greatly marvelling at this, questioned him again regarding the reason for his intention.
The brahmin replied:

"Originally, this beggar intended to use it for his livelihood; however, he reflected deeply that human life in this world is but brief, and all things are impermanent, difficult to preserve from moment to moment. Consequently, his heavy anxieties and bitter sufferings deepen daily. Even if one accumulates treasures as vast as mountains, they are of no benefit to oneself; to scheme with greedy desires only brings needless hardship upon oneself. It is better to quiet the mind and seek the Way of Non-action (wuwei); therefore, he did not take it."
The king’s mind was opened and he resolved to receive the enlightened teaching.
Thereupon, the brahmin manifested the radiant marks of a Buddha, leaped up to stay in mid-air, and spoke these verses for him:
"Though one may accumulate precious treasures Until their height reaches the heavens,"
Even if one fills the world with such [offerings], it is not equal to seeing the path of the Dharma.
That which is unwholesome appears as wholesome; that which is craving appears as non-craving;
taking suffering for the mark of pleasure—this is what the deluded man finds endearing.

Thereupon, the king beheld the Buddha’s radiant marks illuminating heaven and earth; hearing these verses, he leaped for joy. The king and his ministers immediately received the five precepts and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

Chapter 22: Praising the Buddha *Faju Piyu Jing*, Chapter Twenty-Two: Praising the Buddha Formerly, when the Buddha was at the site of the Auspicious Way in the realm of Magadha, beneath the tree of primal auspiciousness, he subdued the Māras through the power of his virtue. Sitting in contemplation, he thought to himself: "The drum of the nectar-like Dharma shall be heard throughout the three thousandfold world system.
In the past, my father the King dispatched five men to provide me with offerings of hemp and rice; they served me with great diligence, and their merit and reward should now be recounted."
"These five men are in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata rose from beneath the tree; his marks and signs were majestic, his radiance illuminated heaven and earth, and his awesome spiritual power caused all to tremble. Those who saw him were filled with joy as he proceeded to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

Before he had reached the Middle Way, he encountered a brahmin named Uruvilvā, who had left his kin and home to seek a teacher and study the Path; beholding the Exalted One’s sublime majesty, he was filled with a mixture of astonishment and joy.
Standing by the side of the road, he raised his voice and sighed in admiration, saying:
"Your majestic spirit moves the hearts of men; your demeanor is elegant and exceptionally distinguished. Under which master did you originally study to attain such a countenance?
For the sake of the one named Youhu (Ugra), the Buddha spoke this verse:

“Having attained the Eightfold Right Awakening by myself, free from departure and untainted, with craving exhausted and the net of desire torn asunder, I have realized this spontaneously without a teacher.
My practice is without a master or protector; my resolve is solitary and without companion.”
"By accumulating [merit], one attains Buddhahood; from this, one penetrates the holy path.
Upon hearing this verse, Uruvilvākāśyapa was bewildered and did not understand it. He immediately asked the World-Honored One Gautama, "How should one practice?"
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"I wish to go to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī to beat the drum of the Dharma of Ambrosia and turn the unsurpassed wheel of the Dharma. Among all the sages of the three realms, none have ever turned the wheel of the Dharma to lead people into Nirvāṇa as I do now."
Uruvilvākāśyapa was greatly overjoyed and said:
"Excellent, excellent!
As the Buddha has spoken, I pray that you will grant me the nectar of the Dharma by preaching the teaching as it truly is."
After the brahmin had saluted him, he departed. Before reaching his teacher’s dwelling, he stayed overnight on the road; at midnight, he suddenly passed away.
With his eye of the Path, the Buddha saw that he had died and, feeling pity for him, said:

"The world is foolish, claiming that life is permanent; yet upon seeing the Buddha depart, he alone has perished. While the Dharma-drum resounds, he alone does not hear it; while the nectar extinguishes suffering, he alone does not taste it. Wandering through the five realms of existence, his cycle of birth and death grows ever longer. Having passed through kalpas of time, when will he attain deliverance?"
The Buddha, out of compassion, spoke these verses:
"Having seen the Truths, pure and free from defilement, He has already crossed the abyss of the five realms of existence.
The Buddha has appeared to illuminate the world, To eliminate the manifold sorrows and sufferings of all beings."
"Difficult is it to be born as a human; difficult is it to obtain a long life.
Difficult is it for a Buddha to appear in the world; difficult is it to hear the Buddha’s Dharma.
When the Buddha spoke these verses, five hundred devas in the air heard them with joy and all attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Chapter 23: On Tranquility (*Aniṅga-varga*). *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-three: On Tranquility.

Formerly, when the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, there was a mountain village of more than five hundred households three hundred *li* to the southeast. The people were stubborn and difficult to transform through instruction. Yet, due to the merit and vows of their past lives, they were destined to receive the Buddha’s salvation.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One manifested as a śramaṇa and went to the village for alms.

Having finished his almsround, he departed from the village and sat down beneath a tree; entering the *nirvāṇa-samādhi*, he remained there for seven days without breathing, without ceasing [his breath], without moving, and without turning.
When the villagers saw this, they thought he had passed away and said to one another, "The śramaṇa is dead;
we should bury him together. Each taking a bundle of firewood, they went to burn him.

As the fire blazed and the wood was consumed, the Buddha rose from his seat and manifested the divine transformations of the Way. His radiance shone forth, moving all ten directions. Having completed these manifestations, he returned to sit beneath the tree; his physical form was calm and composed, as serene and joyful as before.
The villagers, both young and old, were all struck with alarm and fear;

they bowed their heads in prostration and apologized, saying, "We mountain folk are stubborn and uncivilized, ignorant of divine beings. We have recklessly used firewood and flames to burn what was not yet ablaze. We consider ourselves to have incurred a sin heavier than Mount Tai; we only pray that you will grant us compassionate pardon and do not hold us in resentment."
I wonder if you, O divine being, have not suffered any injury or illness?
Are you perhaps beset by sorrow or grief?
Or are you perhaps afflicted by hunger or thirst?
"Will you not experience the heat of affliction?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, with a serene countenance and a smile, spoke these verses:
"My life is already at peace; I do not resent those who harbor enmity toward me. While people everywhere harbor resentment,"
I practice without enmity;
my life is already at peace. While others are afflicted by illness, I practice without illness.
My life is already at peace; I do not grieve over sorrow. While people everywhere possess sorrow, my conduct is free from sorrow.
My life is already at peace, pure and unconditioned; I take joy as my sustenance, like the devas of Ābhāsvara.
"My life is already at peace; I am tranquil and free from affairs. Even if the fires of the kingdom were to increase their fuel, how could they burn me?

At that time, when the five hundred people in the village heard this verse, they all became śramaṇas and attained the path of arhatship; the villagers, both great and small, all placed their faith in the Triple Gem.
The Buddha flew back to the Bamboo Grove with five hundred people.
When the Venerable Ānanda saw the Buddha arriving together with those who had attained the Way, he stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What extraordinary virtue do these bhikṣus possess that has caused the World-Honored One to go in person to guide them?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Before I attained Buddhahood, there was a Pratyekabuddha in this world who constantly dwelt on this mountain. Not far from the village, beneath a tree, he sought to enter parinirvāṇa; manifesting his spiritual power and virtue, he then passed into extinction."
The villagers took firewood and torches and went there to cremate him; they collected the relics and placed them in a precious jar, which they buried on the mountain peak, each making this vow:
"May we later attain the Way, so that our parinirvāṇa may be as blissful as that of this śramaṇa."
"By virtue of this merit, they shall surely attain the Way; therefore, the Tathāgata has gone to deliver them.
When the Buddha spoke these words, countless devas and humans all attained the traces of the Path.
Formerly, when the Buddha was staying at a monastery in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, four bhikṣus were sitting beneath a tree and asked one another:
"What is the most painful thing in all the world?"
One person said,
"Of all the sufferings in the world, none exceeds sensual desire.
Another person said:
"There is no suffering in the world greater than anger," one person said.
"There is no suffering in the world greater than hunger and thirst," another said.
One person said,
"Of all the sufferings in the world, none surpasses fear and terror.
They continued to debate the meaning of suffering at length, without ceasing.
The Buddha, knowing their words, went to where they were and asked the bhikṣus,
"What was the subject of your recent discussion?
They immediately rose, paid their respects, and reported in detail what they had discussed.
The Buddha said, “Bhikṣus!
What you have discussed does not fully investigate the meaning of suffering. Among all sufferings in the world, none surpasses having a body!”
Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, anger, fear, lust, and the calamities of enmity all stem from the body.

Indeed, the body is the root of manifold sufferings and the source of misfortune; it causes the mind to toil and the intellect to exhaust itself through myriad anxieties and terrors. That beings writhing within the three realms harm one another, and that they are bound by the notion of "self" so that birth and death never cease—all this is due to the body.

"Those who wish to leave behind the suffering of the world should seek quiescence; by gathering the mind, maintaining rectitude, and remaining tranquil and free of thought, one may attain Nirvāṇa—this is the supreme bliss.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"No heat exceeds lust; No poison exceeds anger; No suffering exceeds the body."
There is no bliss greater than cessation;
there is no joy in minor joys. For those who seek the Great through minor eloquence and minor wisdom, they shall attain great peace.
"I am the World-Honored One; long since liberated and free from sorrow, I have rightly delivered beings from the three realms of existence and alone have subdued the hosts of Māra.
Having spoken this verse, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, incalculable eons ago, there was a bhikṣu with the five supernatural powers named Vīryabala, who sought the Way in the solitude beneath a tree in the mountains."
At that time, there were four creatures who relied upon him for protection and always found peace and security:
first, a pigeon; second, a crow; third, a venomous snake; and fourth, a deer.
These four animals went out to seek food during the day and returned in the evening.
One night, the four animals asked one another:
"Among the sufferings of the world, which is the most heavy?"

The crow said: "Hunger and thirst are the greatest suffering. When one is hungry and thirsty, the body becomes emaciated, the eyes grow dim, and the consciousness is not at peace; one casts oneself into nets and disregards sharp blades. That we lose our lives is invariably due to this; speaking from this perspective, hunger and thirst constitute suffering."

The pigeon said, "Sensual desire is the greatest suffering; when the fire of lust blazes intensely, one has no regard for anything else, and there is nothing that does not lead to the endangerment of the body and the extinction of life.
The venomous snake said:
"Hatred is the greatest suffering; once a poisonous intent arises, one makes no distinction between kin and stranger—it can kill others and it can lead to one's own suicide.

The deer said: "Terror is the greatest suffering. As I roam the wild forests, my heart is constantly trembling with anxiety. Fearing hunters and various jackals and wolves, at the mere sound of something, I dash toward pits and precipices. Mother and child abandon one another, our hearts trembling with grief. Speaking from this perspective, terror is indeed suffering."
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu immediately told them:
"What you are discussing is merely the branches; it does not investigate the root of suffering.

Among all the sufferings in the world, none surpasses having a body. The body is a vessel of suffering, fraught with immeasurable anxiety and fear. For this reason, I have abandoned the secular life to study the Way, extinguishing the mind and severing conceptualization, no longer craving the four great elements. I seek to cut off the source of suffering, setting my will upon Nirvāṇa."
"The path to Nirvāṇa is tranquil extinction and formless; when anxieties and afflictions are forever ended, there is then great peace.
Upon hearing this, the hearts of the four birds were immediately opened and liberated.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“At that time, the bhikṣu with five supernatural powers was none other than myself;
the four animals were you four people here today.
Since you already heard the meaning of the root of suffering in a previous life, why do you speak thus again today?”
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu felt shame and reproached himself; he immediately attained the path of an arhat before the Buddha.
Chapter 24: Delight in Joy. *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-four: Delight in Joy. Formerly, when the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there were four newly ordained bhikṣus who, having gone together to sit in meditation and practice the Way beneath a mango tree, saw that the mango blossoms were in full bloom, beautiful in color and fragrant. They then said to one another:
"Of all the myriad things in this world, which is most lovable and capable of delighting the human heart?"
One person said:
"In the second month of spring, when the trees are in full bloom, to roam and play upon the plains and fields—this is the greatest pleasure.
Another person said:
"One said: 'To gather with one's kinsmen and relatives, where cups and goblets are passed back and forth amidst music, song, and dance—this is the height of pleasure. Another said:

'To accumulate vast wealth and treasures so that whatever one desires is obtained at will; to have carriages, horses, and finery that distinguish one from the masses; to move about with such brilliance that all who see one take notice—this is the height of pleasure.'"
One man said: "To have a wife and concubines of upright beauty, wearing bright and colorful garments, and to indulge one's desires with the fragrance of perfumes—this is the greatest pleasure.

The Buddha, knowing that these four men were ready to be converted, yet their minds were wandering among the six desires and they did not contemplate impermanence, immediately called out to the four men and asked them:
"What were you discussing while sitting beneath the tree?
The four men reported in detail what they had been enjoying.
The Buddha told the four men:

"What you are discussing is entirely the way of sorrow, fear, and perilous ruin; it is not the Dharma of eternal peace and supreme bliss. All things flourish in spring and wither in autumn and winter;

the joy of one's kinsmen must inevitably end in separation; wealth, treasures, carriages, and horses are shared among the five families [of heirs]; and beautiful wives and concubines are merely the masters of love and hatred."

When ordinary beings dwell in the world, they give rise to resentment and calamity; their lives are endangered and their clans extinguished, leading to immeasurable anxiety and fear. All the myriad forms of suffering in the three evil realms and the eight difficulties arise from this very source.
"Therefore, a bhikṣu renounces the world to seek the Way; with his will set upon non-action (*asaṃskṛta*) and no greed for honor or profit, he attains nirvāṇa by himself—this is the supreme bliss.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"From craving and delight arises sorrow; from craving and delight arises fear. When there is nothing to crave or delight in,"
What is there to fear? What is there to dread?
Attachment gives rise to sorrow; attachment gives rise to fear. When there is nothing to which one is attached, what is there to fear? What is there to dread?
Lust gives rise to sorrow; lust gives rise to fear. When one is liberated from lust, what sorrow and what fear can there be?
One who is devoted to the Dharma fulfills the precepts; being sincere and possessing a sense of shame, their conduct brings them close to the Path, and they are beloved by the multitude.

"When the manifestations of desire do not emerge, one speaks only after reflecting with rectitude; when the mind is free from craving and attachment, one will surely cut off the stream and cross over.
The Buddha told the four bhikṣus:

"In the past, there was a king named Pujian (Universal Peace) who was close friends with four kings of neighboring kingdoms. He invited these four kings for a month-long banquet, where they enjoyed food, drink, and entertainment with incomparable joy."
On the day of their departure, Prince Puan asked the four kings:
"What do people take as pleasure while dwelling in this world?
One king replied:
"Amusement and play are our pleasure," said one king.
"The auspicious assembly of kinsmen and music are our pleasure," said another king.
One king said: "To amass great wealth and treasures so that all desires are fulfilled according to one's will is happiness.
Another king said:
"Indulging one's desires and following the passions is the ultimate pleasure. King Puhuan replied:

"What you discuss is the root of suffering and affliction, the source of anxiety and fear; that there is pleasure first and suffering later, and that myriad forms of grief and sorrow all arise from this."
"It is not as good as tranquility—being without seeking or desire, maintaining a simple purity and abiding in the One, and finding joy in attaining the Way.
When the Four Kings heard this, they rejoiced with faith and understanding.
The Buddha told the four bhikṣus:
"The King Universal Peace at that time was I myself;
the four kings were you four people.
Although I have already explained this previously, you still do not understand it now: how can the spreading vines of birth and death be brought to rest?"

At that time, the four bhikṣus heard this teaching again; they felt shame and repented their transgressions, and their minds were awakened. They extinguished their defilements, severed desire, and attained the path of Arhatship.
Chapter 25: Anger The Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra, Chapter Twenty-five: Anger Formerly, when the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha.

At that time, Devadatta conspired with King Ajātaśatru to slander the Buddha and his disciples; the king issued an edict to the people of the country that they were not permitted to revere the Buddha, nor were they allowed to give alms to the assembly of monks when they went on their begging rounds.

At that time, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Kāśyapa, Subhūti, and others, along with the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrākapilā and her followers, each took their disciples and departed for other lands; only the Buddha and five hundred arhats remained dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Devadatta went to Ajātaśatru and consulted with the king, saying:
"The Buddha's disciples have now been dispersed; there remain only five hundred disciples still by the Buddha's side."

"I pray that Your Majesty will invite the Buddha into the city tomorrow; I shall feed five hundred great elephants until they are intoxicated. When the Buddha enters the city, I will drive these drunken elephants to trample him to death, thereby exterminating his lineage entirely. I shall then establish the Buddha's teachings to transform the world."
Upon hearing this, King Ajātaśatru was filled with joy; he went at once to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself in salutation, and said to the Buddha:
"Tomorrow I shall prepare a modest offering; I pray that the World-Honored One and his disciples will deign to take their meal within my palace."
The Buddha, knowing their plan, replied:
"Very well! I shall go there tomorrow morning."
The king withdrew and returned to tell Devadatta:
"The Buddha has already accepted the invitation; you must remember your previous plan, get the elephants drunk, and lie in wait for him."

On the following day at mealtime, the Buddha entered the city gate together with five hundred arhats. Five hundred intoxicated elephants trumpeted their trunks as they advanced, crashing against walls and breaking down trees; passersby were struck with terror, and the entire city trembled.

Five hundred arhats flew through the air, while Ānanda alone remained by the Buddha’s side. The intoxicated elephant, with its head lowered, charged straight toward the Buddha. The Buddha then raised his hand, and at that very moment, his five fingers transformed into five hundred lion kings. They roared in unison, shaking heaven and earth; thereupon, the intoxicated elephant knelt and prostrated itself upon the ground, not daring to lift its head. Its intoxication soon dissipated, and it shed tears as it repented its transgression.
The king, his ministers, and the common people were all struck with awe and solemnity.
The World-Honored One proceeded slowly to the royal palace, where he and the various arhats finished their meal and offered prayers of blessing.
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:

“By nature my mind was not clear, and I believed those slanderous words; I incited rebellious evil and plotted against the proper order. I pray that you will bestow great compassion and forgive my delusion and folly.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Ajātaśatru and the great assembly:

“There are eight matters in the world that give rise to long-standing slander; all stem from fame and reputation, as well as greed for gain and offerings, which lead to great offenses that persist through kalpas without end.”
What are the eight?
Gain, loss, defamation, praise, honor, contempt, suffering, and pleasure.
From antiquity to the present day, there have been few who have not been deluded by these.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"From antiquity until now, people have slandered one another; they have slandered the talkative and slandered the silent and patient;
they have also slandered those of moderate character— there is no one in the world who is not slandered."
The intentions of the lustful are unholy; unable to find the middle way, they alternate between disparagement and praise solely for the sake of fame and profit.
Those praised by the wise are called only "upright and virtuous. When a person of wisdom observes the precepts, there is nothing to be reviled or slandered.
“As pure as an Arhat, do not slander him; he is praised by the devas and revered by Brahmā and Śakra.
Having spoken this verse, the Buddha again addressed the king:
“In the past, there was a king who delighted in eating goose meat. He constantly dispatched hunters to spread nets and capture geese, sending one goose every day to provide for the king’s meal.”

At that time, there was a king of geese who, leading five hundred geese, flew down to seek food. The king of the geese fell into a net and was captured by a hunter, while the remaining geese flew off in alarm, circling about and refusing to leave.
At that time, there was a wild goose that followed in close pursuit, avoiding neither bow nor arrow; it cried out in grief until it vomited blood, never ceasing day or night.

When the hunter saw this, he was moved by its sense of righteousness and immediately released the goose king so that it might go with him. Having regained their leader, the flock of geese rejoiced and circled around him.
At that time, the hunter reported everything in detail to the king, and the king, moved by his sense of righteousness, decreed that geese were no longer to be captured.
The Buddha told King Ajātaśatru:
"The goose king at that time was none other than myself."
The single goose was Ānanda;
the flock of five hundred geese are now these five hundred arhats;
and the king of the country that ate the geese is now the Great King.
The hunter of that time was none other than Devadatta.

From previous lives until now, he has constantly sought to harm me; yet, through the power of my great compassion, I have been saved by him, and without harboring thoughts of resentment or malice, I have attained Buddhahood myself.
When the Buddha spoke these words, the king and his ministers were all moved to understanding.

Chapter 26: On Dust and Defilement (*Rajomala-varga*) from the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*. Once upon a time, there was a man who had no brothers. When he was a young child, his parents cherished and loved him; with sincere and earnest hearts, they desired for him to achieve success. They took him to teachers and friends, encouraging him to study and learn the arts.

The son was arrogant and haughty, never applying his mind; he would receive instructions in the morning and discard them by evening, never reciting or practicing them. Thus, as the years accumulated, he possessed no knowledge or skill.

His parents summoned him home and ordered him to manage the family estate, but the son remained conceited and indolent, showing no diligence. Consequently, the family’s affairs fell into ruin, and all undertakings were neglected and abandoned.

The son was licentious and heedless, selling off his family’s possessions to satisfy his own whims and desires. He wore his hair in disarray, went barefoot, and his clothing was unclean; he was stingy, greedy, and reckless, showing no regard for shame. Foolish and self-indulgent, he was loathed by others; all the people of the country detested him, calling him a malevolent villain, so that no one would speak to him as he walked in and out.

Unaware of one's own evil, one instead blames others; first resenting one's parents and next reproaching teachers and friends, claiming that the ancestral spirits refuse to grant their protection and have caused me to suffer such misfortunes, one thinks: "It would be better to serve the Buddha so that I may obtain his blessings."
He immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself before him, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Way of the Buddha is vast and expansive, admitting all without exception; I pray that you will grant me permission to become your disciple."
The Buddha said to this man:
"One who seeks the Way must practice pure conduct. You bring worldly defilements into my Way; what benefit is there in your coming and going in vain?"

It is better to return home and serve one’s parents with filial piety, to recite and study the teacher’s instructions without forgetting them even unto death, to diligently cultivate one’s livelihood so as to possess wealth and joy without anxiety, to restrain oneself with propriety and not transgress what is improper, to bathe and dress oneself while being careful in speech and conduct, to hold fast to the mind and maintain a single focus so that all tasks are accomplished, and to be quick in action and refined in cultivation so as to be admired by others; such conduct alone may truly be called the Way.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Failure to recite is the defilement of speech; Lack of diligence is the defilement of the household;
Lack of adornment is the defilement of physical form; Heedlessness is the defilement of one's affairs."
Avarice is the stain of generosity; unwholesome conduct is the stain of action.
In this life as well as in future lives, evil dharmas are constant stains.
Among all stains, none is more severe than delusion; one who studies should abandon this.

The bhikṣu was free from defilement. Upon hearing the verse, the man recognized his own arrogance and delusion; he immediately accepted the Buddha’s teaching and returned home with joy. Contemplating the meaning of the verse, he repented and renewed himself:

he served his parents with filial piety, honored his teachers and elders, recited and studied the scriptures and the Way, and diligently cultivated his livelihood. He upheld the precepts and restrained himself, refraining from all that was not the Path. His clan praised him for his filiality, and his village praised him for his brotherly respect; his good reputation spread far and wide, and he was acclaimed as a worthy throughout the land.
After three years, he returned to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, and earnestly and sincerely declared: "Your Honored Teaching is most true;

I have been able to preserve my physical form, abandon evil, and practice good, so that both those above and below have received blessings. I pray that you will extend your great compassion to receive me and deliver me into the Way."
The Buddha said, "Excellent!

His beard and hair fell away immediately, and he became a śramaṇa. Internally contemplating *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, as well as the Four Noble Truths and the Right Path, he ascended through diligent effort and attained the state of an Arhat.

Chapter 27: On Upholding the Teaching. *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-seven: On Upholding the Teaching. Formerly, there was an elderly Brahmin named Saccaka Nigaṇṭha, who was foremost in his country for his brilliance and great wisdom.

He had five hundred disciples who were arrogant and conceited, disregarding all under heaven; they bound their bellies with iron plates. When people asked them the reason for this, they replied, "We fear that our wisdom might overflow."

Hearing that the Buddha had appeared in the world and that his path and transformation were clear and penetrating, he harbored jealousy in his heart and found no peace whether waking or sleeping. He said to his disciples:

"I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama calls himself a Buddha; we shall now go to question him on profound and subtle matters, causing his heart to tremble with uncertainty so that he knows not what to say."

He immediately went with his disciples to the Jetavana Monastery and stood in a line outside the gate. From afar, they beheld the World-Honored One’s majestic radiance, brilliant as the rising sun; their five senses surged with emotion as joy and fear intermingled. Thereupon, they proceeded straight forward to pay homage to the Buddha, who bade them take their seats.
When he had finished sitting, the Nirgrantha asked the Buddha,
"What is called the Way?
What is called wisdom?"
What is meant by "venerable elder"?
What is meant by "handsome"?
What is meant by "śramaṇa"?
What is meant by a bhikṣu?
What is meant by a benevolent sage?
What is meant by one who possesses the Way?
"What is meant by 'upholding the precepts'?
If you can answer this, I shall be your disciple.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, observing what was appropriate for him, replied in verse:
"Always take pity on those who love learning and rectify their minds through practice; cherish only the treasure of wisdom—this is what is called the Way.
What is called a wise person does not necessarily consist in eloquent speech; one who is without fear or dread and maintains goodness is wise."
What is called "old" does not refer merely to advanced age, a matured physical form, white hair, or even simple-mindedness.
One who cherishes the Dharma of Truth, conforms to harmony, is compassionate and benevolent, and is wise, discerning, and pure—such a person is a true elder.
What is called "handsome" is not merely having a complexion like a flower; for one who is greedy, envious, and hypocritical, their words and deeds are in conflict.
To be able to abandon evil and have its roots already severed, possessing wisdom and freedom from anger—this is what is called being handsome.
What is called a śramaṇa does not necessarily mean one who has shaved his hair; if one speaks falsely, greedily takes, and possesses desires like an ordinary person, he is not a śramaṇa.
One who is able to cease evil, who is expansive and vast in propagating the Way, and who quiets the mind and extinguishes volitions—this is called a śramaṇa.
What is called a bhikṣu is not one who merely maintains the practice of begging for alms while engaging in wrong conduct and seeking fame through such means.
Rather, one who abandons sinful karma and purely cultivates the holy life (brahmacarya), whose wisdom is able to destroy evil—this is a bhikṣu.
What is called benevolent clarity (*renming*) is not something expressed by the mouth; it is when the mind is applied with such refinement that one merely accords with the external.
It means that the mind is non-active while internal conduct is pure and void; that both this and that are in a state of quiescent extinction—this is benevolent clarity.
What is called the Way does not consist in saving a single thing; rather, universally relieving all under heaven and ensuring no harm is done is the Way.
One who upholds the Dharma does not rely on many words; though they may have heard little in the past, their person acts in accordance with the Dharma.
"To guard the Way without forgetfulness is to honor the Dharma.

When Saccaka Nigaṇṭha and his five hundred disciples heard these verses from the Buddha, they were filled with joy and attained understanding. They cast aside their arrogance and all became śramaṇas; one Nigaṇṭha gave rise to the bodhicitta, and all five hundred disciples attained the path of arhatship.

Chapter 28: On the Practice of the Path. From the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Eight: On the Practice of the Path. Formerly, there was a Brahmin who left home at a young age to study the Way, yet by the time he reached sixty years of age, he had not attained the Way.

According to the dharma of the Brahmins, one does not attain the Way until age sixty; thereafter, they return home to marry and establish a household. He was born with a son who was handsome and lovely. By the time he reached the age of seven, he was exceptionally intelligent in his studies of writing and learning; his eloquence was such that his speech surpassed that of others, and he possessed conduct that exceeded the ordinary. At last, he fell gravely ill and passed away at the end of his life.

The brahmin, overcome with grief and unable to restrain himself, fell upon the corpse and fainted; though he revived, his kinsmen admonished him and forcibly took the body away to enshroud it and bury it outside the city.
The brahmin thought to himself:
"My weeping now will be of no avail; it would be better to go to King Yama and beg for my son's life.
Thereupon, the brahmin bathed and observed the fast, taking flowers and incense with him as he departed from his home. Wherever he went, he asked people:
"Where is the realm governed by King Yama?
Traveling further and further for thousands of li, he reached a deep mountain where he encountered several brahmins who had attained the Way; he questioned them as he had before.
The brahmins asked,
"What do you seek by asking about the realm governed by King Yama? He replied:
"I have a son whose eloquence and wisdom surpassed those of others; he passed away recently, and I am so overcome with grief and distress that I cannot find relief.
I wish to go to the abode of King Yama to beg for my son’s life, so that I may bring him back home to raise him until he reaches old age."
The various brahmins, pitying his ignorance, immediately told him: "The realm governed by King Yama is not a place that can be reached by a living person. We shall show you the proper way:

from here, travel westward for more than four hundred *li* until you reach a great river. Within it lies a city; this is the city where the various heavenly deities halt when they tour the world. King Yama always tours the realm on the eighth day of the month and will certainly pass through this city. If you observe the fast and maintain the precepts, you will surely see him if you go there."
The brahmin, filled with joy, accepted the instruction and departed.
Arriving at the middle of the river, he beheld a magnificent city with palaces and dwellings like those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The brahmin went to the gate, burned incense, stood on tiptoe, and offered prayers, seeking an audience with King Yama.
The King commanded his attendants to inquire into the matter, and the Brahmin replied:

"I recently fathered a son to provide for my old age; having raised him for seven years, he has recently passed away. I only pray that Your Majesty will show mercy and grant me the gift of my son's life."
King Yama said: "Excellent!
Your son is currently playing in the Eastern Garden; go there yourself and bring him back."
The brahmin went at once and saw his son playing with other children; he immediately stepped forward and embraced him, weeping as he said to him:
"Day and night I have thought of you, finding neither food nor sleep pleasant; do you not even consider the hardships endured by your parents?"
The child cried out in alarm and rebuked him, saying:

"Foolish old man, you do not understand the principles of the Way! You have resided here for but a brief moment and call me your son; do not speak such idle words, it would be better for you to leave at once. Now, I already have my own parents here; why did you suddenly embrace me so pointlessly?"
The brahmin departed dejectedly, weeping with grief.
He then thought to himself:
"I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama knows the way of the transformations of the human soul and spirit; I shall go and question him."
Thereupon, the brahmin immediately returned to seek out the Buddha’s dwelling.

At that time, the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī, preaching the Dharma to a great assembly. Upon seeing the Buddha, the brahmin prostrated himself in salutation and related the matter from beginning to end to the Buddha:

“Truly, this is my son who refused to acknowledge me; instead, he called me a foolish, senile old man. He stayed with me for but a moment and then claimed me as his father, yet there has never been any feeling of father and son between us.”
"For what reason have you acted thus?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"You are truly foolish!"

When a person dies, the spirit departs and takes on another form; parents, wives, and children meet through the convergence of causes and conditions, like guests who part as soon as they have risen. Fools, deluded and bound by attachment, reckon these things as their own; they are beset by grief, sorrow, and suffering, failing to recognize their fundamental nature, sinking into the cycle of birth and death without end or rest.

"Only those who possess wisdom do not crave affection; they awaken to suffering, abandon habitual tendencies, and diligently cultivate the sutras and precepts, thereby extinguishing perception and thought so that birth and death may come to an end.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"People exalt their wives and children, yet fail to contemplate the law of illness; the arrival of death is as sudden as a rushing torrent."
If father and son do not save one another, what hope can be placed in other relatives?
When life comes to an end, relying on kin is like a blind man clutching a lamp.
One who understands this meaning should cultivate the sutras and precepts; through diligent practice, they shall transcend the world and eliminate all suffering.
To remain far removed from all abysses like the wind dispersing clouds, and to have extinguished all discursive thought—this is knowledge and vision.
Wisdom is the elder of the world; it finds serene joy in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and by receiving the true teaching, birth and death are brought to an end.

Upon hearing the verse, the brahmin attained sudden and clear understanding; realizing that life is impermanent and that wife and children are but guests, he prostrated himself, surrendered his person, and requested to become a śramaṇa.
The Buddha said: "Excellent!"

His beard and hair fell away naturally and the dharma robes appeared upon his body; he immediately became a bhikṣu. Contemplating the meaning of the verse, he extinguished craving and severed conceptualization, attaining the path of arhatship right there on his seat.

Chapter 29: The Chapter on Extensive Explanations (*Vistara-varga*). From the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*. In the past, when the Buddha was dwelling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, he preached the Dharma to transform and guide sentient beings. Devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, and commoners would go to listen to his teachings during the three periods of the day.

At that time, there was a king named Prasenajit, who was arrogant and unrestrained in his passions. His eyes were deluded by forms, his ears distracted by sounds, his nose attached to fragrances, his mouth indulged in the five flavors, and his body craved smooth textures. His food and drink were of the utmost delicacy, yet he was never satisfied; consequently, he ate increasingly more and constantly suffered from hunger and emptiness, never ceasing his culinary preparations as he took eating to be his constant duty.

His body was so stout that his carriage could not support him; when lying down or rising, he suffered from shortness of breath, and his respiration would cease for periods, causing him to wake up in alarm. Whether sitting or reclining, he groaned constantly, suffering from the heaviness of his body; unable even to turn over, he regarded his own body as a source of affliction, and thus ordered his carriage to be prepared and set out for the place where the Buddha was.
Supported by his attendants, he paid his respects, withdrew to sit down with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Having been far removed from attending upon you and receiving your instruction, I have had no means to inquire after you. I do not know what transgression has caused my body to grow so fat?"
"I have been unable to awaken to the reason why this is so;
I have always been troubled by this, and for that reason, I have neglected my duties and failed to pay frequent visits to offer my respects.
The Buddha told the Great King:
“There are five things that cause a person to remain constantly fat:
first, eating frequently; second, being fond of sleep; third, indulgence in pleasure; fourth, freedom from sorrow; and fifth, having no responsibilities.”
"These are the five things that cause one to become fat.
If you wish not to be fat, reduce coarse and dry food; only then will you become thin.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“A person should maintain mindfulness, always knowing moderation in eating;
thereby their suffering will diminish, and by regulating their consumption they shall preserve their life.
Upon hearing this verse, the king was filled with immeasurable joy and immediately summoned his cook, saying to him:
"Recite this verse for me when it is time to serve the meal; only then may the food be served. The King took his leave and returned to the palace.

Whenever the cook served the meal, he would recite the verse. Hearing the verse, the King was filled with joy and reduced his portion by one spoonful each day. As his food intake diminished, his body became light and he grew as thin as before.

Seeing this for himself, he rejoiced and called to mind the Buddha; he immediately rose and walked on foot to where the Buddha was, prostrated before him, and when the Buddha bade him sit, the Buddha asked the king:
"Where are your chariots, horses, and retinue?"
"For what reason are you walking on foot?
The King, filled with joy, addressed the Buddha:
"Having previously received the Buddha's teaching and practiced in accordance with the Dharma, my body is now light."
"The power of the World-Honored One is such that one may know its nature by observing his gait. The Buddha told the Great King: "The people of the world are thus ignorant of impermanence;

they indulge long in sensual desires and do not contemplate the cultivation of merit. When a person dies, the spirit departs while the body remains in the tomb. The wise nourish the spirit, while the foolish nourish the body. If one can understand this, one should reverently practice the holy teaching."
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"A person who lacks learning, though old, is like a solitary ox; he merely grows fat of flesh, yet possesses no wisdom."
Birth and death are wearying; coming and going is arduous. When the mind relies on the craving for the body, further suffering arises without end.
The wise perceive this suffering and therefore abandon the body; they extinguish the will and sever desire, so that with the exhaustion of attachment, there is no further birth.

Upon hearing these verses again, the king was delighted and his mind was liberated; he immediately resolved to attain the unsurpassed, true, and right path (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), and countless listeners all attained the Dharma-eye.

Chapter 30: Hell (*Niraya-varga*). *The Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Chapter Thirty: Hell. Formerly, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a Brahmin teacher named Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, who traveled with five hundred disciples. The king and the people had previously served them together.

When the Buddha first attained the Way, he traveled with his disciples from Rājagṛha to Śrāvastī. His physical marks were resplendent and his teaching was vast and sublime; the king, the ladies of the inner court, and all the people of the land did not fail to revere him.

Thereupon Pūraṇa Kāśyapa gave rise to feelings of jealousy, desiring to destroy the World-Honored One’s exclusive claim to veneration and service. He immediately took his disciples to see King Prasenajit and addressed him himself, saying:

"We elders were the former teachers of this country who learned first; the śramaṇa Gautama appeared later in pursuit of the Way, yet he possesses no divine sanctity and falsely claims to be a Buddha."
Yet the King has abandoned me, wishing to serve him exclusively; now he desires to compete with the Buddha in the practice of the Way and its Virtue to see who is superior.
Whosoever is victorious, the King shall serve them for the rest of his life.
The king said, "Excellent!
He then prepared his carriage and proceeded to the Buddha's location; having completed his prostrations, he addressed him, saying:
"Pūraṇa Kāśyapa wishes to compete with the World-Honored One in the power of the Way and manifest supernatural transformations; I wonder if the World-Honored One would permit this?
The Buddha said, "Very well."

"A period of seven days was set for a contest of supernatural transformations. To the east of the city, on a level, spacious, and auspicious site, the King erected two high seats forty *zhang* in height, adorned with the seven precious jewels. Banners and streamers were displayed and the seating arrangements were prepared; the distance between the two seats was two *li*. The disciples of the two schools sat beneath them respectively, while the king, his ministers, and the great assembly gathered like clouds, desiring to witness the two men compete in their divine transformations."

At that time, Kāśyapa and his disciples arrived at the place of the seats first and climbed the ladder to ascend. A king of the ghost spirits named Pañcaśikha, seeing that Kāśyapa and his followers were full of false jealousy, immediately raised a great wind that blew their high seat; the cushions were overturned, the banners and streamers were scattered, and sand, grit, and stones rained down so that they could not even see.
The World-Honored One’s high seat remained serene and unmoved.
The Buddha, together with the great assembly, approached with dignified composure and suddenly ascended the high seat. All the monks sat down in silence in their respective places.
The king and his ministers, filled with increased reverence, prostrated themselves and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray that you will manifest your divine transformation to subdue false views, and cause the people of this land to clearly believe in the true and correct Dharma."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One suddenly vanished from his seat and ascended into the void, emitting a great radiance; he disappeared in the east and appeared in the west, and likewise in all four directions. From his body he emitted water and fire, alternating between the upper and lower parts, and performed twelve miraculous transformations while sitting and reclining in mid-air. He then vanished and reappeared upon his original seat. Devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts made offerings of flowers and incense, and the sound of their praises shook heaven and earth.
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, realizing he possessed no spiritual power, lowered his head in shame and dared not lift his eyes.
Thereupon, the Vajrapāṇi raised his vajra, flames erupting from its tip as he pointed it at Kāśyapa, saying:
"Why do you not manifest your supernatural transformations?"
Kāśyapa, struck with terror, leaped from his seat and fled, while his five hundred disciples scattered in all directions in a frantic rush.
The World-Honored One’s majestic countenance showed neither joy nor sorrow; he returned to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, where the king and his ministers took their leave with joyful hearts.
Thereupon Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and his disciples departed, having suffered this humiliation. On the way, they encountered an elderly female lay follower (upāsikā) named Maṇi, who cursed them, saying:

"You foolish crowd, you fail to measure yourselves; yet you wish to compete with the Buddha regarding the Way and its virtue. You are madly ignorant and deceitful, lacking any sense of shame. You ought not even to walk about in this world with such faces!"
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, feeling ashamed before his disciples, went to the banks of the river and deceived them, saying:
"I shall now cast myself into the water and will surely be reborn in the Brahma Heaven; if I do not return, you may know that such is its bliss."
The disciples waited for him but he did not return; they deliberated among themselves, saying, "Our teacher must have ascended to heaven; why should we remain here?
One by one, they threw themselves into the water, hoping to follow their teacher, but dragged down by their own karma, they all fell into hell.
On a later day, when the king heard that such was the case, he was greatly astonished and marveled at it. He went to where the Buddha was and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The master Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and his disciples are deluded and ignorant; by what cause has it come to this?"
The Buddha told the king:
"Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and his disciples have two grave offenses:
first, their three poisons are rampant yet they claim to have attained the Way; second, they slander the Tathāgata, desiring to receive his veneration and service."

Because of these two offenses, one should fall into hell; driven by the pressure of such calamity and guilt, one is forced to throw oneself into a river, where upon death and the departure of the spirit, one undergoes immeasurable suffering.
Therefore, the wise guard and restrain their minds; when no evil arises within, external transgressions do not reach them.

It is like a frontier city bordering on enemies; when its defenses are firm and secure, it has nothing to fear, those within dwell in peace, and external invaders cannot enter. The wise person who protects themselves is likewise so.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"False testimony for the sake of seeking bribes, conduct that is already unrighteous, slandering the virtuous to unjustly govern the world—the sins of such a person draw them into a pit."

"Just as the walls of a border city are secure both inside and out, one must guard one's own mind so that unrighteousness does not arise; for a deficiency in conduct leads to sorrow and causes one to fall into hell.
After the Buddha had spoken these verses, he addressed the king again:
"In times long past, there were two monkey kings, each presiding over five hundred monkeys."
One king, conceiving a mind of jealousy and desiring to kill the other king in order to rule alone, went forth to fight him; however, being repeatedly defeated, he withdrew in shame and humiliation.

Reaching the shore of the great ocean, amidst a bend of the sea, there was a mass of water-foam piled up by the wind to a height of several hundred *zhang*. The foolish monkey king, taking it to be the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*), said to his troop:

"I have long heard that within the ocean lies a Snowy Mountain, where one may enjoy happiness and indulge in sweet fruits at will. Today I have finally seen it; I shall go ahead to inspect it. If it is truly pleasant, I shall not return; if it is not pleasant, I shall come back to tell you."
Thereupon, they climbed the tree and leaped with all their might into the mass of foam, drowning at the bottom of the sea.

Seeing that the others did not emerge, the remaining ones marveled, thinking they must surely be enjoying great pleasure; one by one they threw themselves in, joining the throng and perishing by drowning.
The Buddha told the king:
"The envious monkey king at that time was none other than Pūraṇa Kāśyapa;
the troop of followers were the five hundred disciples of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa."
"That monkey king was none other than myself. In a previous life, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa harbored jealousy;

dragged by his own transgressions, he threw himself into a mass of foam, severing his kin and ending his lineage. Now, having again slandered me, he has been cast into the rivers; such is the retribution for his sins, continuing through infinite kalpas."
Upon hearing this, the king believed and understood it, paid his respects, and departed.
Long ago, there were seven bhikṣus who entered the mountains to study the Way; for twelve years they were unable to attain the Way.
They deliberated among themselves, saying:

"The study of the Way is exceedingly difficult; one must disfigure one's appearance and maintain strict discipline, enduring cold and suffering without avoidance. One begs for food for a lifetime, enduring insults that are hard to bear. The Way is ultimately unattainable and offenses are difficult to expiate. To labor fruitlessly until perishing in the mountains is not as good as returning home to establish a household, marry, raise children, and extensively engage in profitable enterprises with a joyful heart and pleasant mind."
"How could they know what would happen later?
Thereupon, the seven men immediately rose and departed from the mountain.
The Buddha perceived from afar that they were destined for deliverance; yet, unable to endure their minor suffering, they would eventually fall into hell—a state truly pitiable and tragic.
The Buddha immediately manifested as a śramaṇa and went to the mouth of the valley, where he encountered seven bhikṣus.
The manifested man asked them, "I have long heard that you have been studying the Way; why have you come out now?"
The seven men replied:

"The study of the Way involves arduous toil, and its roots of affliction are difficult to uproot. To wander for alms and endure humiliation is hard to bear; moreover, there are no donors in these mountains. For many years we have lived in humble austerity, yet in vain we have exhausted ourselves—enlightenment cannot be attained."
Furthermore, he wished to return home to extensively seek profitable enterprises, amass great wealth, and only later, when old, seek the Way.
The transformed śramaṇa said: “Stop! Stop!”
Listen to what I say: human life is impermanent;

one cannot guarantee that morning will be followed by evening. Although practicing the Way is difficult, it brings suffering first and joy later; whereas living as a householder is fraught with hardship, offering no respite for billions of eons. To wish that one’s wife and children remain together and share in peace and benefit, or to desire eternal happiness without encountering calamity, is like taking poison to treat an illness—it only increases the ailment without providing any relief.

"All that has form within the three realms is accompanied by sorrow and affliction; only through faith and precepts, with a mind free from negligence, and through diligence in attaining the Way, can all sufferings be brought to an end forever.
Thereupon, the transformed śramaṇa manifested the physical marks of a Buddha; his radiant image was majestic and sublime as he spoke this verse:
"Learning is difficult, abandoning sin is difficult, And dwelling as a householder is likewise difficult."
To assemble and cease from harm, and to share in common benefit, is difficult; there is no hardship greater than existence.
For a bhikṣu, the difficulty of begging for alms is great; how can one not exert oneself?
Through diligence, one attains spontaneity, and in the end, has no desire for others.
With faith, the precepts are perfected; from the precepts, one attains much treasure.
Likewise, through them one finds a harmonious mate and receives offerings wherever one goes.
Sitting alone in a single place, walking alone without indulgence—
"Guarding the One to rectify the mind, the heart finds joy dwelling among the trees.

Thereupon, the seven bhikṣus beheld the Buddha’s physical marks and, hearing this verse, were filled with shame, fear, and trembling. Prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet; composing their minds and repenting their transgressions, they paid homage and departed. Returning to the mountains, they exerted themselves with life-risking diligence, contemplating the meaning of the verse, guarding the One and rectifying the mind while dwelling in quietude and extinction, and thereby attained the path of Arhatship.

Chapter 31: The Elephant. *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Chapter Thirty-one on the Elephant. Formerly, when Rāhula had not yet attained the Way, his nature was coarse and wild, and his speech lacked sincerity and faith.
The Buddha commanded Rāhula:
"Go and dwell within the Kṣemaka Vihāra; guard your speech, restrain your mind, and diligently cultivate the sūtras and precepts.
Rāhula received these instructions, paid his respects, and departed. He stayed there for ninety days, feeling shame and remorse, repenting day and night without ceasing.

The Buddha went to see him; Rāhula, filled with joy, approached and prostrated before the Buddha. He prepared a corded seat and received the Buddha with reverence. As the Buddha sat upon the corded seat, he addressed Rāhula, saying:
"Take water from the basin and wash my feet."
Rāhula received the instruction and washed the Buddha’s feet.
When the washing of the feet was finished, the Buddha said to Rāhula:
“Do you see the water used for washing the feet in the basin?”
Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Indeed, I have seen it.
The Buddha said to Rāhula:
"Can this water be used for drinking, eating, washing,
or rinsing? Rāhula replied,
"It cannot be used anymore."
Why is this? This water was originally pure and clear, but having now been used to wash the feet and thus received the dust and grime, for this reason it can no longer be used.
The Buddha said to Rāhula:

"You are just like this. Although you are my son and the grandson of a king, having renounced worldly glory and emolument to become a śramaṇa, you do not contemplate diligence, nor do you restrain your body or guard your speech. With the filth of the three poisons filling your breast, you are just like this water—no longer fit for use."
The Buddha said to Rāhula,
"Discard the water in the basin.
Rāhula immediately discarded it.
The Buddha said to Rāhula,
"Even though a washbasin is empty, can it be used to hold food and drink?
Rāhula replied to the Buddha:
"It cannot be used. Why is this?
Because although it bears the name of a washing basin, it has already been defiled by impurities.
The Buddha said to Rāhula:

"You are just like this: though you have become a śramaṇa, you lack sincerity and faith; your character is stubborn and you do not contemplate diligence. Having once borne an evil reputation, you are like a washbasin unfit for holding food."
The Buddha pushed away the basin with his toe; at that moment, the basin spun around and ran off, leaping up and falling down several times before finally coming to rest.
The Buddha said to Rāhula, "Do you cherish this basin, fearing it might break?"
Rāhula said to the Buddha, "The vessel for washing the feet is an object of little value; though I cherish it in my mind, I do not regard it with great earnestness.
The Buddha said to Rāhula:
"You are just like this.

Although you have become a śramaṇa, you do not restrain your body or speech; your coarse words and evil talk cause much injury. You are not loved by the multitude and are not cherished by the wise. When your body dies and your spirit departs, you will transmigrate through the three miserable realms, experiencing immeasurable suffering as you are born and die again and again."
"The Buddhas and the worthy sages do not cherish [their bodies], just as you said they do not spare their basins.
When Rāhula heard this, he was filled with shame, remorse, and trepidation.
The Buddha said to Rāhula:
“Listen to a parable I shall tell.
Once there was a king who possessed a great elephant, fierce and capable in battle; its strength and power were calculated to surpass those of five hundred small elephants.”

That king raised an army intending to attack a rebellious state. He equipped the elephants with iron armor, and elephant-riders drove them forward. Pairs of spears and halberds were fastened to the two tusks of the elephants; furthermore, two swords were tied to their two ears, curved-blade knives were bound to their four legs, and iron clubs were attached to their tails. Thus, all nine weapons upon the elephants were made formidable and sharp.
Although the elephant conceals its trunk and protects it so as not to use it in combat, the elephant trainer rejoices, knowing that the elephant is protecting itself. Why is this?
Because the elephant's trunk is soft and fragile; were it struck by an arrow, it would die immediately. Therefore, it does not extend its trunk to fight.

The elephant fought for a very long time and extended its trunk to seek the sword; the elephant-keeper did not give it to him. Thinking that this fierce elephant would not spare his own life, he extended his trunk to seek the sword, wishing to place it upon the tip of his trunk. The king and his ministers, pitying this great elephant, ceased making him fight.
The Buddha told Rāhula:
"When a person commits the nine evils, they must guard their speech alone, just as this great elephant guards its trunk and does not fight.
