The reason for this is that it fears death by being struck by an arrow."
Human beings are also like this: the reason one guards one's speech is that one should fear the suffering of the three miserable realms and the hells.

Those who commit all ten evil deeds and fail to guard their speech are like this great elephant, which loses its life because it does not consider that it has been struck by an arrow, but instead sticks out its trunk and flaps its ears to fight.
Human beings are also like this: if they commit all ten evil deeds, they will not only suffer the bitter pains and torments of the three miserable realms.

If they practice the ten wholesome deeds by restraining their speech, body, and mind, and do not commit any evils, they can attain the Way and remain forever free from the three miserable realms, devoid of the afflictions of birth and death.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"I am like an elephant in battle, Unafraid of being struck by arrows; Always with sincerity and faith, I deliver those who lack precepts."
"Just as an elephant, when well-tamed, is fit to be the king's mount; so too, one who is tamed becomes a noble person and receives sincere trust.

Having heard the Buddha’s earnest and compassionate instruction, Rāhula was moved with gratitude and exhorted himself to diligence, never forgetting it even to the marrow of his bones. Through his diligent effort, gentleness, and earth-like patience, his perceptions became tranquil, and he attained the path of an Arhat.

In the past, when the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove Monastery in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, he expounded the Great Dharma for the fourfold assembly of disciples, as well as for devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, ministers, and commoners.

At that time, there was an elder householder named Hatthaka who came to where the Buddha was staying. He paid homage to the Buddha, withdrew to sit on one side, and with palms joined and kneeling for a long time, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"I have long received your grand transformation and have revered and yearned to behold your countenance; however, due to private constraints, I have not been able to do so. I pray you will grant me your compassionate forgiveness."
The World-Honored One bade him sit and asked where he had come from and what his name was.
Kneeling with his right knee on the ground, he replied:
"I am of the householder caste; my name is Khadira. In the time of the former king, I served as the king’s elephant trainer."
The Buddha asked the householder,
"How many methods are there for training an elephant? He replied:
"One always uses three things to tame a great elephant.
What are these three?

First, using a strong hook to catch its mouth and attach it to the harness; second, reducing its food so that it is constantly hungry and emaciated; third, striking it with a staff to inflict pain and suffering."
"By means of these three matters, one attains discipline and excellence.
He asked again:
"By what are these three matters governed and treated?"
He replied:

"An iron hook is used to hook the mouth in order to control a strong mouth; food and drink are withheld to control the wildness of the body; and the application of the whip and staff is to subdue the mind—it is through these very means that it becomes tamed."
He asked, "For what purpose is this prostration performed? He replied:
"Once they have been thus subdued, they may be mounted upon the king’s vehicle and made to fight; they will advance or retreat at will without any obstruction.
He then asked the householder:
"Is this the only method?"
"Is there any other method? He replied,
"The method for taming elephants is precisely like this."
The Buddha told the householder:
"One who can tame an elephant can likewise tame oneself. He then said:
“I do not understand the meaning of ‘self-discipline.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will clarify and expound upon what I have not yet heard.
The Buddha told the householder:
“I also have three matters by which I discipline all people, and by which I have disciplined myself to reach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

First, through utmost sincerity, I control the karma of speech; second, through compassionate integrity, I subdue the rigidity of the body; third, through wisdom, I extinguish the delusive veil of the mind.”

"By upholding these three matters, one delivers all beings, leaves behind the three evil realms, attains the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) for oneself, and does not encounter the sorrows, lamentations, suffering, and afflictions of birth and death.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Just as the elephant named Dhanapāla, Fierce and harmful, difficult to restrain,"
Bound by the tether and denied food, he still yearns for the wild elephant;
yet with the original intent to practice purity, and through the constant practice of what brings peace,
he completely abandons and subdues the fetters, just as a hook restrains and tames an elephant.
Delighting in the Path and being heedless not, one who can always guard their own mind thereby uproots bodily suffering, like an elephant emerging from a bog.
Though well-trained, it is like a newly harnessed steed; it is also the most excellent of elephants.
It is better to discipline oneself;
for others cannot reach that which no one else has reached—only those who discipline themselves can arrive at the realm of self-mastery.

Upon hearing these verses, the householder experienced immeasurable joy and celebration; his inner mind was liberated, and he immediately attained the Dharma-eye. Among those who heard them, countless beings all attained the fruit of the Path. **Chapter 32:

On Craving and Desire (Kāma-varga)** *Faju Piyu Jing* (Verses on the Dharma with Parables), Chapter Thirty-Two: On Craving and Desire. Formerly, when the Buddha was staying at the Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain Monastery in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, he turned the Great Wheel of Dharma for devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits.

At that time, there was a man who left his home, wife, and children and came to where the Buddha was; he paid homage to the Buddha and requested to become a śramaṇa. The Buddha immediately accepted him and ordained him as a śramaṇa, commanding him to sit beneath a tree and contemplate the Way and its virtue.

Having received these instructions, the bhikṣu entered the deep mountains, traveling more than a hundred li from the vihāra. Sitting alone among the trees, he contemplated the Way for three years; yet his mind lacked firm resolve, and he desired to retreat. He thought to himself, "I have left my home to seek the Way through such diligent hardship, yet it would be better to return early and see my wife and children."
Having formed this thought, he rose and departed from the mountain.
The Buddha, perceiving through his holy penetration that this bhikṣu ought to attain the Way but was returning due to folly,
employed his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to manifest as a śramaṇa and went out to meet him on the road, where they encountered one another.
The manifested person then asked: "Whence have you come?
This ground is level; we may sit together here and converse."
Thereupon, the two men sat down to rest and spoke, immediately replying to the transformed person:

"We left our homes, wives, and children to seek the life of śramaṇas; yet dwelling here in these deep mountains we have been unable to attain the Way. Parting from our wives and children has not accorded with our original vows; our lives are being wasted in vain labor without gain. We now wish to repent and return to see our wives and children, to enjoy ourselves together as we please, and thereafter make further plans."
After a short while, there was an old monkey who had long since left the midst of the trees and lived in a place where no trees grew.
The transformed śramaṇa asked the bhikṣu,
"For what reason does this monkey stay alone on the level ground?"
"There are no trees here; why do you find pleasure in this?
The bhikṣu replied to the transformed person, "I have observed these monkeys for a long time, and it is for two reasons that I have come to dwell here."
What are these two?
First, because they have many wives, children, and attendants, they cannot obtain food and drink or enjoy themselves at their pleasure.
Second, they constantly climb up and down trees day and night until the soles of their feet are worn through, finding no rest.
"It was for these two reasons that we abandoned the trees and came to dwell here.
While the two men were speaking, they saw the monkey run back and climb up the tree again.
The transformed śramaṇa said to the bhikṣus:
"Do you see that monkey returning to the trees?
He replied, "I see it.
This foolish insect, having escaped from the trees, returns to them in the midst of a noisy, chaotic crowd, never wearying of its toil."
The transformed person spoke again:
"You are just like this; how are you any different from this monkey?
You originally came into these mountains for two reasons."
What are these two? First, because one regards wife, children, and home as a prison; second, because one regards sons, daughters, and kinsmen as shackles.

You have come for this reason—to seek the Way and sever the suffering of birth and death—yet now you wish to return home, once again donning shackles and entering the prison, where your attachment to affection and longing will lead you directly to hell.

The transformed śramaṇa immediately manifested the marks and signs of a buddha, sixteen feet tall and golden-hued, with radiance that illuminated and moved the entire mountain. Birds and beasts flew and ran toward the light; they all recognized their past lives and felt remorse within their hearts.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"As when a tree's roots are deep and firm, Though it be cut, it grows again;
If the mind of craving is not utterly eliminated, One shall inevitably undergo suffering once more."
As a monkey leaves one tree only to find release and yet run back to another, so it is with the multitude:
having emerged from prison, they enter it again.
When habit is joined with arrogance, and thought dwells upon sensual desire, [suffering follows].
Self-conceit blinds one so that nothing is seen;
the fetter of craving is like a creeping vine. Only through the discernment of wisdom can one sever the very root of the mind.
"Thoughts spread like creeping vines; craving is deep and bottomless. Thus do old age and death increase.

Seeing the Buddha’s radiant countenance and hearing these verses, the bhikṣu was struck with awe and trembled. Prostrating himself on the ground, he repented and apologized for his transgressions. He inwardly reproached himself, immediately withdrew his mind, and practiced counting, following, stopping, and contemplating. In the presence of the Buddha, he attained arhatship.
The various devas came to hear [the teaching] and all rejoiced; they scattered flowers as an offering and praised it immeasurably.
From the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Volume Three: Formerly, four thousand *li* south of Rājagṛha there was a kingdom where several thousand Brahmins were served and honored.

At that time, the kingdom suffered a great drought for three years with no rain. The king offered prayers and sacrifices to all the various deities without exception, yet to no avail. He questioned the brahmins regarding the cause of this misfortune, and the brahmins replied:
"Once we have completed our fasts and purifications, we shall dispatch someone to communicate with Brahmā to inquire about these calamitous portents."
The king said: "Excellent!
Please inform me of whatever may be lacking for the observance of the fast."
The brahmins said:
"We shall require twenty cartloads of firewood, ghee, honey, oil, flowers, incense, banners, and canopies, as well as gold and silver sacrificial vessels—all of these we must have."

The king immediately prepared the materials and went outside the city. At a level and expansive site seven *li* from the city, he piled firewood into a mountain-like heap. They exhorted one another, saying that whoever was not sparing of their own body would ultimately be reborn in the Brahma Heaven (*Brahmaloka*). Seven men were selected; they were to be cast into the fire and dispatched to the Brahma Heaven.
Once the seven men had finished receiving the sacrificial offerings and the prayers for blessing, they were crowded onto the woodpile; fire was set from below to burn them to death.

As the smoke and flames blazed up and the heat reached them directly, the seven men were filled with terror and sought help to their left and right, but there was no one to save them. Raising their voices, they cried out:
"Within the three realms, surely there is one of great compassion who will take pity on our distress! We pray that you accept our taking refuge!"

The Buddha, knowing this from afar, went to rescue them at once; appearing in the midst of space with his marks and signs of excellence, the seven men saw the Buddha and leaped for joy in grief and delight, saying:
"We pray only that you will take refuge in us and save us from our burning pain."
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Many take refuge in themselves, In mountains, rivers, and tree spirits; They fashion images and establish shrines, Praying and sacrificing in pursuit of blessings."
Taking refuge in such [a way] is neither auspicious nor supreme; they cannot come to deliver you from your manifold sufferings.
But those who take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and in the Path, the Virtue, and the Four Truths, will surely behold right wisdom.
Birth and death are extreme suffering; one attains deliverance through the Truths. Having crossed over the world’s eight hardships, these manifold sufferings are eliminated.
Taking refuge in the Triple Gem is the most auspicious and supreme; it alone exists for the purpose of delivering one from all suffering.
When the Buddha had finished speaking, the sound of the "thirst-fire" (tṛṣṇāgni) immediately ceased. The seven men attained peace of mind and experienced immeasurable joy.

The brahmins and the people of the country were all struck with awe; they gazed upward at the World-Honored One’s radiant and magnificent countenance as he manifested his body in various ways—disappearing in the east and appearing in the west, moving freely between existence and non-existence—and as water and fire issued from his body, shimmering in five colors. Upon seeing this, the multitude prostrated themselves, offering their lives in refuge.
Thereupon, the seven men emerged from beneath the firewood; with grief and joy mingled within them, they spoke these verses:
"To see a noble person is a joy; To have one to rely upon is a joy; To be free from fools is a joy;
To practice virtue alone is a joy."
Maintaining right view brings joy; teaching the Dharma to one another brings joy; being without contention with the world brings joy; and possessing the precepts brings constant joy.
It causes the virtuous to dwell in joy, like a gathering of kinsmen; those who draw near to the benevolent and wise become learned, lofty, and far-reaching.
When these seven men had spoken this verse, they and the various brahmins requested to become his disciples.
The Buddha accepted them, and they all became śramaṇas, attaining the path of arhatship.

The king and his subjects all practiced the Way; soon the heavens sent down great rain, the country became abundant, and the people were at peace. The transformation through the Way flourished, and there was none who did not rejoice to hear it.
*Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Volume Four, translated by the Śramaṇas Dharmakṣema and Dharmayaśas during the Jin Dynasty.
The Thirty-second Chapter on Similes Regarding Desire, Part Two.

In the past, when the Buddha was in Śrāvastī preaching the Dharma to devas and humans, there lived in the city a brahmin householder of immeasurable wealth. He was stingy and greedy by nature and took no pleasure in giving alms; he always kept his doors closed when eating and disliked the company of guests. Whenever it was time for him to eat, he would invariably command his gatekeeper to shut the doors firmly, ensuring that no one should enter the interior by mistake, so that beggars and seekers, as well as śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, could not even obtain a sight of him.
At that time, the elder suddenly craved fine food and commanded his wife to prepare a meal, instructing her to slaughter a plump chicken, season it with ginger and pepper, and roast it until cooked.

The food and delicacies were prepared immediately; he ordered the gates outside to be closed, and the husband and wife sat down together with their young son seated in the center, where they ate and drank together.
The parents took pieces of chicken and placed them in the child’s mouth, doing this repeatedly without ever ceasing.

The Buddha, knowing that this elder possessed the merit from past lives to be delivered, transformed himself into a śramaṇa. While the family was sitting down to eat, he appeared before them and, offering a blessing, said:
"By giving even a small amount in alms, one may attain great wealth."
The elder raised his head and saw the transformed śramaṇa, whereupon he reviled him, saying:
"You are a man of the Way, yet you have no sense of shame; why do you intrude upon my family while they are sitting here eating?"
The śramaṇa replied, "You yourself are foolish and do not know shame; why, then, should I, a mendicant, feel shame?
The householder asked:
"I am enjoying myself with my wife and family; why should I feel shame?
The śramaṇa replied, "You have killed your father and taken your mother's wife to provide for an enemy, yet you know no shame. Instead, you ask why I, a beggar, should not feel ashamed."
Thereupon the śramaṇa spoke these verses:
"The branches of what is born do not cease; One merely uses food to feed greed and desire.
It nourishes enmity and increases the burial mounds; The foolish person is always in a state of frantic haste."
Though a prison has iron hooks and cangues, the wise do not call it secure;
the fool sees the adornments of wife and children and becomes so deeply stained by attachment that his love is very secure.
The wise declare that love is a prison, deep and firm, from which it is difficult to escape.
"Therefore, you should sever and cast them away; do not associate with desires for the sake of peace.
Upon hearing this verse, the elder was startled and asked him, "O practitioner, for what reason do you speak these words?"
The practitioner replied, "The chicken on the table was your father in a previous life; because of his stinginess and greed, he was constantly reborn among chickens to be eaten by you."

This child was formerly a rākṣasa. When you were a great merchant leader traveling by ship into the sea, you repeatedly drifted and fell into the land of the rākṣasas, where you were devoured by them.
When his lifespan of five hundred such lives has ended, he will come to be born as your son; because your remaining karmic retribution is not yet exhausted, he comes now with the intent to harm you.
As for this wife, she was your mother in a previous life; because their bonds of affection were so deep and firm, she has now returned to become your wife.

Now you are foolish and do not recognize your past lives; you have killed your father to nourish your enemy and taken your mother as your wife. Wandering through the cycle of birth and death across the five realms without end—who could know the extent of your circuiting through these five paths?
"Only those who are practitioners of the Way can see this and perceive that; how could the ignorant not feel shame?

Thereupon, the elder’s hair stood on end suddenly as if he were struck with fear. The Buddha manifested his majestic spiritual power to cause him to recognize his past lives. Upon seeing the Buddha, the elder immediately recognized his own past existence; he then immediately repented and apologized to the Buddha, received the five precepts, and as the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Once, when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, preaching the Dharma at Jetavana, there was a young bhikṣu who entered the city for alms.

He saw a young woman of incomparable beauty; his mind became fixated on sensual desire, and he was so entangled in delusion that he could not resolve it. Consequently, he fell ill; his appetite vanished, his complexion grew haggard, and he lay prostrate, unable to rise.
A fellow practitioner went to inquire after him, asking, "What is troubling you?
The young bhikṣu explained his situation in detail:
he wished to destroy his resolve for the Path, yet because his desires were not fulfilled, he was bound by grief, which had become his illness.

His fellow students’ admonitions and exhortations did not enter his ears; they then forcibly supported him and brought him to the Buddha’s presence, reporting the circumstances of the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the young bhikṣu:
“Your wish is easily obtained; there is no need for such distress and anxiety. I shall employ skillful means to resolve it for you.”
"Arise and eat and drink!
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu’s mind became serene and joyful, and his constricted breath was immediately released.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, taking this bhikṣu along with the great assembly, entered the city of Śrāvastī and went to the house of the beautiful woman. The beautiful woman had already died, and her corpse had lain for three days; the family wailed in grief, unable to bear the thought of burying her, as her body festered with a foul stench and impurities flowed forth.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

"That woman whom you coveted and were deluded by is now like this; all things are impermanent and change in the space of a breath. The fool observes only the external and does not see its evil, remaining entangled in the net of sin while regarding it as pleasure."
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Seeing forms, the mind becomes deluded; It does not contemplate or observe impermanence.
The fool deems them beautiful and good, How could he know they are not real?"
Enveloped by sensual pleasure, like a silkworm making its cocoon, the wise are able to sever and cast it aside; without looking back, they eliminate all suffering.
Those whose minds are set on heedlessness perceive sensual desire as pure.
When the sentiment of affection increases intensely, from this one constructs a prison.
One who awakens the mind to extinguish lust, constantly mindful of the impurity of desire,
emerges from that evil prison and is able to sever the affliction of old age and death.

Thereupon, the young bhikṣu saw this woman; though she had been dead for three days, her face was bloated and rotting, and its stench was unbearable. Furthermore, hearing the World-Honored One’s verses of pure instruction, he was struck with regret and attained awakening, realizing his own delusions and errors. He prostrated himself before the Buddha, bowing his head in repentance.
The Buddha granted them refuge and led them back to the Jetavana Monastery; there, they applied themselves with life-long diligence and attained the path of Arhatship.

The countless members of the great assembly who witnessed the impurity of form and desire, and who gained faith in the evidence of impermanence, had their cravings and expectations cease, and likewise attained the traces of the Path.
Once, when the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī, preaching the Dharma for devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits,
there lived at that time a great elder of immense wealth who had an only son about twelve or thirteen years of age.

When his parents passed away, the son was still young and did not yet understand the principles of livelihood or managing a household; he squandered his wealth until it was exhausted within a few years, and later, when he went begging for alms, he could not even provide for himself.

His father had a close friend who was a householder of immeasurable great wealth. One day, seeing him, the householder inquired about his circumstances; out of compassion, he took him back to manage his affairs, gave him his daughter in marriage, and provided him with countless servants, carriages, horses, and riches, further building him a residence so that he might establish a household.
Being lazy and lacking the capacity for planning, he was unable to support himself; as his wealth was exhausted through dissipation, he fell into even greater hunger and distress.
Because of his daughter, the elder provided him with further resources, yet it was just as before, until he once again reached a state of poverty.

The elder frequently sent provisions, but [the husband] used them without restraint; thinking he could not achieve success, the elder wished to seize his wife and remarry her to another, so the clan members discussed the matter together.
The woman heard of this in secret and returned to tell her husband:
"My family’s powerful group can seize you because they believe you cannot make a living; what do you intend to do, and what plan will you devise?"
Upon hearing his wife’s words, the husband was filled with shame and reflected to himself:

"It is because of my meager merit that I have been born without protection; I have not practiced the methods for managing a household or sustaining a livelihood. Now I shall lose my wife and must once again resort to begging as before."
"Having indulged in affection and become attached through lustful passion, how can we now endure the separation that must arise?

Thinking this over repeatedly, he gave rise to an evil thought; taking his wife into the room, he said, "I shall now die together with you," and he immediately stabbed his wife and then stabbed himself, so that both husband and wife died together.

The servants and slaves fled in alarm to inform the elder; the elder, along with his family members, came in haste to look at him. Seeing that it was already so, they encoffined and dispatched him according to the customary laws of the land.

The elder was filled with great sorrow for his daughter, his grief never leaving him for even a moment. Suddenly, he heard that the Buddha was still in the world teaching and preaching the Dharma, and that those who saw him would rejoice, forgetting their sorrows and casting off their afflictions. He took his family and household members and went to where the Buddha was; having paid homage to the Buddha, they withdrew to sit at one side.
The Buddha asked the householder:
"Where have you come from?
Why do you have such an unhappy and sorrowful expression?"
The elder replied: "Our family lacks virtue;

previously we gave one daughter in marriage, but she encountered a foolish man who could not provide for her livelihood. He sought to seize her from me, so I killed both my wife and myself, that we might die together in this manner."
"I have sent him back to pay his respects to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the elder:

"Greed and anger are the common ailments of the world; ignorance and lack of wisdom are the gateways to calamity. It is because of these that beings fall into the abyss of the three realms and five destinies, transmigrating through birth and death for countless kalpas. They endure myriad forms of suffering yet still do not repent—how much less could a foolish person recognize this?"
"The poison of greed destroys the individual and the clan; its harm extends to all sentient beings, let alone between husband and wife.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The fool binds himself with greed, Seeking no way to cross to the other shore."
Because greed is a craving for wealth, it harms others and harms oneself as well.
With the mind of desire as the field, and lust, anger, and delusion as the seeds,
one who gives to those who have transcended the world obtains immeasurable merit.
"With few companions but much wealth, the merchant is struck with trepidation and fear;
for sensual desires are thieves that harm one's life, therefore wisdom does not crave desire.

At that time, having heard the Buddha recite this verse, the elder was filled with joy and gladness, forgetting his sorrows and casting off his afflictions. There and then, upon his seat, he and all those present—both great and small, as well as the entire assembly—destroyed twenty billion evils and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

Once, when the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī, preaching the Dharma for devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, ministers, and commoners, there were two wandering sons who were close friends.

They always followed one another as if they were one body, never differing. The two of them deliberated together, wishing to become śramaṇas, and immediately brought each other to the place where the Buddha was. They paid homage to the Buddha, knelt with palms joined, and said to him:
“We wish to become śramaṇas; we pray only that you will grant us permission.”
The Buddha accepted them, and they immediately became śramaṇas.
The Buddha ordered the two men to dwell together in one room.

While living together, they thought only of worldly affection, love, and glory; they further conversed with one another about sensual desires and physical forms, praising their beauty and remaining exclusively attached to them without letting go, without ceasing their thoughts, and without reflecting on impermanence, filth, or impurity. Because of this, they became oppressed, and illness arose within them.
With his eye of wisdom, the Buddha knew that her thoughts were disordered; her mind ran toward desire and could not remain settled, and for this reason she was not yet liberated.
The Buddha sent one person away and then himself manifested as another person who entered the room and asked her:
"The intentions we both contemplate do not differ; let us go together to observe it, so that by seeing its physical form we may know what it is like."
"It is merely empty conceptualization; it is exhausting and of no benefit.
The two followed each other to a village of courtesans. There, within the village, the Buddha transformed himself into a courtesan. They entered her house together, and he addressed her, saying:

"We are practitioners who have received the prohibitions and precepts of the Buddha and do not violate the matter of the body. We wish to observe the appearance of women; you should receive our payment according to the law."

Thereupon, the transformed woman immediately removed her necklaces, perfumed garments, and stood naked, her foul odor making her difficult to approach. As the two men looked at her, they saw her impurity exposed in its entirety. The transformed śramaṇa then said to one of them:

"The beauty of women consists merely of cosmetics, fragrant powders, various flowers, bathing, and the application of scented ointments; they wear garments of many colors to cover their impurities and forcibly mask them with perfumes, desiring to be viewed by others. It is like a leather bag filled with excrement—what is there to covet?"
Thereupon, the transformed bhikṣu spoke these verses:
“I know your origin, O Desire: You are born from the mind through conceptualization.
If I do not conceptualize you, Then you shall no longer exist.”
If the mind finds approval, it becomes desire; why need one limit it only to the five desires?
To be able to swiftly sever the five desires is what constitutes true courage and strength.
Without desire, there is nothing to fear; in tranquil detachment, there is no sorrow or affliction.
"Desiring to eliminate the latent tendencies and fetters, this is to emerge forever from the abyss.

When the Buddha had finished speaking these verses, he manifested his radiant form. Upon seeing this, the bhikṣu felt shame and remorse for his transgressions; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he paid homage to the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma to him once more, and he joyfully attained liberation, immediately becoming an arhat.
One man returned and saw that his companion’s countenance was more joyful than usual; he immediately asked his companion why he alone appeared thus. The companion then related the facts as they were:
how the Buddha’s great compassion delivers beings in such a manner, and how, by the grace of the World-Honored One, he had been spared from all suffering.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu spoke these verses again:
"Day and night one thinks of sensual desires, The mind runs toward them without ceasing.
Seeing that women are impure and exposed, When such thoughts are extinguished, there is no sorrow."
Upon hearing this verse, the companion bhikṣu reflected within himself; he severed desire and extinguished conceptualization, immediately attaining the Dharma-eye.

Chapter 33: On Gain and Honor (*Liyang-pin*). The *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Chapter Thirty-three: On Gain and Honor. In the past, the Buddha led his disciples to the country of Kutumbī, to the Monastery of Beautiful Sound (*Meiyin Jingśe*), where he preached the Dharma for the sake of devas, humans, spirits, and nāgas.

At that time, the king of that country was named Udayana. He had a chief consort who practiced benevolence and love, whose reputation for purity was manifest, and whom the king prized for her integrity, privately honoring her with constant respect.

Hearing that the Buddha had come to convert them, they prepared their carriages and went out together to the place where the Buddha was. Having arrived, they paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew to sit in their usual places.

For the sake of the king, his consort, and the court ladies, the Buddha preached on impermanence, suffering, and emptiness; how beings arise from causes and conditions, the suffering of meeting with those one dislikes and being separated from those one loves, and how through merit one is born in heaven while through evil one enters the abyss.

The king’s consorts were filled with joy and faith; they each received the five precepts and became lay disciples (upāsakas and upāsikās). Having paid homage to the Buddha, they took their leave and returned to the palace.

At that time, there was a brahmin named Puṣya who had given birth to a beautiful daughter, rarely equaled in the world. When she reached the age of sixteen, no one could find fault with her. He hung out a reward of a thousand pieces of gold for ninety days, seeking out a wise person, saying:
"To whoever can point out a flaw in this girl's appearance and declare her not to be beautiful, I shall give the gold to them."
No one dared to respond.
As the girl grew up and reached the age for marriage, she thought to herself,
"To whom shall I be given?"
"If there should be one as handsome as my daughter, I shall give her to him.
Having heard that the śramaṇa Gautama is of the Śākya clan and possesses a golden complexion rarely seen in the world, I shall take this daughter and go to wed her to him."
He immediately brought her to the Buddha’s presence and prostrated before him, saying to the Buddha:

“My daughter is pure and beautiful, peerless in this world. She has reached marriageable age, yet there is no match for her in the world. Since Gautama is so handsome, he can serve as her counterpart; therefore, I have traveled a great distance to bring her here to be wedded to the World-Honored One.”
The Buddha told Puṣya:

"Your daughter's beauty is the kind of beauty prized by your own family; the beauty I prize is the kind prized by all Buddhas. What I prize follows a different path from yours, yet you yourself praise your daughter for her upright and exquisite beauty."
For example, what is so extraordinary about filling a painted vase with excrement and urine?
What is there to admire?

The eyes, ears, nose, and mouth are the great thieves of the body; though the face and head may be handsome, they are the body’s greatest affliction. That families are ruined, clans are extinguished, and that parents are killed and children harmed—all this stems from female beauty.
"I am a śramaṇa, standing alone with but one body; I am already fearful of peril, let alone accepting goods that bring calamity and are tainted by violence.
You may take them yourself; I will not accept them."
Thereupon, the brahmin departed in anger and went to King Udayana. Praising the woman’s exquisite beauty, he addressed the king, saying:
"This woman is worthy to be your queen; I now send her to you, O King, as she has reached maturity."

The King, seeing this, was filled with joy and immediately accepted her, appointing her as his second left consort; he then bestowed upon Jixing seals, silks, gold, silver, and precious jewels, appointing her as a minister of state.
This woman, having found her opportunity, constantly incited jealousy and practiced sorcery to delude the king, slandering the chief consort in this manner on numerous occasions.
The king rebuked them, saying:
"Your wiles and charms are perverse and insolent; that woman’s conduct is noble and worthy of respect, yet you slander her."

This woman harbored jealousy in her heart and still wished to harm him; she slandered him incessantly until the king was somewhat deluded by her. She and her confederates conspired together, waiting for his time of fasting, and then urged the king, saying:
"For today's pleasure, you should invite the Right Consort."

The king then issued a general summons, commanding everyone to assemble; however, the chief consort, who was observing the fast, alone did not respond to the call. Though summoned three times in succession, she remained steadfast in her observance of the fast and would not move. The king’s anger flared up, and he dispatched men to drag her out, binding her before the palace hall with the intent to shoot her to death.

The lady was not afraid; with single-minded devotion she took refuge in the Buddha. When the king himself shot at her, the arrows turned back toward the king. Each time he shot, they returned, and this was likewise true for many arrows.
At that moment, the king was struck with great terror. He untied his own garments and asked her, "What sorcery do you possess that it should come to this?"

The lady replied, "I have served only the Tathāgata and taken refuge in the Triple Gem; morning after morning I observe the Buddha’s fast, abstaining from food after midday, and I practice the eightfold discipline so that no ornaments remain upon my person. It must be that the World-Honored One has looked upon me with such compassion."
The King said: "Excellent! How could one say no?"
He immediately sent the maiden Śubhā back to her parents and had the Chief Queen govern the inner palace with proper discipline.

The King, together with the Chief Queen, the members of the harem, and the Crown Prince, prepared their carriages and accompanied by the ministers, went to where the Buddha was staying; they paid their respects, withdrew to sit down, and with palms joined, listened to the Dharma.
The King immediately addressed the Buddha, reporting the matter to him in full detail.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"A woman who practices sorcery possesses eighty-four manners; there are eight major manners among them, which are loathed by the wise."

What are these eight? First is jealousy; second is false anger; third is verbal abuse; fourth is cursing; fifth is malevolent suppression; sixth is stinginess and greed; seventh is fondness for ornamentation; eighth is harboring poison. These are the eight great dispositions.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

"The heavens rain down the seven treasures, yet desire remains insatiable; pleasure is slight while suffering is great—those who realize this are called wise. Though one possesses celestial desires, one who uses wisdom to renounce them without greed finds joy in departing from affection and love, becoming a disciple of the Buddha."
The Buddha told the Great King:

"When people perform deeds of merit or transgression, each has its own inherent nature; the retributive shadows they receive differ ten-thousandfold. If one practices the six virtues and observes the fast, the merit is great and praised by all Buddhas; in the end, one will be born in the Brahma Heaven, where blessings and joys are spontaneous."
When the Buddha spoke these words, the king, his consort, the court ladies, and the ministers all attained liberation of mind and realized the stage of the Path (srotāpanna).

Chapter 34: The Chapter on the Śramaṇa (*Śramaṇavarga*). From the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*. Chapter Thirty-Four: The Śramaṇa. Formerly, when the Buddha was staying in a monastery in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, he preached the Dharma for the devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, and the common people.
At that time, there was a young bhikṣu who, at dawn, dressed himself, took up his staff and bowl, and went into a large village to beg for alms.

Along the great road, there was an official vegetable garden; its exterior was planted with millet and sorghum, and beyond the field, arrows were set among the grass. If any insects, beasts, or thieves came near, they would trigger the nets and arrows; struck by the arrows, they would die.

There was a beautiful young woman who guarded this garden alone; anyone wishing to enter would have to call out from afar for her to show the way, only then gaining access to the garden—for those who did not know the path were certain to be killed by her arrows.

This woman alone maintained her mournful song, its tone so enchanting and clear that all who heard it could not help but halt their chariots and stop their horses; they turned about, paced restlessly, and desired to approach her, lingering and refusing to depart—all because of the resonance of her voice.

At that time, as this bhikṣu was returning from his almsround, he heard the sound of singing along the way. Leaning his ear to listen to the melody, his five senses were filled with delight; his mind became bewildered and his thoughts disordered as he greedily clung to it and could not let go. He imagined that the woman must be exceedingly beautiful, and his thoughts turned toward the desire to see her—her sitting, rising, and speaking. He then turned and hurried toward her, yet before he had reached her, his will became dazed and confused; his hand dropped the *khakkhara* staff, and the robes and bowl slipped from his shoulder, all without his own awareness.

The Buddha, perceiving this with his threefold knowledge (*trividyā*), saw that the bhikṣu would soon be killed by an arrow as he walked forward a short distance. Although his merit was such that he should have attained the Way, he was deluded by folly and shrouded by desire. Out of compassion for his ignorance and wishing to deliver him, the Buddha transformed himself into a layman and went to his side, rebuking him with a verse:

“O śramaṇa, why do you act so unrestrainedly? With every step you become stuck, merely following where your thoughts run. Though the saṃghāṭī robe covers your shoulders, it does nothing to diminish your evil. One who practices such evil conduct shall fall into the evil realms.”

One must cut off the stream, maintain self-restraint, and subdue the mind to repel desire; for if a person does not sever desire, their single-mindedness will still wander. One must practice this again and again with firm self-control; even if one has left the household life, if the mind is lax, it will surely become defiled once more.
For one whose practice is lax, the enticements of the mind are not eliminated; how can one who does not practice pure brahmacarya attain the Great Treasure?
One who is undisciplined is difficult to admonish, like a withered tree in the wind; since you have created this body for yourself, why do you not exert yourself with diligence?

Having spoken this verse, he immediately restored his original form; his marks and signs were radiant, illuminating heaven and earth. Those who beheld him had their delusions dissolved and their distractions stilled, each attaining their proper place.

When the bhikṣu saw the Buddha, his mind was suddenly opened like the appearance of light in the darkness; he immediately prostrated himself on the ground to pay homage to the Buddha, bowing his head to repent for his transgressions and offering a confession of remorse to the Buddha. Internally realizing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, he immediately attained arhatship and followed the Buddha back to the vihāra.
Those who heard it were innumerable, and all attained the Dharma-eye.

Chapter 35: The Brahmins, from the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*. Chapter Thirty-Five: The Brahmins. Long ago, in the kingdom of Sihakṣatra, there was a great mountain named Sihakṣatra. On this mountain lived more than five hundred brahmins, each of whom had mastered supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
They said to one another, "What we have attained is precisely Nirvāṇa."

When the Buddha first appeared in the world, he first beat the Dharma drum and opened the gate of the Deathless; yet these brahmins heard him but did not approach. Since their past merit merited deliverance, the Buddha went to them alone, without a companion.

Arriving at the crossroads, he sat beneath a tree; with his mind settled in samādhi, he emitted a radiance from his body that illuminated the entire mountain, appearing like a mountain of lost fire burning in its entirety.

The brahmin, filled with fear, cast spells over water to extinguish it, yet even by exhausting his supernatural powers he could not put it out. Marvelling at this, he fled by another path out of the mountain; from afar he saw the World-Honored One sitting in meditation beneath a tree, like the sun rising beside a mountain of gold, his marks and signs radiant like the moon among the stars.
Wondering what deity this was, he approached to observe it.
The Buddha ordered him to sit and asked where he had come from.
The brahmin replied:
“Having resided in this mountain for a long time practicing the Way, this morning a fire suddenly broke out, burning the trees and vegetation of the mountain; we fled in terror.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
“This is the fire of merit, which does not harm people; it seeks to extinguish the defilement of your own fetters of ignorance.”
The Brahmin master and his disciples looked at one another and said,
"Who is this practitioner? Among the ninety-six types [of heterodox schools], there has never been such a person."
The Master said:
"I have heard that there was a prince of the Śuddhodana clan named Siddhārtha, who took no pleasure in the position of a noble ruler and left the home life to seek Buddhahood. Could this be him?"
The disciples addressed their teacher, saying,
"We should go together to question the Buddha as to whether the practices performed by this brahmin are in accordance with the Dharma.
Then the teacher and his disciples rose together and addressed the Buddha:

“The *Brahmacārin Sūtra* is named ‘The Four Unhindered Knowledges. It contains the methods of astronomy and geography, the principles for kings to govern states and lead their people, as well as the practices to be followed by the ninety-six kinds of heterodox paths. Is this sūtra the Dharma of *nirvāṇa*?”
"I pray that the Buddha will explain and transform those who have not yet heard this.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Listen well and reflect upon it."

Since incalculable kalpas past, I have constantly practiced this sutra and attained the five supernatural powers, such as moving mountains and stopping flowing waters; yet, having undergone births and deaths beyond counting, I have neither attained nirvana nor heard of anyone who has attained the Way.
"Those who act as you do are not called brahmins.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"One who has severed the stream like crossing over, who is free from desire like Brahmā, and who knows that all conditioned activities have been exhausted—such a one is called a brahmin."
One who crosses the abyss by means of the purity of non-dual dharmas, whose fetters of desire are all untied—such a one is called a *brahmin*.
It is not by wearing matted hair that one is named a *brahmin*; rather, one who acts with sincerity and according to the Dharma, being pure and clean, is truly noble.
What is the use of adorning one's hair with grass garments if there is no wisdom?
If one is not free from attachment within, what benefit is there in renouncing external things?
One who has cast off lust, anger, delusion, pride, and all evils—like a snake shedding its skin—is called a *brahmin*.
One who has severed worldly affairs and whose speech is free from harshness, who examines the Eightfold Path with discernment—such a one is called a brahmin.
One who has already cut off affection and love, who has left home and is free from desire, and whose attachment has been completely exhausted—such a one is called a brahmin.
One who leaves behind the assembly of humans and does not fall into the assembly of devas, who returns to no assembly whatsoever—this is a brahmin.

One who knows his own past lives and the origins from which he has come, for whom birth and death have been exhausted, whose wisdom penetrates the profound Way, and who is as radiant as one capable of silent stillness—this is called a brahmin.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these verses, he addressed the brahmins:
"You practitioners who claim to have already attained nirvana—how can you possess lasting joy when you are like fish in shallow water?"
"It is to be united with that which is originally non-existent.
Upon hearing this sutra, the brahmin felt joy arise within his five senses; he knelt on both knees and addressed the Buddha:
"I pray to become your disciple."

His hair fell off of its own accord and he immediately became a śramaṇa; through his originally pure conduct, he attained the Way and became an arhat, while devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits all attained the fruits of the path.

Chapter 36: On Nirvana The Dharmapada-avadāna Sūtra, Chapter Thirty-six: On Nirvana In the past, when the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, he was accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, the King of Magadha was named Ajātaśatru. He ruled over five hundred kingdoms, each with its own name. There was a neighboring kingdom called Vaiśālī that did not obey the king’s commands; wishing to go and subdue it, he immediately summoned his ministers to deliberate, saying:
"The people of Vaiśālī are wealthy, prosperous, and flourishing, and they produce many rare treasures, yet they do not submit to me."
"Would it not be better to raise an army and go to attack him?
There was a worthy minister and chancellor in the state named Yu She, who replied,
"Indeed it would."
The King said to Varṣākāra, "The Buddha is not far from here;

as a holy sage possessed of the three types of supernormal knowledge, there is nothing he does not penetrate. Take my words and go to the Buddha's presence; using your own wisdom and insight, inquire of him in full detail: 'If I wish to go and attack him, will I be able to achieve victory?'"

Having received these instructions, the Prime Minister immediately prepared his carriages and horses and went to the vihāra. Upon arriving before the Buddha, he prostrated himself with his head to the ground to pay homage to the Buddha.
The Buddha bade him sit; the official then took his seat. The Buddha asked the Prime Minister:
"From where have you come?"
The Duke said: "The King has sent me here.
He bows his head to the Buddha's feet and inquires after your well-being and whether your daily meals are as usual."
The Buddha then asked the official:
"Are the King, the people of the land, and the ministers all in peace?
The official replied:
"The sovereign and his subjects alike have received the Buddha’s grace.
The Duke addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The King has a grievance with the kingdom of Vaiśālī and intends to go and attack it; in the Buddha’s holy view, will he be able to achieve victory?"
The Buddha told the Prime Minister:
“The people of the kingdom of Vaiśālī practice seven dharmas that cannot be overcome.
Your Majesty should reflect carefully; do not act rashly.”
The Duke then asked the Buddha,
"What are these seven dharmas?
The Buddha said:

"The people of the Vṛji country frequently gather in groups to discuss the True Dharma, cultivate merit, and maintain self-restraint; this they take as their constant practice—this is called the first.

The rulers and subjects of the Vṛji country are always in harmony; those appointed to office are loyal and virtuous, and they offer counsel and advice which is respectfully accepted and never opposed—this is called the second."

The people of Vaideha uphold the Dharma and lead one another by example, neither grasping nor rejecting; they do not dare to commit transgressions, and both superiors and subordinates follow established custom—this is called the third.

The people of Vaideha are refined by ritual and diligent in their reverence; there is distinction between men and women, and elders and juniors succeed one another without failing in propriety or law—this is called the fourth.

The people of Vaideha are filial and supportive toward their parents and respectful and deferential toward their teachers and elders; they receive admonitions and instructions as the standard for the state—this is called the fifth.

The people of Vaideha follow the pattern of Heaven and the laws of Earth; they revere the altars of soil and grain, accord with the four seasons, and do not neglect agriculture—this is called the sixth.

The people of the country of Vaiśālī revere the Way and honor virtue; if there are śramaṇas who have attained the Way and become arhats and come from afar, they provide them with robes, bedding, seats, and medicine—this is called the seventh [quality].
"If a ruler of a state practices these seven dharmas, he is difficult to endanger; even if the entire world’s armies were to go forth together to attack him, they could not achieve victory.
The Buddha told the Prime Minister:
"If the people of Vaiśālī were to uphold even a single one of these dharmas, they would still be unassailable; how much more so if they all uphold these seven dharmas?"
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Victory through gain is not to be relied upon; even victory remains suffering.
One should seek the Dharma of true victory for oneself; having attained such victory, nothing more arises."

Upon hearing the Buddha’s verse, the Prime Minister Yusha immediately attained the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), and all those present, both great and small, likewise attained the path of the Stream-enterer.
The Duke then rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying, “My state affairs are many and pressing; I wish to take my leave and return.”
The Buddha said, "It is well;
you should know that now is the time.

He immediately rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed. Returning, he reported the matter in full to the king, who then ceased his assault and, upholding the Buddha’s solemn teaching, used it to transform the kingdom.
The people of Vaṅga immediately came to submit to his command; superiors and subordinates honored one another, and the kingdom subsequently flourished.

Chapter 37: On Birth and Death (*Saṃsāra-varga*). Long ago, when the Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī, he extensively expounded the sublime Dharma for devas, humans, kings, and great ministers.

There was a brahmin householder living by the side of the road, possessing immeasurable wealth. He had an only son, twenty years of age, who had recently married; it had not yet been seven days since the wedding, and the husband and wife respected one another and spoke in harmony. The wife said to her husband:
"I wish to go to the rear garden to watch the festivities; would that be possible?"

In the third month of early spring, the husband and wife went together to the rear garden. There was a large and tall *nyagrodha* tree with beautiful blossoms; the wife desired some flowers, but there was no one to gather them for her. Knowing his wife’s desire for the *nyagrodha* flowers, the husband immediately climbed the tree to pick one. Desiring another, he moved further up the tree until he reached a slender branch; the branch snapped, and he fell to the ground, sustaining a mortal injury and dying instantly.

The family members, both old and young, rushed and ran toward the place where the child was, crying out to heaven in grief and wailing until they collapsed and revived again. Countless kinsmen from both within and outside the clan arrived, all of them deeply pained; none who heard of it failed to feel sorrow, and none who saw it failed to mourn with anguish. The parents and their children blamed heaven and earth, claiming that they did not provide protection. They prepared the coffin, shrouds, and offerings according to the rites and sent the body forth; returning home, they wept and sobbed, unable to restrain themselves.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for their folly, went to inquire after them. When the elder and his entire household, both great and small, saw the Buddha, they were moved with grief; they paid homage and recounted their hardships in detail.

The Buddha said to the elder: "Cease your weeping and listen to the Dharma. All things are impermanent and cannot be maintained for long; where there is birth, there is death, and transgressions and blessings follow one another. For this child, you have wept in three places; such overwhelming grief and despair are difficult indeed to overcome."
"In the end, whose child is he?
Who is his kinsman?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Life is like fruit ripening on a flower; one always fears it will fall away.
All that is born possesses suffering; who can attain immortality?
From the very beginning, one delights in sensual desires, entering the shadow of the womb through lust."
Receiving a physical form, life is like a flash of lightning; day and night it flows on, difficult to stop.
This body is but a thing destined for death, while the spirit is a formless dharma.
Even if one dies and is born again, neither sin nor merit shall perish.

"From beginning to end, it is not for a single lifetime; following craving and delusion for a long time, one creates suffering and pleasure for oneself. When the body dies, the spirit does not perish.
Upon hearing this verse, the elder understood its meaning and forgot his grief. He knelt down and addressed the Buddha:
"What transgression did this child commit in his past lives that his full and flourishing life was cut short?
We only pray that you will explain the offenses he previously committed.
The Buddha told the elder:
"In the distant past, there was a young boy who entered a sacred tree with a bow and arrow to play, while three other men were watching from nearby.
There was a sparrow in the tree, and as the boy wished to shoot it, the three men urged him, saying:
'If you can hit that sparrow, you shall be called a hero in this world.'"

The boy, his mind filled with delight, drew his bow and shot at it; the sparrow was struck and immediately fell dead to the ground. The three men laughed together, rejoiced in his success, and then each departed on their own way.

Throughout countless kalpas of birth and death, these three individuals have encountered one another in various places, together undergoing the retribution of their sins. Of these three, one possessed merit and now dwells in the heavens; one was born in the ocean as a nāga king through miraculous transformation; and the third is this present elder.

This child was, in a previous life, the son of a deva in the heavens; when his life there ended, he descended to become the son of an elder. Upon falling from a tree and dying, he was immediately reborn in the ocean as the son of a transformation-born nāga king; on the very day of his birth, a transformation-born garuḍa king seized him and ate him.
"Today, my distress and weeping at these three places—how can they even be described?
Because I assisted them in their joy in previous lives, these three people have repaid me with tears and wailing."
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The consciousness-spirit creates the three realms, The five destinations of the wholesome and unwholesome.
Moving through the aggregates in silence, Its destination is like an echo responding."
"Existence in the realm of form, the realm of desire, and the formless realm—all are caused by past actions.
Just as a seed follows its original form, the natural retribution is like a shadow.

Having spoken this verse, the Buddha, wishing to cause the elder to understand, employed his power of the Path to reveal his past lives, whereby [the elder] saw all the matters concerning the heavens and the dragon realms.
The elder, his mind enlightened and filled with joy, immediately rose, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that you and your followers, both great and small, may become disciples of the Buddha; I shall receive the five precepts and become an upāsaka."

The Buddha immediately conferred the precepts upon them and again expounded for them the meaning of impermanence. Both the great and the small were filled with joy, and all attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.

**Chapter 38: The Benefits of the Path (Mārga-hita-varga)** *Faju Piyu Jing* (Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra) In the past, there was a king who governed according to the True Dharma (*saddharma*), and the people admired his transformation. However, as he had no crown prince, he was filled with sorrow and anxiety.

When the Buddha entered the kingdom, she went out to pay her respects to the Honored One; having listened to the sutras with great joy, she immediately received the five precepts. With single-minded devotion and reverence, she prayed only for the birth of a son, practicing with diligence day and night, never flagging during the three periods of the day.

There was a servant boy, eleven years of age, who constantly served the King. He was loyal and faithful, observed the Dharma, and never failed in his dignified deportment. Humble, patient, and single-mindedly diligent, he studied and recited the sūtras and gāthās. Knowing the proper time, he would rise before others and prepare the incense and lamps. For several years he practiced with such diligence that he did not consider it wearisome; eventually, he fell gravely ill and passed away.
That spirit returned and became the king’s son; nursed and raised until he reached the age of fifteen, he was established as the crown prince.

When his father, the king, passed away, he succeeded him to the throne. Becoming arrogant and self-indulgent, he abandoned himself to licentiousness and sensual pleasure; day and night he remained steeped in dissipation and neglected the affairs of state. Consequently, the ministers abandoned their court duties and the people suffered from his tyranny.
The Buddha, knowing that the king’s conduct did not accord with fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), led his disciples to that kingdom.

When the king heard that the Buddha had arrived, he followed the customs of former kings and, together with a great assembly, went out to welcome him. Prostrating himself upon the ground, the king withdrew to take his seat on the royal throne. The Buddha addressed the king, saying:
"Are the people of the land, the various ministers, and the hundred officials all as usual?"
The king said, “As they were young, they were unable to bring peace and transformation; yet, through the Sage’s grace, the kingdom has remained free from harm.
The Buddha told the king:
"Your Majesty, you yourself now know from where you originally came; what merit did you perform to obtain this royal throne?
The king replied, "I do not know."
"Stubborn and ignorant, he does not understand that one does not know from where one has come in previous lives.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Originally, it is by means of five matters that one becomes a king."
What are these five?
First, by means of giving, one becomes a king, and the myriad people offer him palaces, halls, and pavilions, such that his wealth and resources are boundless.

Second, by establishing temples and making offerings to the Triple Gem with beds, couches, curtains, and canopies, one becomes a king who governs the nation from the imperial throne within the main hall.
Third, by personally revering the Three Jewels and all those of superior virtue, one becomes a king such that all the myriad people do not fail to pay him homage.
Fourth, by practicing patience regarding the three actions of the body, the four of speech, and the mind being free from evil, one becomes a king such that all who see him are filled with joy.
Fifth, one should constantly seek wisdom through study and take this as one's sovereign; thus, when deciding state affairs, all shall follow and implement them.
By practicing these five matters, one shall become a king in every lifetime.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"When a person knows how to honor their superiors— Their ruler, father, teacher, and spiritual guide;
And when they possess faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom— They will meet with ultimate good fortune and dwell in peace wherever they are born."
Having merit and auspiciousness from past lives, he was born as a sovereign among men;
he brought peace to the world through the Way, and none failed to follow him in honoring the Dharma.
As a king and lord of his subjects, he always treated those below him with compassion and love.
One leads oneself by means of the Dharma and precepts, and demonstrates to others the signs of fortune and misfortune.
Dwelling in peace, one does not forget danger; with clear deliberation, blessings grow ever more abundant.
As for the reciprocal retribution of merit and virtue, it makes no distinction between the noble and the lowly.
The Buddha told the king:

"In a previous life, you were a servant to a great king. You served the Buddha with faith, the Dharma with purity, the Sangha with reverence, your parents with filial piety, and your sovereign with loyalty. You constantly practiced single-minded diligence and generosity, toiling your body and exhausting your strength without ever becoming weary."
This merit follows one’s person, enabling one to become a prince and attain the glory of royalty.
Yet now, though wealthy and noble, you have instead become indolent.
As a king, one ought to practice five things.
What are the five matters?
First, governing the myriad people without injustice or excess.
Second, nourishing and raising the generals and soldiers by providing them with provisions according to the season.
Third, one should mindfully cultivate one's fundamental karma so that merit and virtue are never exhausted.
Fourth, one should trust the upright admonitions of loyal ministers and not accept slanderous speech that would harm those who are righteous.
Fifth, one must restrain desires and greed for pleasure so that the mind remains heedful.
By practicing these five matters, one's fame will spread across the four seas and fortune and prosperity will come of their own accord.

If these five matters are abandoned, the fundamental principles will not be upheld; when the people are distressed, they contemplate rebellion, and when the officials are exhausted, the state cannot be sustained.
Without merit, spirits and deities do not provide assistance;
when one acts according to one's own will, one loses the Great Principle, and loyal ministers dare not offer admonition;
when the mind is indolent, the state is not governed, and when ministers are negligent, the people become resentful.
"If it is thus, one will lose one's reputation and, in the end, possess no merit.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"One who acts as a general of the world, Practices rectitude without crookedness,"
One who tames the mind surpasses all evils; such a one is a Dharma King.
Seeing correctly, they are able to bestow kindness; being benevolent and loving, they delight in benefiting others.
Having benefited them with impartiality, the multitude thus becomes attached and close to them.

When the Buddha had finished speaking these verses, the king was filled with great joy. He rose and stood before the Buddha, prostrating himself on the ground to repent and apologize to the Buddha. He immediately received the five precepts, and as the Buddha further expounded the Dharma for him, he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

In the past, when the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove Monastery in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, he preached the unsurpassed Great Dharma for the sake of devas and humans, kings and ministers, and the fourfold assembly of disciples.
At that time, there was a deep mountain to the south of Śrāvastī where wild elephants were constantly born; these elephants were of three colors: white, blue, and black.

Whenever the king desired a fine, famous fighting elephant, he would dispatch men to capture one and bring it back to be entrusted to an elephant trainer; within three years, it could be ridden and also trained for combat.

At that time, there was a divine elephant born of a dragon; its body was white as snow and its tail red as vermilion, while its two tusks were like gold. When the hunter saw this exceptionally fine elephant, he returned and informed the king:
"There is a great elephant of such a form; it would be fitting for Your Majesty to ride it."
The king immediately recruited more than thirty elephant trainers and dispatched them to capture this elephant.

When the men arrived at the elephant's location, they spread nets intending to catch it; however, this divine elephant, knowing the intentions of the people, came forward and fell into the nets himself. As the crowd all rushed forward to seize him, the elephant became enraged and trampled them with his leaps; those nearby died instantly while those further away fled, yet the elephant pursued them without ceasing.

At that time, there were several young practitioners dwelling on the mountain slope who were strong, powerful, and courageous. Having studied the Way in the mountains for a long time, they had not yet attained meditative concentration. Seeing from afar this elephant pursuing and killing people, these practitioners, out of compassion for them, relied upon their own strength and courage and desired to go and rescue them.

The Buddha saw this from afar and feared that the bhikṣu might be killed by the divine elephant; he immediately went to its side and emitted a great radiance. Upon seeing the Buddha’s light, the elephant’s anger ceased and its resentment was dissolved, so that it no longer pursued or sought to kill the man.
When the bhikṣu saw the Buddha, he went forward to pay him homage.
The Buddha then spoke this verse for the bhikṣu:
"Do not recklessly harass the divine elephant, lest you invite suffering and affliction."
"Malice leads to suicide; / In the end, one does not reach the realm of goodness.

Upon hearing this verse, the bhikṣu immediately prostrated himself, repented, and apologized for his transgression. He inwardly reproached himself, deeply reflecting on his wrongdoing, and there before the Buddha attained arhatship.
At that time, the elephant-keepers all returned; those who had fainted and fled soon came back, and they all attained the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpatti*).
Long ago, when the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*) in Rājagṛha.

At that time, King Bimbisāra had a high minister who was dismissed for an offense and banished to the Southern Mountains, a thousand *li* from the capital. Previously, there was no one there who did not cultivate the five grains;

however, once the minister arrived, spring waters overflowed and the five grains ripened in great abundance. People from various kingdoms throughout the four quarters who were suffering from hunger and cold all came to this mountain. Within a few years, three or four thousand households had gathered there, and the minister provided them with fields and land so that they might sustain their livelihoods.
Among them, the elders, chiefs, and those of advanced age deliberated together:
"A state without a ruler is like a body without a head.
They went together to the residence of the chief minister and proposed him for the position of king.
The minister replied to the elder, saying:

"If you consider me to be the king, I shall follow the laws of other kings: my ministers on the left and right, civil and military officers, and those on duty above and below shall be summoned from the palace; and the collection of taxes in grain and silk shall be according to the laws for the common people."
The elders of the various states replied, "So be it;
we shall obey your command and follow the royal law.

They immediately established him as king and appointed the various ministers, both civil and military, high and low. They conscripted the people to build city walls, houses, palaces, and towers. The people were so afflicted by this bitter suffering that they could no longer endure it; they all conceived rebellious thoughts and plotted against the king.
A group of treacherous ministers took the king out on a hunt; after traveling thirty or forty *li* from the city, they led him into a vast wilderness marsh and intended to kill him.
The king asked his attendants, "For what reason do you wish to kill me?"

He replied: "When the people enjoy abundance and happiness, they serve the king with propriety; when the people are in distress, they contemplate disorder, ruining their own houses to plot for the state. The King told him:
"You have acted on your own account; this was not my original doing. May the gods and spirits bear witness that you have wrongfully slain me.
Grant me the fulfillment of one vow, and I shall die without regret."
He then made this vow:

"I originally reclaimed the wasteland to produce grain and nourish the people; all who came were sustained, and their wealth and joy were boundless. We ourselves raised him up and established him as king, following the precedents of various nations and acting together in this way. Now, they have instead turned against me and killed me."
"I truly have no ill will toward these people; however, if I am to die, I pray that I may become a rākṣasa and re-enter my former body, so that I may take revenge for this grievance."
Thereupon, they strangled him, abandoned his corpse, and departed.

Three days later, the King’s spirit manifested as a rākṣasa and returned to his former body; calling himself Ārāva, he immediately rose and entered the palace, where he strangled the new king, along with the ladies of the harem, attendants, and treacherous ministers, killing them all.
The rākṣasa, filled with rage, left the palace, intending to kill everyone.
The three elders of the kingdom bound themselves with grass ropes and came before the rākṣasa to confess:
"This was the deed of treacherous ministers; it was not something the common people could have known. We beg for your pardon and pray that you will return to govern the state."
He said, "I am a rākṣasa; how could I engage in common affairs with humans?
My food and drink must be human flesh, and as a rākṣasa, I have a quick temper and do not consider difficulties."
The elders said, "The kingdom belongs to the King; therefore, it must be as previously arranged. As for the food and drink required, we shall establish a sequence.

The state elders went out together and issued a proclamation to the people that they should all draw lots to determine their order. Each household was to send forth one small child, alive, to serve as food for the Rākṣasa King.

Among some three or four thousand households, there was exactly one family that were disciples of the Buddha; they lived with such diligence that they never violated the five precepts. When the people drew lots according to custom, this family obtained the first lot.
There was a young child who was to be the first meal for the King of Ghosts.

The wise man, both great and small, was filled with distress and wept as he faced Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa from afar, prostrating before the Buddha to repent and reproach himself. With his eye of the Way, the Buddha beheld his suffering and spoke these words:
"Because of this young child, I shall deliver countless people."
He then flew alone to the gate of the rākṣasa and manifested a transformative radiance that illuminated the interior of his palace.

Seeing the light, the rākṣasa suspected it was a supernatural being and immediately went out to see the Buddha. He then gave rise to a malicious intent, wishing to lunge forward and swallow the Buddha; however, the light pierced his eyes, and his mountain-lifting and fire-spewing were all transformed into dust. After a long time of exhaustion and fatigue, he finally submitted and was converted, inviting the Buddha to enter and sit, bowing his head to the ground in prostration.
The Buddha preached the sutra for him; with single-minded devotion, he listened to the Dharma and immediately received the five precepts to become an upāsaka.

The village official, hastening to collect the food, seized the boy and brought him away. The family members wailed and wept as they followed along the road; countless onlookers were moved to profound sorrow for them.
The official took the child, placed food in his hands, and brought him before the rākṣasa. The rākṣasa immediately took this small child and, holding the food, went before the Buddha.

Kneeling for a long time, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "The people of this country take turns providing children as food for me. Now that I have received the five precepts from the Buddha, I can no longer eat these children. I pray that you accept this child as an offering to the Buddha, so that he may serve as the Buddha’s attendant."
The Buddha accepted them and immediately recited a prayer of blessing; the rākṣasa was filled with joy and attained the stage of srotāpanna.
The Buddha placed the children in his almsbowl, carried them out through the palace gate, and returned them to their parents, telling them:
"Raise these children well and no longer grieve."
When the multitude saw the Buddha, there was none who was not struck with amazement, wondering, "What deity is this?
By what merit does this child alone receive such protection,
that he has been snatched back from his parents' hands by the Rākṣasa?"
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, standing in the midst of the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"The virtue of precepts is worthy of reliance; The retribution of merit constantly follows one.
Seeing the Dharma, one becomes a leader among men, And in the end remains far removed from the three evil realms."
"Vigilance in the precepts removes suffering and fear; Merit and virtue are honored throughout the three realms.
Ghosts, dragons, and malevolent poisons Cannot harm one who possesses the precepts.

When the Buddha had finished speaking these verses, countless people beheld the Buddha’s radiant image and realized that the Supreme One was peerless within the three realms. They all returned to him and became his disciples; hearing the verses with joy, they all attained the fruits of the Path.
