In the past, when the Buddha was at the Deer Park in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, he preached the Dharma for an immeasurable multitude of devas, humans, nāgas, and ghosts, as well as kings, ministers, and citizens.

At that time, the crown prince of a great king, accompanied by more than five hundred sons of minor kings, went to where the Buddha was, paid homage to the Buddha, and withdrew to sit to one side to listen to the Dharma.
The various princes then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The Way of the Buddha is pure, subtle, profound, and remote, difficult to attain. Since ancient times, have there been any sons of kings, princes, great ministers, or elders who abandoned their kingdoms, officials, subjects, and the joys of affection and honor to become śramaṇas?"
The Buddha told the princes:
"The prosperity, pleasures, and endearments of worldly realms are like illusions, transformations, dreams, and echoes; they come and go suddenly and cannot be maintained forever."
Furthermore, there are three reasons why a king’s crown prince cannot attain the Way.
What are these three?
First is arrogance and self-indulgence, whereby he does not contemplate the study of the subtle meanings of the Buddha’s scriptures to save his spiritual foundation.

Second is greed and grasping: failing to contemplate giving to those who are lowly, poor, or in distress; and regarding all the wealth and treasures of ministers and soldiers, not sharing them with the people to cultivate the foundation of prosperity.

Third, being unable to distance oneself from the objects of desire and attachment to form, nor abandoning the afflictions of the prison-like anxieties, yet acting as a śramaṇa to extinguish all sufferings and difficulties, thereby taking the cultivation of the body as one's foundation.
Therefore, when a Bodhisattva is born as a king, by setting aside these three matters, he shall personally attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, there are another three matters. What are these three?
First, during his youth, he pursued learning, governed the realm, and led the common people through transformation, causing them to practice the ten wholesome deeds.
Second, in his middle years, he bestowed wealth upon the poor, the destitute, the orphaned, and the widowed, so that his ministers, generals, and soldiers shared in the joy of the people.

Third, one should constantly reflect that life is impermanent and does not remain long; one ought to leave the household life to become a śramaṇa, severing the causes and conditions of suffering so as not to undergo birth and death again.
"Since these three things were not bestowed, I alone have obtained nothing.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke of himself, saying:

"In a former life, I was a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Emperor Nambang. Seven treasures escorted me; there were eighty-four thousand each of palaces, pavilions, bathing pools, traveling palaces, pleasure gardens, ministers, crown princes, ladies, court attendants, elephants, horses, and cooks."

He has a thousand sons, brave, fierce, and sharp; each single one can match a thousand men. They fly through the void and roam the four quarters, acting with such mastery that there is no one who can oppose them.
His lifespan was eighty-four thousand years; he governed according to the Dharma and did not oppress the people.
At that time, the Holy King suddenly thought to himself:
"Human life is brief and impermanent, difficult to preserve; I must cultivate merit in order to seek the truth of the Way."

Reflecting that one should constantly practice giving to the people of the world, sharing all one's wealth and possessions with them, and having already planted the seeds of merit, one should only then leave the household life to become a śramaṇa; by severing greed and desire, one can attain the cessation of suffering.
The King immediately commanded his hairdresser:
"If you see a single white hair among my locks, you must inform me at once.
After many tens of thousands of years had passed, the hairdresser addressed him, saying:
"White hair has already grown," he said,
ordering it to be plucked out and placed upon the table.
When the king saw the white hair, he wept and commanded, saying:
“The first messenger has suddenly arrived again; now my head has turned white, and I ought to leave the household life to become a śramaṇa and seek the path of spontaneity.
Holding his hair in his palm, he spoke this verse himself:
“Now upon the crown of my head, Whiteness has grown as if by theft.”
"A celestial messenger has already summoned me; now is the very time to leave the household life.

He immediately summoned his ministers and established the crown prince as king. He then became a śramaṇa, entered the mountains to cultivate the Way, and at the end of his human lifespan, was reborn in the second heaven as Śakra, Lord of Devas.
Later, when the Crown Prince governed the world just as the Great King had done, he again commanded his barber:
"If you see a white hair, you must inform me immediately."
After a long time, he reported again:
"White hair has already grown.
The Emperor ordered it to be plucked out; holding it in the palm of his hand, he spoke this verse:
"Now that my head and upper body have become white, as if plundered by age,
and since the divine messengers have already summoned me, this is precisely the time to leave the household life."

"Furthermore, he summoned his ministers and installed the crown prince as king; he then immediately went forth to become a śramaṇa, entered the mountains to cultivate the Way, and at the end of his human life, was reborn in the heavens as Śakra, Lord of Devas."

In a previous life, Śakra, Lord of Devas, having completed his celestial lifespan, descended to be born in the world as the crown prince of a holy king. These three holy lords became father and son: one was the Lord of Devas above, one was the holy king below, and one was the crown prince in between. Each of them underwent this cycle thirty-six times for many tens of millions of years; ending and beginning again, they performed these three deeds until they themselves attained Buddhahood.
At that time, the father was my current self;
the crown prince was Śāriputra;
and the grandson of the king was Ānanda.
"Successively following one another in birth, they have turned in succession to become kings to transform the world; for this reason, he is uniquely honored as peerless within the three realms.

When the Buddha spoke these words, the king’s crown prince and all the other princes were filled with great joy; they received the five precepts from the Buddha, became upāsakas, and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

Chapter 39: On Auspiciousness. *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Chapter Thirty-Nine: On Auspiciousness. Formerly, when the Buddha was on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, he turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles for devas, humans, nāgas, and ghosts.

At that time, on the banks of the Ganges River to the south of the mountain, there was a Nirgrantha Brahmin who was among the most eminent elders, profoundly learned, and possessed vast knowledge. His virtue approached the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and he clearly understood both past and present. He maintained five hundred disciples whom he instructed and taught; they were all thoroughly versed in astronomy, geography, the stars, and human nature, leaving nothing unexamined. Surveying both the internal and external worlds, they encompassed all knowledge regarding auspicious and inauspicious signs, calamities and blessings, abundance and scarcity, and the emergence and disappearance of phenomena.

The disciples of the brahmin, who had previously practiced under the Buddha and were destined to attain the Way, suddenly took one another by the hand and went to the edge of a riverbank. Sitting apart in private, they discussed their words and asked one another:
"Regarding the conduct of the people in all the kingdoms of the world, by what means do they consider themselves to possess worldly auspiciousness?"
The disciples, not yet understanding, went to their teacher’s place and paid him homage. With palms joined, they said to him:
“We disciples have studied for a long time and have mastered what was to be learned; however, we have not heard what constitutes auspiciousness in various countries.”
The Nirgrantha replied: "Excellent is your question! In the land of Jambudvīpa there are sixteen great kingdoms and eighty-four thousand small kingdoms;

each of these kingdoms has its own auspicious omens. These may be gold or silver, crystal or lapis lazuli, the divine cintāmaṇi pearl, elephants, horses, and chariots, jade maidens, coral, conch shells, music, phoenixes, and peacocks; or they may be the sun, moon, and stars, jeweled vases, the four flowers, brahmins, and ascetics. These are the auspicious and favorable responses cherished by the various kingdoms. If one should behold such things, one praises them immeasurably, for these are the auspicious responses that bring fortune to a kingdom."
The disciples asked,
"Is there perhaps some other extraordinary auspiciousness that would benefit the body and lead to rebirth in the heavens?
The Nirgrantha replied:
"Since the time of our former masters, none has surpassed this; it is not recorded in the books.

The disciples said, "We have recently heard that a member of the Śākya clan has left home to practice the Way, sitting upright for six years to subdue demons and attain Buddhahood, possessing the three types of perfect knowledge without obstruction. Let us go together to question him; let us see how broad and profound his learning is compared to that of our Great Master."

The master and his disciples, numbering more than five hundred, traveled along mountain paths until they reached the Buddha’s dwelling. They paid homage to the Buddha and took their seats in the position of brahmins; with palms joined and kneeling on their right knees, they addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Such are the auspicious objects favored in various kingdoms; we wonder if there are any superior to these?”
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"Regarding the worldly matters you have discussed, if one follows them, there is auspiciousness; if one goes against them, there is misfortune. Yet they cannot cause a person to rescue their spirit or transcend suffering."
"According to the auspicious Dharma as I have heard it, the practitioner attains merit and is forever separated from the three realms, personally reaching Nirvana.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Buddha is honored above all devas; The Tathāgata constantly manifests the ultimate meaning."
There was a brahmin ascetic who came and asked, "What is the most auspicious?
Thereupon the Buddha, out of compassion, explained for him the essential truth:
"To have faith and delight in the True Dharma—this is the supreme auspiciousness."
Nor from gods or humans, nor by seeking luck through hope;
nor by praying at shrines—this is the most auspicious.
Associate with the virtuous, choose a good dwelling, and always prioritize the cultivation of merit.
To govern oneself with integrity and rectitude is the greatest auspiciousness.
To abandon evil and follow what is good, to avoid alcohol and know self-restraint,
and not to be lustful toward women— this is the greatest auspiciousness.
To be learned as one who observes the precepts, to study the Dharma and Vinaya with diligence,
to cultivate oneself without contention— this is the greatest auspiciousness.
To dwell in filiality and serve one's parents, to manage the household and support one's wife and children.
To act without indigence— this is the most auspicious thing.
To be neither arrogant nor conceited, to be content and mindful of the past,
and to recite and study the sūtras at the proper times— this is the most auspicious thing.
Always wishing to endure what one hears, Delighting in seeing śramaṇas,
and listening whenever a discourse is given— this is the most auspicious.
Observing the fasts and practicing the pure life, Constantly wishing to see the wise and virtuous— this is the most auspicious.
To rely upon the wise is the greatest auspiciousness.
Having faith in virtue and morality, with a right intention free from doubt,
desiring liberation from the three evil realms— this is the greatest auspiciousness.
Practicing generosity with an impartial mind, honoring those who have attained the Way,
and likewise revering all devas and humans— this is the most auspicious.
Constantly desiring to be free from greed, lust, ignorance, and anger— this is the most auspicious.
To be able to cultivate the vision of the Path— this is the most auspicious thing.
If one abandons what is not one's duty and is able to diligently apply oneself to the practice of the Path,
always attending to what ought to be done— this is the most auspicious thing.
To act for the sake of all under heaven, to establish a mind of great compassion,
to cultivate oneself as a person and bring peace to sentient beings— this is the most auspicious thing.
When the wise dwell in the world, they constantly practice auspicious conduct.
"To personally attain the realization of wisdom and insight—this is the most auspicious.

When the brahmin master and his disciples heard these verses spoken by the Buddha, their minds were joyfully resolved; filled with great rapture, they stepped forward and said to the Buddha, "Most wonderful, World-Honored One!"
This is something rare in the world; from time immemorial we have been deluded and have not yet attained clear understanding.

We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and deliver us! We wish to personally take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and hope to become śramaṇas, following in the lower ranks.
The Buddha said, “Excellent! Welcome, bhikṣu!”
He immediately became a śramaṇa; contemplating internally the *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing), he attained arhatship.
Those who heard him were innumerable, and all obtained the Dharma-eye.
*Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*, Volume Four.
